Version: Current (v6.11.1)

7.x Upgrade Guide

Breaking changes​

Reading Form internals through a ref​

Form is now a function component. Its ref exposes FormRef<T> instead of a class instance, and FormState, the class component's state type, is no longer exported: IChangeEvent is the public shape of what reaches your callbacks.

First, change the ref's type. Use your form-data type in place of MyData:

-import Form from '@rjsf/core';
+import Form, { type FormRef } from '@rjsf/core';

-const formRef = useRef<Form<MyData>>(null);
+const formRef = useRef<FormRef<MyData>>(null);

The same change applies to createRef. Then replace any access to class internals:

If your code uses…Change it to…
formRef.current.state.formDataformRef.current.getFormData()
.state.errorSchema or .state.errorsRead event.errorSchema or event.errors in onChange/onSubmit.
.setState(...)Call .setFieldValue(path, value), or .setFieldValue('', data) to replace the whole value.
.state.schemaUtilsUse registry.schemaUtils in a custom field, or create one with createSchemaUtils({ validator }, schema).
.state.registryUse the registry prop in a custom field, widget or template. Outside Form, use buildRegistry(props, schemaUtils.getRootSchema(), schemaUtils).
.formElementUse .reset() if you need to reset the form. The handle does not expose the DOM element.

For example, save the data using the handle and keep error information from events:

-const data = formRef.current.state.formData;
+const data = formRef.current.getFormData();

-const errors = formRef.current.state.errors;
+const onChange = (event) => setErrors(event.errors);

submit(), setFieldValue(), validateForm(), validateFormWithFormData() and focusOnError() keep their existing signatures. reset() takes an optional seed, see reset() goes back to the seed. For the separate change to validate(), see the validate migration.

Form owns its data BREAKING CHANGE​

This is the change most forms will notice. Read the model first. Then use the table to find the cases that apply to your code.

The model​

React has two kinds of input. A controlled <input value={text}> shows exactly what its parent passes, and changes only when the parent passes something new. An uncontrolled <input defaultValue={text}> reads the prop once and then keeps its own value. The parent hears about edits through onChange and reads the current value when it needs it.

Form is the uncontrolled kind:

  • initialFormData is the seed, like defaultValue. The form reads it when it mounts and when reset() is called, and fills it in with the schema's defaults. On every other render the form ignores it.
  • After mount, the data belongs to the form. Each edit is applied, validated and shown before onChange reports it, whatever your handler does with the event.
  • getFormData() reads the current value at any time, from anywhere you hold the form's ref.
  • formData is a deprecated name for the seed. It still works, so that forms written for v6 keep compiling and, for the common patterns, keep working, and when you pass both props, formData is the seed. Its @deprecated tag flags it in your editor and linter: rename it to initialFormData. React's docs use the same convention: a prop that is read once should start with initial or default, so readers know its later values are ignored.

Only undefined means "not passed". null seeds the schema's defaults, as undefined does. false, 0 and '' are values.

What to change​

If your code…Then…
Stores every edit: formData={data} onChange={(e) => setData(e.formData)}Change nothing. The value you pass back is the form's own, so passing it changes nothing, even if you store it late (after an await, say).
Passes formData at allRename it to initialFormData, which reads the same. formData is deprecated.
Passes a formData that changes after mount: a record that loads, the next record, an outside editRemount the form under a key, or call setFieldValue().
Refuses an edit by not storing it, or stores a rewritten copy, such as a trimmed stringMove that decision into transformChange.
Computes a field from other fields and passes it back as formDataCompute it in transformChange, and into initialFormData.
Writes formData inline, such as formData={{}}, and doesn't store what onChange reportsChange nothing. A re-render no longer throws the user's edits away.
Expects onChange on mount: for the defaults, or for a type: 'null' field's nullRead getFormData().
Calls reset()Check which seed it goes back to.
Reads the DOM inside onChangeRead the event.
Edits a field and calls submit() in the same handlerMind the browser's validation.
Makes several edits that should be validated togetherMake them as one edit.
Renders the form inside <Activity>A hidden form is treated as unmounted.
Has a custom field that hands ArrayField or ObjectField a sorted or filtered copyPass formData through unchanged.
Relies on an error boundary to catch an onChange that throwsHandle the error in the callback.
Wraps a FormRef call in startTransition()Remove the wrapper. The call is synchronous either way.

Show other data after mount​

A formData that changes after mount no longer replaces the data. In development the form logs a warning the first time it ignores one. There are two ways to show other data. Which one to use depends on whether it is a different record or the same one.

A different record: remount the form under a key. This is how React recommends resetting all state when a prop changes. The new form starts clean: its errors and the fields' own state are cleared, and the record gets the values the form fills in on mount only, such as a ui:initialValue or the defaults of additional properties.

-<Form schema={schema} validator={validator} formData={record} onChange={save} />
+<Form key={record.id} schema={schema} validator={validator} initialFormData={record} onChange={save} />

For a record that loads after mount, render the form once the record is there:

if (!record) {
  return <Spinner />;
}
return <Form key={record.id} schema={schema} validator={validator} initialFormData={record} onChange={save} />;

The same record, changed from outside: call setFieldValue() on the form's ref. setFieldValue('', data) replaces the whole value, and setFieldValue(path, value) replaces one field. The errors and the fields' state stay, and the change goes through transformChange and is reported through onChange, like any edit. Make the call where the new value arrives, such as the handler of a button or the callback of a request. A useEffect that watches a prop and copies it into the form adds a render and a step for no gain (You Might Not Need an Effect).

Refuse or rewrite an edit in transformChange​

By the time onChange runs, the form has already applied the edit, so not storing the event no longer refuses it. onChange reports an edit; it does not decide one. That decision goes in transformChange. This is a pure function that receives the data the edit produced (next) and the data before it (previous), and returns the data the form should keep. The form calls it for every edit, from a field or from setFieldValue(), and for those alone, before it stores, validates and reports the result. What the form derives on its own (its defaults, the live omit a blur runs and a reset()) is stored without it, and only the last two are reported through onChange. The defaults are filled in on mount and again when the schema, a ui:emptyValue, defaultFormStateBehavior or additionalPropertiesWhenAbsent changes. An onChange that refused or rewrote an edit becomes:

-const onChange = ({ formData }) => {
-  if ((formData.title ?? '').length > 80) return;
-  setData({ ...formData, code: formData.code?.toUpperCase() });
-};
+const transformChange = (next, previous) => {
+  if ((next?.title ?? '').length > 80) return previous;
+  return next?.code === undefined ? next : { ...next, code: next.code.toUpperCase() };
+};
+const onChange = ({ formData }) => setData(formData);

Return next to take the edit, previous to refuse it, or another value. It runs for every keystroke, so a rewrite has to hold for a value the user is still typing, and for a field they cleared, which is undefined: upper-casing does, while trimming would remove a space as soon as it is typed. Return next's unchanged subtrees as they are, so their fields don't render again. Keep the function pure: the form may call it more than once for the same edit, the way React may call a component more than once. If you have used Downshift's stateReducer or React Final Form's parse, this is the same idea applied to the whole form. A decision that has to wait, such as a server check, can still undo an edit afterwards with setFieldValue(). When an edit switches a oneOf/anyOf option, the selector stays on the option the user picked unless you refuse the switch or rewrite that field's data; a rewrite elsewhere in the form, such as stamping another property, keeps the choice, while one at the field keeps it only while the rewritten data still fits the picked option, and otherwise moves the selector to the option that data fits.

Defaults are filled in without onChange​

The form fills its seed in with the schema's defaults on mount, and again when the schema, a ui:emptyValue, defaultFormStateBehavior or additionalPropertiesWhenAbsent changes. That filling-in is something the form works out from its props, not an edit, so it no longer calls onChange. v6 called onChange for those defaults from its constructor, and the field of a type: 'null' schema called onChange(null) from an Effect as it mounted. Both were ways of telling the parent about state from outside the event that caused it, which React advises against. A missing type: 'null' value is now filled in as null like any other default, and whatever emptyObjectFields says, as the field used to, so the submitted data is unchanged wherever that field rendered. Where it didn't, the null is filled in too, as a default or a { "const": null } already was: a type: 'null' property left out of a LayoutGridField layout, or under a ui:field that doesn't render it, is now submitted as null where it was absent. The one other difference is an object holding such a field that you set to undefined, with setFieldValue() or transformChange: the field put its null back, re-creating the object with its defaults, where the form now leaves it undefined, as it leaves an object holding no such field.

If you keep a copy of the data from onChange, that copy has no defaults until the first edit. Read getFormData() when you need the value with its defaults, or take it from the onSubmit event.

If you call getDefaultFormState() yourself, it now fills in a missing type: 'null' value as null too (except inside an anyOf/oneOf option that is rendered), and its return type includes null.

setFieldValue() fills in the defaults of the value it writes​

Under mergeDefaultsIntoFormData: 'useDefaultIfFormDataUndefined', setFieldValue(path, undefined) at a field with a default left the field empty, while setFieldValue('', data) filled the same field's default back in. Both now fill it in, as the form does for any data it holds. The fields the user cleared elsewhere in the form stay empty, and only those: an undefined that setFieldValue() or the seed put there also takes a default that arrives later, such as one a new schema prop gives an object holding the field. A form that has to leave a field empty from code can keep mergeDefaultsIntoFormData at its default, 'useFormDataIfPresent', under which a field set to undefined stays undefined.

A cleared field gives way or stays as its field does​

Two cases of a field the user cleared behave differently now, and neither can be turned off:

  • When a field's type, const, enum (or the constants of its anyOf/oneOf), maxItems or default changes, through an if/then, an option switch or a new schema prop, a clear of it gives way to the new field's default, under every mergeDefaultsIntoFormData, where the field stayed empty. A disabled or readonly form keeps and gives way to its clears the same way, and so does any other key holding undefined, as in an enabled form. It leaves every value as it is, a null item the user didn't clear included.
  • Under mergeDefaultsIntoFormData: 'useDefaultIfFormDataUndefined', an anyOf/oneOf field of constants with a default stays cleared, as any other field does, where its default came back.

If your form relied on the old result, restore it from transformChange, which gets the data an edit settled on: write undefined back for a field that has to stay empty, or the default for one that has to take it again. A new schema prop runs no transformChange, so a field that has to stay empty through one needs its data set after the change.

A transformChange that drops a cleared key loses the clear under mergeDefaultsIntoFormData: 'useDefaultIfFormDataUndefined': a clear holds only while the key is there holding undefined, where a missing key used to count as cleared too. Pass the undefined through to keep it:

-const transformChange = ({ code, ...rest }) => (code ? { ...rest, code: code.toUpperCase() } : rest);
+const transformChange = (next) => (next.code === undefined ? next : { ...next, code: next.code.toUpperCase() });

The same goes for a copy made with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(next)), which drops every undefined; copy with structuredClone().

reset() goes back to the seed​

reset() with no argument works as in v6, until you first pass it a seed. It reads the seed from the current props (formData if you pass it, otherwise initialFormData) and fills it in with the defaults. It clears the submit count and every error except extraErrors, and reports the result through onChange.

reset(saved) makes saved the seed instead, for this and every later reset(), which then goes back to saved rather than the props' seed, even after the props pass another one; remount the form under a key to read the props' seed again (see Making the saved data the baseline). So reset passed as an event handler now receives the event as its seed: see FormRef.reset() passed as an event handler seeds the form with the event.

Mind which seed you pass. If you pass formData={data} and store every edit in data, the seed is the latest edit, so reset() clears the errors and leaves the data as it is. To reset to the original record, pass the record as initialFormData and keep your copy of the edits in a separate state. Or remount the form under a key.

Read the event, not the DOM​

onChange now runs before the inputs show the new value. Take the value from the event:

 const onChange = (event) => {
-  const title = document.querySelector('#root_title').value;
-  saveDraft({ title });
+  saveDraft(event.formData);
 };

Outside onChange, call getFormData(). It returns the form's current value, including edits made earlier in the same tick. Code that needs the updated DOM itself belongs in an Effect.

Submit in the same handler as an edit​

submit() submits the form's current value, including an edit made in the same handler, and calls onSubmit or onError before it returns:

formRef.current?.setFieldValue('status', 'final');
formRef.current?.submit(); // submits { status: 'final' }

There is one limit. The browser's own constraint validation (required, pattern and the rest on the inputs) checks the DOM, and React has yet to show such an edit in the inputs. So a submit in the same handler as an edit is checked by schema validation alone. A submit made while the inputs show the current value, such as a submit button's, is checked by both. To check a value without storing or submitting it, call validateFormWithFormData(nextData).

Make several edits as one​

Live validation and liveOmit now run for every edit, where the v6 class validated a run of queued edits once. Several edits in one event still build on each other: each one reads the form's current value, so a second setFieldValue() keeps the first one's change. When the edits are one operation, replace the whole value in one call, so they are validated together:

-formRef.current.setFieldValue('city', 'Paris');
-formRef.current.setFieldValue('country', 'France');
+const data = formRef.current.getFormData();
+formRef.current.setFieldValue('', { ...data, city: 'Paris', country: 'France' });

A form inside a hidden <Activity>​

React asks components to treat content hidden by <Activity> as unmounted: it cleans up the hidden content's Effects and expects nothing in there to keep acting. Form does what React asks. While hidden, it keeps its data, but drops anything that reaches it: a draft a widget flushes from an Effect cleanup, a timer or a file read that finishes late, and a setFieldValue(), reset() or submit() through its ref. A validateForm() returns its result without calling onError. In development, the form warns once about the first setFieldValue(), reset() or submit() it drops this way, through a handle you kept: React clears the ref while the form is hidden, so ref.current is null then, and ref.current?.setFieldValue() skips the call without reaching the form. Everything works again once the form is shown. A form shown again by an <Activity> gets its ref back after its fields' layout Effects have run, so an onChange a widget reports from one finds ref.current still null. React also cleans up the Effects of content a <Suspense> fallback replaces, after it has been shown, so a form inside one drops the same things while the fallback shows. A form that has unmounted drops the same things, as in v6. Otherwise, a late change would be reported through a stale onChange and stored as the data of a form the user can't see.

Custom fields that wrap ArrayField or ObjectField​

ArrayField and ObjectField add, remove, rename and reorder by reading the form's current value at their fieldPath, so that several edits in one event build on each other. A custom field that wraps one of them has to pass formData through unchanged. If it passes a transformed copy, such as a sorted list, those operations act on positions the form doesn't hold, and in development the field warns once that it was rendered with other formData than the form holds at its fieldPath. The same goes for a field that hands it part of its own data under its own fieldPath, as <ArrayField {...props} formData={props.formData.items} /> does: the operations read the whole value at that path, so an add can replace it with an array of one new item and a remove does nothing. Render the part at its own fieldPath, or render the container for that part through SchemaField.

Handle callback errors in the callback​

An error thrown by your onChange, onBlur or onFocus no longer unmounts the form or reaches an error boundary. One thrown during a FormRef call comes out of that call. One caused by the user editing a field is reported as an uncaught error. If you need to act on the error, catch it inside the callback.

Changes and submits are validated as before 6.11.1​

6.11.1 changed how Form applies a change (#5631), and v7 doesn't keep all of it. If you upgrade from 6.11.1, check these:

  • A throw from customValidate or transformErrors during setFieldValue() comes out of setFieldValue(), as it did before 6.11.1, not from a timeout. A try/catch around the call catches it.
  • A throw from focusOnFirstError on submit comes out of the submit handler before onError is called, so onError isn't called for that submit. Catch the error inside focusOnFirstError if you need onError.
  • A change made in the same event as the parent setting schema, liveValidate or extraErrors is applied and validated with the props from before that event, as before 6.11.1. To apply it with the new props, make the change after they have rendered, such as from an effect.
  • noValidate doesn't hide a custom error a widget raised; it shows at once. To keep it hidden while validation is off, don't raise it then: pass your noValidate flag to the widget, for example through formContext, and call onChange without an errorSchema while it's set.

Also note​

  • With omitExtraData, a submit both passes the data with its extra fields removed to onSubmit and keeps it as the form's data.
  • Without live validation, an edit clears the validator's errors of the fields it changed. v6 did this only for a form passed formData; it now holds for every form. The errors that an item reorder, a property rename or an option switch moved stay with the values they moved with.
  • In development, the formData passed to onChange is deep-frozen, so mutating it throws instead of silently corrupting your state. Only plain objects and arrays are frozen. The object you seed the form with, initialFormData or formData, is frozen too from the form's first edit, validation, submit or reset on, since the form's data shares it: all of it, except the objects and arrays the form filled a default into, which it copied. v6 code that goes on mutating that object, such as this.state.data.address.city = 'x', throws in development; change a copy instead.

Why​

v6 looked controlled, but it wasn't. The form kept its own copy of the data, showed every edit whether or not you stored it, and re-read formData whenever any prop changed. Several long-standing bugs came from reconciling those two copies. An edit you didn't store stayed on screen until an unrelated prop changed, then snapped back. A oneOf switch could revert. Every prop change re-ran default generation.

There were two ways to get to one copy. One was to make the form truly controlled. That was tried during v7's development and dropped. A form holds state its data can't express, such as the selected oneOf option, which array row is which, a property name halfway through a rename, and each field's errors. Keeping all of that consistent while the parent decides about each edit took a lot of machinery, and a list of rules for you to follow. The other way was to let the form own its data, the way an uncontrolled input does. That is what React Hook Form (defaultValues), Formik (initialValues), React Final Form (initialValues) and TanStack Form (defaultValues) do too. A key starts it over, as React recommends.

ESM-only packages​

Every @rjsf/* package now ships only ESM: per-file modules and declarations in lib/. The CommonJS (dist/index.cjs), bundled ESM (dist/<name>.esm.js) and UMD (dist/<name>.umd.js) builds are gone, along with the ./dist and ./dist/*.cjs export paths.

  • import from any bundler or from Node works as before; require() also keeps working on every supported Node version, which can load ESM packages natively.
  • Deep imports through @rjsf/<package>/lib/<file>.js no longer resolve: see deep imports are removed.
  • If you loaded a UMD bundle from a CDN with a <script> tag, switch to an ESM CDN (for example import Form from 'https://esm.sh/@rjsf/core') or a bundler.

Deep imports are removed BREAKING CHANGE​

Each package's exports lists only its public entry points, so an import of @rjsf/<package>/lib/<file>.js or @rjsf/<package>/lib throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED in Node, and fails to resolve in every bundler and TypeScript resolution that reads exports (node16, nodenext and bundler). A tool that ignores exports, such as webpack 4 or TypeScript's node10 resolution, still finds the file, but nothing there is part of the public API any more. What still resolves:

  • each package's root, such as @rjsf/core or @rjsf/utils;
  • @rjsf/core/markdown, @rjsf/core/testing, @rjsf/core/rjsf.css and @rjsf/core/rjsf-theme.css;
  • @rjsf/validator-ajv8/compileSchemaValidators and @rjsf/validator-ata/compileSchemaValidators, in place of their lib/compileSchemaValidators paths.

Most deep imports name something the package root exports too, so import it from there:

-import SchemaField from '@rjsf/core/lib/components/fields/SchemaField.js';
-import { getUiOptions } from '@rjsf/utils/lib/getUiOptions.js';
+import { SchemaField } from '@rjsf/core';
+import { getUiOptions } from '@rjsf/utils';

GridType, Operators, LAYOUT_GRID_OPTION, LAYOUT_GRID_UI_OPTION and the GridProps, GridSchemaType, LayoutGridSchemaType and LayoutGridFieldProps types, which only lib/components/fields/LayoutGridField.js exported, are exported from @rjsf/core now, and so is getMatchingPatternProperties(), which only lib/schema/retrieveSchema.js exported, from @rjsf/utils. Label, from lib/components/templates/FieldTemplate/Label.js, is exported from @rjsf/core as FieldLabel. These have no import path any more:

  • A theme's individual components, such as @rjsf/mui/lib/SelectWidget/SelectWidget.js: read them from the theme's Widgets or Templates export, or from registry.widgets and registry.templates in a custom component.
  • @rjsf/core's LayoutGridField and LayoutMultiSchemaField helpers, such as getSchemaDetailsForField() and computeEnumOptions().
  • @rjsf/core's LOOKUP_REGEX, which LayoutGridField.js exported beside LAYOUT_GRID_OPTION.
  • @rjsf/utils' getDefaultFormState() internals, such as computeDefaults(), getObjectDefaults(), getArrayDefaults(), getDefaultBasedOnSchemaType() and AdditionalItemsHandling: call getDefaultFormState() or schemaUtils.getDefaultFormState().
  • @rjsf/utils' calculateIndexScore(): call getClosestMatchingOption().
  • @rjsf/snapshot-tests/package.json, the one package metadata file a package exported: a tool that needs it can read it from node_modules.
  • Every other module that a package's root doesn't export.

@rjsf/shadcn no longer ships prebuilt stylesheets BREAKING CHANGE​

The compiled dist/<theme>.css files (default, amethyst-haze, caffeine, claude, clean-slate, neo-brutalism, pastel-dreams, soft-pop, twitter, vercel) are gone, and so is the src/css directory they were built from. Each was a full Tailwind build — preflight reset included — for one fixed set of design tokens, which is the wrong shape for a library: importing one restyled the whole page and could not follow your own shadcn theme.

@rjsf/shadcn is now styled the way shadcn components are, by the application's Tailwind build. Add the package to your Tailwind sources:

@import 'tailwindcss';
@source "../node_modules/@rjsf/shadcn/lib";

The form then picks up the CSS variables from your shadcn init setup. If you were importing a prebuilt theme for its colors, generate the equivalent variables with tweakcn into your global CSS; the playground's theme sources hold the token sets the old stylesheets were built from.

getDefaultRegistry() removed BREAKING CHANGE​

getDefaultRegistry() bundled the core fields, widgets and templates together with placeholder rootSchema, formContext, translateString and globalFormOptions values that the Form overwrote anyway. Use generateTheme() for all three dictionaries, or the individual generator for the one you need:

-import { getDefaultRegistry } from '@rjsf/core';
+import { generateTheme } from '@rjsf/core';

-const { fields, widgets, templates } = getDefaultRegistry();
+const { fields, widgets, templates } = generateTheme();
-import { getDefaultRegistry } from '@rjsf/core';
+import { generateFields } from '@rjsf/core';

-const { StringField } = getDefaultRegistry().fields;
+const { StringField } = generateFields();

To reuse a single component, import it directly instead — import { StringField } from '@rjsf/core' — so the rest of the core components stay out of your bundle.

Form.getRegistry() is now the buildRegistry() export BREAKING CHANGE​

getRegistry() was a static on the Form class. It is now a standalone buildRegistry() export from @rjsf/core, taking the same arguments:

-import Form from '@rjsf/core';
+import { buildRegistry } from '@rjsf/core';

-const registry = Form.getRegistry(props, schema, schemaUtils);
+const registry = buildRegistry(props, schema, schemaUtils);

Most code never needs it. Inside a field, widget or template, use the registry prop you already receive — it is the registry the Form actually rendered with, including its real schemaUtils. To build one for a test, use getTestRegistry() from @rjsf/core/testing. For the core component dictionaries on their own, use generateTheme().

_internalFormWrapper removed BREAKING CHANGE​

The private _internalFormWrapper prop, and its entry in the ThemeProps a theme passes to withTheme(), have been removed. It existed so @rjsf/semantic-ui could wrap the <form> element in that library's own Form component, and it was the only theme that ever used it. Use the public tagName prop to render a different element in place of <form>.

getTestRegistry() moved to @rjsf/core/testing BREAKING CHANGE​

Update the import and add @rjsf/validator-ajv8 to your dev dependencies:

-import { getTestRegistry } from '@rjsf/core';
+import { getTestRegistry } from '@rjsf/core/testing';
npm install --save-dev @rjsf/validator-ajv8

@rjsf/validator-ajv8 is now an optional peer dependency of @rjsf/core that only this entry point needs, so it no longer ships as a transitive dependency of the main entry. The arguments are unchanged: getTestRegistry(schema, {}, templates) still works. It takes an optional classMap after presentation, layered over @rjsf/core's as a Form's is, so a theme can test a core template under its own class map.

Registry members are read-only BREAKING CHANGE​

Every member of the Registry type in @rjsf/utils is now readonly. The registry is the plumbing Form builds from its props and hands down to fields, widgets and templates; nothing is supposed to write back into it, and now nothing can.

This is only a breaking change if you assigned into a registry you received, e.g. registry.globalUiOptions = {...} or registry.formContext = {...}. Build a modified copy instead and pass that down:

-registry.globalUiOptions = { enableMarkdownInHelp: true };
+const registry = { ...baseRegistry, globalUiOptions: { enableMarkdownInHelp: true } };

Only the registry's own members are read-only. The component maps it holds are not deeply read-only, so registry.widgets.MyWidget = ... still compiles; override widgets, fields and templates through the Form props or withTheme() rather than by writing into the maps.

The registry that getTestRegistry() returns is additionally frozen at runtime, along with its fields, templates and widgets maps and the nested ButtonTemplates, so a test that mutates it throws instead of silently affecting later assertions. The freeze is shallow by design: a deep freeze would reach objects the caller owns, such as formContext, rootSchema and the validator's internal caches.

SchemaExamples is a memo component BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/core exports SchemaExamples wrapped in memo(), so that a keystroke in an input does not render its <datalist> of suggestions again. Render it as an element. A template that calls it as a function still type-checks, and throws SchemaExamples is not a function on its first render:

// Before
{SchemaExamples({ id, schema })}

// After
<SchemaExamples id={id} schema={schema} />

Registry has a required presentation BREAKING CHANGE​

The Registry type in @rjsf/utils has a new required member, presentation: the MergedThemePresentation that declares which parts of a field each registered field and widget draws itself, merged from @rjsf/core's declarations, the theme's and the Form's new presentation prop.

This is only a breaking change if you build a Registry object by hand, e.g. in a test. Build it with buildRegistry() or getTestRegistry() from @rjsf/core/testing, which fill it in, or add it yourself:

+import { mergeThemePresentation } from '@rjsf/utils';

 const registry: Registry = {
   fields,
   templates,
   widgets,
+  presentation: mergeThemePresentation(),
   // ...
 };

getTestRegistry() takes the presentation as a new last argument, and freezes it along with the component maps.

Registry has a required classMap BREAKING CHANGE​

The Registry type in @rjsf/utils has a new required member, classMap: the MergedClassMap of class names the elements @rjsf/core renders carry, one key per element, merged from @rjsf/core's defaults, the theme's classMap and the Form's new classMap prop. @rjsf/core's components read their classes from it, beside the rjsf- markers they always render.

This is only a breaking change if you build a Registry object by hand, e.g. in a test. Build it with buildRegistry() or getTestRegistry() from @rjsf/core/testing, which fill it in, or add it yourself with every key of ClassMap, leaving a key without a class undefined rather than '', which renders an empty class attribute, or an empty object cast to MergedClassMap where nothing reads it:

+import type { MergedClassMap } from '@rjsf/utils';

 const registry: Registry = {
   fields,
   templates,
   widgets,
   presentation: mergeThemePresentation(),
+  classMap: {} as MergedClassMap,
   // ...
 };

@rjsf/core's Label, which only lib/components/templates/FieldTemplate/Label.js exported, is exported from @rjsf/core as FieldLabel now that deep imports are removed. It takes a className and no longer renders control-label itself; pass joinClassNames('rjsf-field-label', registry.classMap.fieldLabel), as core's templates do, to give it the label marker and the theme's label class.

@rjsf/core renders unstyled markup; Bootstrap 3 moved to @rjsf/bootstrap3 BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/core's widgets and templates render toolkit-independent HTML5 markup. No Bootstrap 3 class is rendered: its default classMap is empty, the inline pixel offsets tuned to Bootstrap 3 are gone, a hidden field uses the hidden attribute, and the buttons are <button class="rjsf-button rjsf-button-{kind}"> with an inline SVG icon in place of a glyphicon; IconButton draws only the plus, copy, arrow-up, arrow-down and remove icons, and renders no icon for any other name, so pass another icon as an element. The array item, the additional-property row, the add button and the GridTemplate lay themselves out through the optional layout stylesheet, @rjsf/core/rjsf.css, in place of Bootstrap's grid classes, and @rjsf/core/rjsf-theme.css adds an optional default look on top of it; every rule in both is a zero-specificity :where(.rjsf …) in @layer rjsf, with --rjsf-* custom properties, so your own CSS overrides it, and without them a form renders with the browser's own controls. An array item's buttons, and an additional property's key input and remove button, sit level with the field's control: rjsf.css lays the field's label, description and control out on the row's grid rows, which it finds by core's rjsf-field-label class and by the description's rjsf-field-description class or id, so a custom FieldTemplate keeps that layout by keeping those on its parts; see Lining up a custom FieldTemplate. A field's state is an attribute rather than a class: data-invalid on the field's wrapper, label, description and help while it shows its own errors, and data-disabled on a disabled or read-only checkbox or radio option, so CSS reading Bootstrap's has-error selects [data-invalid] instead; the wrapper keeps its rjsf-field-error class too, which every theme's wrapper carries. The GridTemplate takes a column's width as a span prop ('ui:col': { span: 4 }) in place of a col-xs-4 class, and adds rjsf-grid-row and rjsf-grid-column itself. Every marker class core renders carries the rjsf- prefix, so CSS or tests reading the unprefixed ones follow: rjsf-field-description, rjsf-error-detail, rjsf-errors, rjsf-required, rjsf-unsupported-field, rjsf-field-radio-group, rjsf-checkboxes, rjsf-file-info, rjsf-range-view, rjsf-btn-now, rjsf-btn-clear and the like, with new markers such as rjsf-field-label, rjsf-field-help, rjsf-checkbox and rjsf-radio on the elements that carried only a Bootstrap class. The <form> keeps its rjsf class beside the className prop rather than in place of it, so a form given a className to keep .rjsf rules off it now takes them, rjsf.css and rjsf-theme.css included. TitleField renders a <div class="rjsf-title"> rather than a <legend> where it heads no <fieldset>: a layout grid's header, so a legend selector aimed at that title aims at .rjsf-title. DateElement in @rjsf/utils no longer defaults its className to Bootstrap 3's form-control, so a theme whose SelectWidget renders the className it is handed, and which renders DateElement without one, as core's AltDateWidget does, no longer puts form-control on its date selects; @rjsf/shadcn's alt-date selects lose a class the theme doesn't style, while @rjsf/fluentui-rc's SelectWidget adds it itself, so its date selects carry it once rather than twice. A theme that wants it passes className='form-control'.

An app that keeps Bootstrap 3 moves to the deprecated @rjsf/bootstrap3 package, which renders the markup @rjsf/core rendered through v6, with the prefixed markers, and is removed in v8:

-import Form from '@rjsf/core';
+import Form from '@rjsf/bootstrap3';

or withTheme(Theme) with its Theme export. A layout grid written for the Bootstrap 3 grid keeps its className: 'row' and className: 'col-xs-4' properties there; under @rjsf/core it uses span:

 'ui:row': {
-  className: 'row',
   children: [
-    { 'ui:col': { className: 'col-xs-4', children: ['first'] } },
+    { 'ui:col': { span: 4, children: ['first'] } },
   ],
 },

The other themes fall back to core for a few components, UnsupportedField in every one, FileWidget and ColorWidget in most, and AltDateWidget in @rjsf/daisyui, @rjsf/fluentui-rc, @rjsf/mui, @rjsf/react-bootstrap and @rjsf/shadcn, which render the prefixed markers too; @rjsf/react-bootstrap gives the AltDateWidget Bootstrap 5 classes through its classMap, @rjsf/daisyui daisyUI ones through its own, and @rjsf/shadcn Tailwind ones through its own. @rjsf/daisyui and @rjsf/shadcn go further and render most of core's templates through a class map of their own; their sections below list which.

@rjsf/daisyui renders core's components through its class map BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/daisyui used to copy most of @rjsf/core's templates and widgets with daisyUI classes on them, and the copies had drifted: its TextareaWidget dropped placeholder and options.emptyValue, its BaseInputTemplate disabled a read-only input rather than marking it read-only. The theme now declares a classMap and renders core's components wherever its own were such copies, keeping only the ones whose markup is its own: FieldTemplate, ObjectFieldTemplate, WrapIfAdditionalTemplate, ArrayFieldTemplate, ArrayFieldItemButtonsTemplate, TitleField, ArrayFieldTitleTemplate and GridTemplate, and the checkbox, toggle, select, date, time and rating widgets.

What that changes in the rendered form:

  • The removed components' form-control wrappers are gone. daisyUI 5 has no such class, so nothing is styled differently, but CSS or a test that reached an input through one has to use core's markers: rjsf-field-description, rjsf-field-help, rjsf-error-detail, rjsf-errors, rjsf-checkbox, rjsf-radio, rjsf-field-range-wrapper, rjsf-alt-date-list.
  • The removed components' own marker classes are gone with them, so CSS or a test selecting one uses core's: rjsf-field-error-template → rjsf-error-detail, rjsf-field-help-template → rjsf-field-help, description-field → rjsf-field-description, error-list → rjsf-errors and btn-add → rjsf-btn-add. A field's errors carry its error id on the <ul> itself: ul#root_x__error.
  • The add, remove, copy, move and clear buttons are core's IconButton, with its inline SVG icons in place of Font Awesome's. A className a custom template passes them lands beside the theme's btn btn-sm. Those classes now come from the class map's iconButton, which core's IconButton reads, rather than from the className the theme hands the button templates, so a custom AddButton, RemoveButton, CopyButton, MoveUpButton or MoveDownButton that renders its own <button> with that className adds btn itself, or reads registry.classMap.iconButton.
  • The error list has an Errors heading, as core's does.
  • A textarea has the browser's default number of rows unless ui:options.rows sets one; it was 5.
  • The alt-date widget renders its selects in one row with the Now and Clear buttons, with no label above each select; each select is still named <field label>, <part> for assistive technology.
  • ui:options.multiple no longer makes a file input accept several files. The file input is core's, which accepts several where the field is an array of files (type: 'array' with items of format: 'data-url'), as in every other theme; a single string field holds one file.
  • ui:enumDisabled dims a whole checkbox or radio option, not only its text, through data-disabled: variants on the data-disabled attribute core sets on it.
  • An array item is core's <div class="rjsf-array-item"> rather than a <fieldset>, rounded at the top of the first item and the bottom of the last by first: and last: variants, so a lone item is rounded at both ends; the items no longer stack by a per-index z-* class.
  • The radio and checkboxes widgets are core's, and CheckboxesWidget names its group from the field's presentation alone. A custom field that renders registry.widgets.CheckboxesWidget without passing the presentation it was handed leaves the group unnamed, and one that renders RadioWidget that way leaves it named by the label it hands it, else its placeholder, else a generic prompt, where the theme's own widgets pointed it at the FieldTemplate's label; pass presentation on.

To restyle one of these elements, pass a classMap to the Form: a class replaces the theme's class for that element, and a function of the theme's class extends it, as the custom themes page describes. The theme's classes carry spacing too, such as checkboxInput's and radioInput's mr-2 before the option's text, so extend them with a function to keep it. A Form put together from the theme's generateTemplates() and generateWidgets() rather than generateTheme() passes classMap={generateClassMap()} too, or core's components render without the theme's classes:

-import { generateTemplates, generateWidgets } from '@rjsf/daisyui';
+import { generateClassMap, generateTemplates, generateWidgets } from '@rjsf/daisyui';

-const Form = withTheme({ templates: generateTemplates(), widgets: generateWidgets() });
+const Form = withTheme({ templates: generateTemplates(), widgets: generateWidgets(), classMap: generateClassMap() });

A custom template or widget that imported one of the removed components from the theme imports it from @rjsf/core instead, or reads it from registry.templates or registry.widgets.

@rjsf/shadcn renders core's plain-HTML templates through its class map BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/shadcn declares a classMap and renders @rjsf/core's FieldTemplate, DescriptionField (core's DescriptionFieldTemplate), FieldErrorTemplate, FieldHelpTemplate, MultiSchemaFieldTemplate, ArrayFieldTemplate, ArrayFieldItemTemplate and ObjectFieldTemplate with Tailwind classes, in place of its own copies, and styles core's AltDateWidget, which it falls back to, through the same class map: its parts in one wrapping row, with Now and Clear as outline buttons. Its widgets and the templates built on its components/ui primitives (BaseInputTemplate, the buttons, ErrorList, CyclicSchemaExpandTemplate, OptionalDataControlsTemplate, TitleField) stay, and so do WrapIfAdditionalTemplate and GridTemplate.

What that changes in the rendered form:

  • An object or an array renders in a <fieldset>, and an array's items in core's rjsf-array-item-list, each item a grid with its buttons in an rjsf-array-item-toolbox beside the field, in place of the nested divs. The buttons are top-aligned and sit level with the field's input, past its label and description however far they wrap or however a classMap restyles fieldLabel or fieldDescription, as core's rjsf.css lays them out; a custom FieldTemplate keeps that by keeping core's classes.
  • TitleField draws an object's or array's title in a <legend>, which names its <fieldset>, followed by the separator, in place of a div holding both.
  • A field's description is drawn above its widget, as core draws it, rather than below. CheckboxWidget rendered without a plan draws no description of its own where ui:widget is the checkbox alias, since core's FieldTemplate draws it there, as @rjsf/core's checkbox does.
  • A field's errors are core's <ul class="rjsf-error-detail"> of <li> items, in place of a div of spans.
  • A field's label, description and help turn destructive through a data-invalid:text-destructive variant beside their class, on the data-invalid attribute core sets while the field shows its own errors.
  • A hidden field uses the hidden attribute rather than a hidden class.
  • AddButton renders its button with no row around it; the arrayFieldset and objectFieldset class-map entries align it to the end of the array or object, so one placed in a custom template carries no margin of its own.
  • WrapIfAdditionalTemplate lays an extra key's label and input, the value and the remove button out on shared grid rows, rather than by pixel offsets, so the key input and the remove button sit level with the value's input however far its label or description wraps, whatever errors or help follow it, as under @rjsf/core (see Lining up a custom FieldTemplate).

CSS or tests that reached these elements through the old div structure use core's markers instead. To restyle one of them, pass a classMap to the Form, as the custom themes page describes. A Form put together from the theme's generateTemplates() and generateWidgets() rather than generateTheme() passes classMap={generateClassMap()} too, or core's templates render without the theme's classes. A custom template that imported one of the removed templates from the theme imports it from @rjsf/core instead, or reads it from registry.templates.

schema, uiSchema and registry props are read-only BREAKING CHANGE​

schema, uiSchema and registry are now readonly on RJSFBaseProps, which every field, widget and template props type extends, and on SubmitButtonProps, which declares its own. These are values the form builds and passes down; writing back into them never reached the form and now fails to compile.

This is only a breaking change if you assigned into the props your custom component received, e.g. props.schema = modifiedSchema. Spread a copy and use that instead, which also drops the modifiers:

-props.schema = { ...props.schema, title: 'Custom' };
+const schema = { ...props.schema, title: 'Custom' };

Note that these props are read-only, not deeply immutable. The objects behind them are shared with the form, so mutating props.schema.title in place is still a bug even though it compiles.

Markdown is an opt-in template​

markdown-to-jsx is no longer part of the @rjsf/core bundle (it was a third of it) and is now an optional peer dependency instead of a dependency, so @rjsf/core no longer installs it. Markdown is rendered through the MarkdownTemplate, whose core default is plain text; @rjsf/core/markdown provides the markdown-to-jsx implementation. Install markdown-to-jsx and register it:

import Form from '@rjsf/core';
import MarkdownTemplate from '@rjsf/core/markdown';

<Form
  schema={schema}
  validator={validator}
  templates={{ MarkdownTemplate }}
  uiSchema={{ 'ui:enableMarkdownInDescription': true }}
/>;

The ui:enableMarkdownInDescription and ui:enableMarkdownInHelp options remain independent, default to false, and can still be set through ui:globalOptions. Translatable strings that allow markdown go through RichDescription, so they also need ui:enableMarkdownInDescription. RichDescription.TEST_IDS and RichHelp.TEST_IDS no longer exist, since neither component renders markdown itself any more; the markdown test id lives on the renderer as MarkdownTemplate.TEST_IDS.markdown from @rjsf/core/markdown. Raw HTML is never parsed, including in FileWidget's file information, which used to allow it.

The English InvalidObjectField, UnsupportedField* and FilesInfo translatable strings no longer use markdown syntax. FileWidget's file information used to render through markdown-to-jsx unconditionally, which is what made the file name bold; it now goes through RichDescription like every other translatable string, so it is plain text unless you register a MarkdownTemplate, set ui:enableMarkdownInDescription, and supply a translateString that marks the name up. A custom translateString that returns markdown keeps working when the template is registered and ui:enableMarkdownInDescription is enabled.

Theme removals​

@rjsf/primereact​

This theme has been removed because its latest version (11) now requires a paid subscription and violates our MIT licensing.

If you want to continue using PrimeReact with your v11 paid subscription, you are welcome to migrate the v6 version of @rjsf/primereact yourself.

@rjsf/semantic-ui​

This theme has been removed as it does not support React 19 and has become unmaintained.

Theme version support changes​

@rjsf/antd​

Version 7 is dropping official support for antd version 5. You must upgrade to antd 6.7 or later. Earlier releases won't do: antd 6.0.0-6.3.5 crash @rjsf/antd forms on first render, fixed upstream in ant-design/ant-design#57636, and releases before 6.7 don't understand a labelAlign of 'start' or 'end'

@rjsf/mui​

Version 7 is dropping official support for @mui/material/@mui/icons-material version 7. You must upgrade to version 9.

@rjsf/mantine​

Version 7 is dropping official support for mantine version 8. You must upgrade to version 9.6.3 or later, which requires React 19.2 or later.

Mantine 9 also renamed Grid's gutter prop to gap. GridTemplate maps a gutter value from ui:row/ui:col options to Mantine's gap prop for backward compatibility (an explicit gap wins if both are provided), but existing ui:row/ui:col options that use gutter should be renamed to gap going forward.

@rjsf/chakra-ui no longer requires chakra-react-select BREAKING CHANGE​

chakra-react-select has been removed from @rjsf/chakra-ui's peerDependencies; nothing in the package imports it any more, now that SelectWidget is built on Chakra's own Select.

No code change is required. If you installed chakra-react-select only to satisfy this peer dependency, you can drop it; if your own code uses it, keep it and declare it as a direct dependency of your app.

@rjsf/chakra-ui applies the chakra option, and getChakra() takes the options BREAKING CHANGE​

The chakra option never reached a widget: each one called getChakra({ uiSchema }), and getChakra() read ui:options off that wrapper and found none. The widgets now apply it, so a uiSchema that carries a chakra option changes how its field looks. Remove the option where the styling is not wanted.

getChakra() takes the widget's options, the merged ones getUiOptions() returns, instead of a uiSchema, so a chakra set through ui:globalOptions or the ui:chakra shorthand applies as one in ui:options does. A custom widget or template that calls it passes its options:

// Before
const chakraProps = getChakra(uiSchema);

// After
const chakraProps = getChakra(options);

A template whose props carry no options, such as a FieldTemplate or an ObjectFieldTemplate, merges them from its uiSchema first:

const chakraProps = getChakra(getUiOptions(uiSchema, registry.globalUiOptions));

A call that still passes a uiSchema, or a uiSchema in a { uiSchema } wrapper, no longer compiles.

It returns JsxStyleProps instead of Field.RootProps, and keeps every Chakra style prop, including the ones that share a name with an HTML attribute, such as color and width. The chakra option of the theme's UiSchema type is JsxStyleProps too, so a non-style prop, such as invalid, required or onClick, no longer compiles in the ui:options of the uiSchema's root. In a nested field's ui:options and under ui:chakra the option is not typed, so such a prop still compiles there; under ui:globalOptions it is typed by ChakraGlobalUISchemaOptions. getChakra() always dropped those, wherever they are set; set them on your own widget or template instead.

@emotion/is-prop-valid is no longer a dependency of @rjsf/chakra-ui. If your own code imports it, declare it as a direct dependency of your app.

@rjsf/snapshot-tests no longer requires @testing-library/jest-dom BREAKING CHANGE​

@testing-library/jest-dom has been removed from @rjsf/snapshot-tests's peerDependencies; none of its suites use a jest-dom matcher.

No code change is required. If your own tests use jest-dom's matchers, declare @testing-library/jest-dom as a direct dev dependency, since npm no longer installs it as a peer of @rjsf/snapshot-tests.

Each RJSF warning is logged once BREAKING CHANGE​

The warnings @rjsf/utils, @rjsf/core and the validators raise while rendering now go through logOnce(), which logs each one only the first time it is seen on the page, so a warning is no longer repeated on every re-render (#3051). What has been logged is remembered until the page reloads, so if your tests assert on an RJSF warning, call resetLogOnce() before each test in your Vitest or Jest setup file; otherwise only the first test to trigger a warning sees it logged.

+import { resetLogOnce } from '@rjsf/utils';
+
+beforeEach(resetLogOnce);

Under Vitest's default globals: false, also import beforeEach from vitest.

Node support​

Version 7 supports only the active Node.js LTS lines: ^22.18.0 || ^24.11.0 || >=26.0.0. Node 20, Node 23, Node 25, and Node 24 releases before 24.11.0 are no longer supported, as they are not maintained versions. Node 22.18.0 is the floor because it is the first release to enable native TypeScript type stripping by default.

All PR and branch builds are running against Node 22, 24 and 26

Dropping Node 20 also let us upgrade pnpm past version 10, which had been pinned because pnpm 11+ requires Node >=22.13. We're now on the latest pnpm release (12).

React version​

RJSF is no longer actively supporting React version < 19.2.x. React 19 is officially supported on all the themes. @rjsf/core declares react >=19.2 as its peer dependency, the release that added <Activity>, whose hidden content Form treats as unmounted.

react-dom is a peer dependency of @rjsf/core BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/core declares react-dom >=19.2 as a peer dependency, for the useFormStatus() hook its submit button reads (see Submitting). A project that renders a Form in the browser already has react-dom at the version of its react, so it has nothing to change. A project that installs @rjsf/core without react-dom, such as a test setup on another renderer, gets a missing peer dependency: add react-dom at the version of react.

Removal of defaultProps support on widgets BREAKING CHANGE​

A widget no longer gets its component's (deprecated) defaultProps.options merged into the options it renders with. React 19 removed defaultProps support for function components, so this merging behavior was already broken for function widgets there and only ever worked for forwardRef/memo-wrapped ones.

If you relied on defaultProps to supply default options for a custom widget, apply the defaults inside the widget itself instead, e.g. via destructuring defaults: const { color = 'red' } = options;. See Custom widget options.

Widget type BREAKING CHANGE​

The Widget<T, S, F> type in @rjsf/utils is now SlotComponent<WidgetProps<T, S, F>>, the slot type Field and every TemplatesType entry share: any function or class component taking those props, including one annotated as a React ComponentType or FunctionComponent. It no longer carries the optional MergedWidget property, which getWidget() used to stamp onto a widget component to cache the wrapper it created for merging defaultProps.options (see above). That caching is gone along with the merging behavior it supported.

This breaks code that referenced Widget['MergedWidget'] directly, and code that assigns a Widget to a React ComponentType annotation, which a SlotComponent does not satisfy; annotate such a value as Widget instead. Passing your own ComponentType into widgets is unaffected.

withTheme() BREAKING CHANGE​

withTheme() now returns a plain function component instead of a forwardRef-wrapped one, now that React 19 supports passing ref as a regular prop to function components.

This is a breaking change if you pass the return value of withTheme() directly to useState() or a state setter, e.g. useState(withTheme(theme)) or setFormComponent(withTheme(theme)). React treats a bare function passed to either as a lazy initializer/updater and calls it immediately with no arguments, which throws (a forwardRef object isn't a function, so this pattern happened to work before). Wrap it in a lazy initializer instead: useState(() => withTheme(theme)).

Its return type changed too; see withTheme() returns a ThemedForm.

FormProps['onSubmit'] event type BREAKING CHANGE​

The event parameter passed to onSubmit is now typed as SubmitEvent<HTMLFormElement> instead of the deprecated FormEvent<any> (both from react; FormEvent doesn't correspond to a real event type and is annotated @deprecated in @types/react in favor of SubmitEvent, ChangeEvent, InputEvent, or SyntheticEvent). This is only a breaking change if you referenced FormEvent directly for your onSubmit handler's event parameter type.

SubmitEvent was added to @types/react in version 19.2.18; earlier 19.2.x patches don't have it and will fail to compile against @rjsf/core's published types with TS2305: Module 'react' has no exported member 'SubmitEvent'. Make sure your project's @types/react is at least 19.2.18.

A promise onSubmit returns makes the form pending BREAKING CHANGE​

When onSubmit returns a promise, as every async function does, the form now ignores another submit until that promise settles, from a submit button, from Enter pressed in a field or from FormRef.submit(), and meanwhile the submit button gets pending and aria-disabled (see Submitting). An onSubmit that returns nothing, or a value that isn't a promise, behaves as before, except that a FormRef.submit() it calls before it returns is ignored, since the form can't tell yet whether it will return a promise. The browser already ignored one that reached requestSubmit() then, while the submit event ran, so only a submit of an edit the inputs have yet to show is newly ignored. Submit the next step once onSubmit has returned instead.

  • A form that should take a second submit while the first is saving, such as one that queues saves, has to return before the save settles: start it without returning its promise, onSubmit={(data) => { void save(data); }}, and handle its errors inside save.
  • A rejection is reported as before: an async onSubmit that throws is reported as one unhandled rejection, from the form's copy of the promise rather than from the promise itself. Only a handler that handled the promise it returned, such as const saving = save(data); saving.catch(log); return saving;, now gets an unhandled rejection it didn't before. Catch inside onSubmit and return a promise that resolves instead.
  • A custom SubmitButton that spreads the props of ui:submitButtonOptions gets aria-disabled, and an onClick that cancels the click, while pending. An onClick those props set still runs first, with the click event, and the submit is ignored. Style [aria-disabled='true'], or read the new pending prop, to show it.

FormRef.reset() passed as an event handler seeds the form with the event BREAKING CHANGE​

FormRef.reset(seed?) now reads its argument, as reset(values) does in react-hook-form and TanStack Form: given data, it makes that data the form's seed and baseline (see reset() goes back to the seed). So reset passed straight as an event handler receives the event as its seed, and a click resets the form to the click event:

<button type='button' onClick={formRef.current?.reset}>
  Reset
</button>

Wrap it, so it is called with no argument:

<button type='button' onClick={() => formRef.current?.reset()}>
  Reset
</button>

ObjectFieldTemplatePropertyType BREAKING CHANGE​

ObjectFieldTemplatePropertyType in @rjsf/utils is now generic (<T, S, F>, defaulted like every other RJSF generic type), and its content field is typed as ReactElement<Pick<FieldProps<T, S, F>, 'schema' | 'uiSchema'>> instead of a bare ReactElement. ObjectFieldTemplateProps['properties'] threads its own <T, S, F> through to it.

This is only a breaking change if you referenced ObjectFieldTemplatePropertyType with explicit (non-default) generic arguments, or relied on content.props being typed as any.

Removal of deprecated APIs BREAKING CHANGE​

The following APIs, deprecated in prior releases, have been removed:

  • UiSchema['ui:rootFieldId']: use the Form.idPrefix prop instead.
  • Form.getUsedFormData() and Form.getFieldNames() instance methods, and the underlying getUsedFormData/getFieldNames exports from @rjsf/utils: there is no direct replacement.
  • Form.omitExtraData() instance method: use SchemaUtils.omitExtraData(schema, formData) instead (build one with createSchemaUtils, or use the registry.schemaUtils your fields, widgets and templates already receive).
  • FormProps.removeEmptyOptionalObjects: this prop had already stopped doing anything; use omitExtraData instead, which now prunes empty optional objects as part of its filtering.
  • removeOptionalEmptyObjects() exported from @rjsf/utils: use omitExtraData instead, which has the equivalent pruning built in.
  • toPathSchema() exported from @rjsf/utils, and SchemaUtils.toPathSchema(): there is no direct replacement.
  • PathSchema type exported from @rjsf/utils: there is no direct replacement.
  • The boolean options for FormProps.liveValidate and FormProps.liveOmit: use 'onChange' in place of true, or omit the prop (or pass undefined) in place of false.

Generic defaults are unknown instead of any BREAKING CHANGE​

The RJSF generics are <T, S, F>: the form data, the schema, and the form context. T and F used to default to any, so anything read out of formData was unchecked and stayed unchecked however far it travelled. They now default to unknown and FormContextType.

FormContextType is object, so reading a key of an untyped formContext is a type error; see any members of the public types are specific types.

Passing your own type is still the way to get typed form data: Form<MyData>, FieldProps<MyData> and IChangeEvent<MyData> behave as before (apart from IChangeEvent.formData, described below), and Form infers T from formData when you pass it, so <Form formData={data} onChange={…} /> types the handler with no type argument at all. The validators and the theme exports were retyped so they keep working with a typed form; see ValidatorType and customizeValidator() take the schema as their first type argument and withTheme() returns a ThemedForm below.

Values annotated without a type argument still fit a typed form. A const uiSchema: UiSchema = …, a CustomValidator or ErrorTransformer, a handler taking a bare IChangeEvent, and a widget, field or template written against the bare props (function MyWidget(props: WidgetProps), class components included) all go into a Form<MyData>, except a bare UiSchema where MyData, or the element of an array MyData, has a string index signature of a type narrower than unknown, such as Record<string, string>; see any members of the public types are specific types. Passed next to formData they do not change what Form infers either: T comes from formData/initialFormData, and from the other props only when no data is passed, so a typed onSubmit handler still types a form that has no formData. Component slots check their props bivariantly, the way React checks event handlers, which is what lets a component written for unknown data fit a slot typed for MyData.

For refs, supply the form-data type explicitly: createRef<FormRef<MyData>>() or useRef<FormRef<MyData>>(null). A bare FormRef defaults to unknown and can make Form infer unknown even when formData is typed. See Reading Form internals through a ref.

The reverse does not hold: a typed handler does not fit a bare FormProps, since FormProps means FormProps<unknown>. A props object or a wrapper component that takes typed handlers (customValidate: (formData: MyData | undefined, …), onSubmit: (e: IChangeEvent<MyData>) => …) fails with TS2322; type it FormProps<MyData>, as in function MyForm(props: FormProps<MyData>) { return <Form {...props} />; }.

IChangeEvent.formData and FormRef.getFormData() are typed EventFormData<T>: T itself when the data is an object or array, since no change below the root replaces such a root with undefined, and T | undefined for a scalar, which is undefined once its field is cleared. A write at the root itself can empty an object root: setFieldValue('', undefined), or a root-level custom field or widget calling onChange(undefined, ROOT_FIELD_PATH). The type does not reflect that, and the event reaches onChange either way, so allow for undefined in the handler's state if your form does either. So const [data, setData] = useState(initial) with onChange={({ formData }) => setData(formData)} needs no annotation for an object form. For a scalar root the state has to allow undefined:

-const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
+const [theme, setTheme] = useState<string | undefined>('light');
 <Form schema={{ type: 'string' }} formData={theme} onChange={({ formData }) => setTheme(formData)} … />

Beyond those, what changes is code that relied on the any default. The form data now arrives as unknown, so you either name its type or narrow it.

Name the type — preferred, and what the default is there to encourage:

-const onChange = ({ formData }: IChangeEvent) => save(formData.name);
+const onChange = ({ formData }: IChangeEvent<MyData>) => save(formData.name);

Or narrow it, when the data really is unknown at that point:

-function MyField({ formData }: FieldProps) {
-  return <input value={formData} />;
+function MyField({ formData }: FieldProps) {
+  return <input value={typeof formData === 'string' ? formData : ''} />;
 }

A custom validator receives unknown for the same reason:

-const customValidate = ({ pass1, pass2 }, errors) => {
+const customValidate: CustomValidator<MyData> = (formData, errors) => {
+  const { pass1, pass2 } = formData ?? {};
   if (pass1 !== pass2) {
     errors.pass2?.addError("Passwords don't match");
   }
   return errors;
 };

One declaration changed along with the defaults: Registry.schemaUtils is SchemaUtilsType<T, S, F> rather than SchemaUtilsType<T, S>. The omitted F was a latent bug that the any default had been hiding; it only matters if you wrote the type out by hand.

The templates prop of Form and withTheme() checks declared templates BREAKING CHANGE​

The templates prop of Form, and with it the templates of the theme passed to withTheme(), now checks a declared template such as FieldTemplate against its own props, where it accepted any component, so a template written for other props no longer compiles. Type its props as the template's, such as FieldTemplateProps. A custom template written inline in the prop needs a type on its props too; see any members of the public types are specific types.

TemplatesType has a string index signature for custom entries, so an Omit of it with literal keys, such as Omit<TemplatesType, 'ButtonTemplates'>, collapses to that signature and checks none of the declared templates. Type a set of templates as the new PartialTemplatesType, the type of the templates prop of Form, which checks each declared template, takes any of the ButtonTemplates on their own and takes custom entries:

-import { TemplatesType } from '@rjsf/utils';
+import { PartialTemplatesType } from '@rjsf/utils';

-const templates: Partial<Omit<TemplatesType, 'ButtonTemplates'>> = {
+const templates: PartialTemplatesType = {
   FieldTemplate: MyFieldTemplate,
   MyTemplate,
 };

A PartialTemplatesType doesn't fit where a Partial<TemplatesType> is expected, such as the return type of a theme's generateTemplates(), because its ButtonTemplates may leave buttons out. Type a value that goes there as Partial<TemplatesType>, which checks the declared templates too but needs every button in a ButtonTemplates it holds.

To leave out other templates, omit them from the new DeclaredTemplatesType, the part of TemplatesType without that signature, and add the new CustomTemplateEntries, the part with it, if the type holds custom entries too. That signature takes a key you omitted unchecked, so declare it again with the type you want. See Typing a set of templates.

A declared template read back out of the templates prop, such as props.templates?.FieldTemplate in a component that wraps Form, was a ComponentType<any> and is now that template's SlotComponent, such as SlotComponent<FieldTemplateProps>. Rendering it with props the template doesn't take, such as <FieldTemplate {...fieldProps} extra='x' />, no longer compiles; pass only the template's own props. A React ComponentType annotation doesn't take a SlotComponent, so a typeof check before passing it on as one no longer compiles either. Name its props with isComponentType():

+import { isComponentType } from '@rjsf/utils';
+
 const { FieldTemplate } = props.templates ?? {};
-if (typeof FieldTemplate === 'function') {
+if (isComponentType<FieldTemplateProps>(FieldTemplate)) {
   wrap(FieldTemplate); // wrap(component: ComponentType<FieldTemplateProps>)
 }

any members of the public types are specific types BREAKING CHANGE​

Members of the @rjsf/utils types that were typed any now have the type their values really have. This affects code that reads these members, and code that builds the props objects that contain them, such as a custom ArrayField or a test that renders a template directly.

MemberWasIs
onAddItem, onCopyItem, onMoveUpItem, onMoveDownItem, onRemoveItem (ArrayFieldItemButtonsTemplateProps, which ArrayFieldItemTemplateProps.buttonsProps holds) and onAddClick (ArrayFieldTemplateProps)(event?: any) => void(event?: SyntheticEvent<HTMLElement>) => void
style (FieldTemplateProps, UIOptionsType, ui:style)StyleHTMLAttributes<any>CSSProperties
RJSFValidationError.paramsanyRecord<string, unknown>
ValidatorType.rawValidation()rawValidation<Result = any>(…): { errors?: Result[] }rawValidation(…): { errors?: unknown[] }; each validator returns its own error type
A custom template's entry in TemplatesType, alone or in a groupComponentType<any>, Record<string, ComponentType<any>>SlotComponent<never>, Record<string, SlotComponent<never> | undefined>
A nested entry of a UiSchema for unknown data, or for data whose index signature holds unknown values, such as Record<string, unknown>anyunknown
additionalProperties in a UiSchema whose T has no index signatureanyUiSchema<unknown>
WidgetProps.value (and BaseInputTemplateProps.value)anyunknown
The value WidgetProps.onChange and FieldProps.onChange take, and the one WidgetProps.onBlur/onFocus and FieldProps.onBlur/onFocus takeany, T | undefinedunknown
useFileWidgetProps()'s value, and the value its onChange takesstring | string[] | undefined | null, string | null | (string | null)[]unknown
DateElementProps.value, and the value select and handleChange take in useAltDateWidgetProps()any, stringnumber | undefined, unknown
Props FieldProps, WidgetProps and BaseInputTemplateProps don't declareanynot accepted
onKeyRename, onKeyRenameBlur, onRemoveProperty in FieldTemplateProps and WrapIfAdditionalTemplatePropsrequiredoptional, undefined for a field ObjectField doesn't render
An option UIOptionsType doesn't declare, read from ui:options, a uiSchema's ui: key or a widget's optionsanyunknown
FormContextType, the constraint and default of every FRecord<string, any>object
RJSFSchemaJSONSchema7 & Record<string, any>JSONSchema7, which declares the later-draft, OpenAPI and Ajv keywords RJSF or its validators read
RJSFMarkedSchemaJSONSchema7 & Record<string, any> & Record<symbol, boolean | string>JSONSchema7 & Record<symbol, unknown>; see RJSFMarkedSchema has no index signature
GenericObjectType, which isObject() narrows to, @rjsf/mui's mui option holds and @rjsf/core's GridProps and LayoutGridSchemaType build onRecord<string, any>Record<string, unknown>
mergeObjects() and mergeSchemas()take and return GenericObjectTypetake any objects and return GenericObjectType
GenericSymbolObjectTypeGenericObjectType & Record<symbol, boolean | string>removed, so declare it yourself if you use it
GridTemplateProps' other props, and the undeclared keys of UISchemaSubmitButtonOptions.props (ui:submitButtonOptions.props)anyAny object, of which only the declared props read back: GridTemplateProps now also declares className and style, and props declares disabled, className, onClick and onClickCapture
The entry of a field typed any in a typed UiSchema, such as UiSchema<{ meta: any }>['meta'] or a UiSchema<GenericObjectType> fieldanyunknown

Pass these handlers straight to a button's onClick, or call them with no argument. A handler you write for one of these props has to accept any React event on an HTML element, and undefined. An SVG element's event, such as the MouseEvent<SVGSVGElement> of an icon's own onClick, doesn't fit: handle the click on the button around the icon instead.

The currentTarget type says it is never null, but React clears it once dispatch ends. A handler that reads it after an await gets null, so read it first: const target = event?.currentTarget; await confirm(); target?.blur();.

onAddItem, onCopyItem, onMoveUpItem, onMoveDownItem and onRemoveItem act on the index the item rendered with, so a template that calls one after an await has to know the item still sits there: if another item was added, moved or removed meanwhile, the call acts on the row now at that index.

The handlers also read whether the button can act, such as the form's disabled, from the render that handed them out. A call after an await still acts if the form was disabled or made read-only meanwhile, so call the handler before awaiting, or check the lock again before calling it.

-const onAddClick = (event: MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>) => { … };
+const onAddClick = (event?: SyntheticEvent<HTMLElement>) => { … };

style was typed as the props of a <style> element, so it accepted keys such as media and nonce that aren't CSS. It now takes the same CSSProperties a style prop does; move anything that isn't a CSS property elsewhere.

RJSFValidationError.params can be missing and its values are unknown, so narrow a value before using it:

-const missing: string = error.params.missingProperty;
+const missing = error.params?.missingProperty;
+if (typeof missing === 'string') { … }

A custom validator that sets params to a value typed with an interface no longer type-checks, since an interface has no index signature. Spread it, as params: { ...params }, or declare it with type.

rawValidation() no longer takes a type argument. Each validator returns the errors of its engine, from customizeValidator(), the default export and createPrecompiledValidator() alike: ErrorObject from Ajv for @rjsf/validator-ajv8, ValidationError from ata-validator for @rjsf/validator-ata, and CFWorkerValidationError for @rjsf/validator-cfworker. Each validator package exports its error type, so an app that doesn't depend on the engine itself can import it from there. Through a bare ValidatorType the errors are unknown[]. To type a stored result, use RawValidationResult from @rjsf/utils, such as RawValidationResult<ErrorObject>:

-import type { ErrorObject } from 'ajv';
+import type { RawValidationResult } from '@rjsf/utils';
+import type { ErrorObject } from '@rjsf/validator-ajv8';

-const [result, setResult] = useState<{ errors?: ErrorObject[] }>();
-setResult(validator.rawValidation<ErrorObject>(schema, formData));
+const [result, setResult] = useState<RawValidationResult<ErrorObject>>();
+setResult(validator.rawValidation(schema, formData));

That diff needs validator to have a concrete type, as customizeValidator(), the default export and createPrecompiledValidator() give it. Code that holds it as ValidatorType, as Form and Registry do, has only unknown[] errors, so it has to assert the engine it knows it has: setResult(validator.rawValidation(schema, formData) as RawValidationResult<ErrorObject>).

A custom validator that hands back another validator's rawValidation() drops its own Result type parameter too, since that call's errors are no longer Result[].

Any component still fits a custom entry in registry.templates, alone or in a group, except a class whose constructor requires a second argument, and naming it in the uiSchema works as before. Reading one back out of registry.templates, or from getTemplates() under a custom name, gives a component whose props type is never, so code that narrowed the lookup and rendered it, or passed it on as a ComponentType, no longer compiles. Name the template's props in the lookup:

+import { isComponentType } from '@rjsf/utils';
+
 const { MyTemplate } = registry.templates;
-return typeof MyTemplate === 'function' ? <MyTemplate {...props} /> : null;
+if (!isComponentType<MyTemplateProps>(MyTemplate)) {
+  return null;
+}
+return <MyTemplate {...props} />;

For an entry in a group, narrow the group first, since isComponentType() is false for it, then name the props on the member. A typeof check alone isn't enough to find the group, because what memo(), forwardRef() and lazy() return is an object too:

const { MyGroup } = registry.templates;
if (typeof MyGroup !== 'object' || isComponentType(MyGroup)) {
  return null;
}
const { MyTemplate } = MyGroup;
if (!isComponentType<MyTemplateProps>(MyTemplate)) {
  return null;
}
return <MyTemplate {...props} />;

Keep reading it from the registry: importing the component directly ignores a theme or templates prop that registers another one under its name.

A template written inline with no type on its props parameter takes never from the same entry, so reading a prop from it no longer compiles. That goes for any custom entry, including one in the templates prop of Form. Annotate the parameter:

-<Form schema={schema} validator={validator} templates={{ MyTemplate: (props) => <div>{props.children}</div> }} />
+<Form schema={schema} validator={validator} templates={{ MyTemplate: (props: MyTemplateProps) => <div>{props.children}</div> }} />

An untyped UiSchema still accepts any nesting, but an entry read back from it is unknown, since nothing says what it holds. So is the entry of a field typed any in a typed one, such as meta in UiSchema<{ meta: any }> or any field of UiSchema<GenericObjectType>. Cast the uiSchema you read to one typed by the data it describes, and narrow the value. Keep WidgetProps' own type argument, which is the widget's value type: the widget's uiSchema is typed by that value, so it needs a cast rather than an annotation to read it as another type. The cast checks nothing, so a wrong one compiles:

 function MyWidget({ uiSchema }: WidgetProps<string>) {
-  return <span>{uiSchema?.custom['ui:options'].hint}</span>;
+  // the uiSchema is typed by the widget's value, which says nothing about the `custom` entry read from it
+  const ui = uiSchema as UiSchema<{ custom?: string }> | undefined;
+  const hint = ui?.custom?.['ui:options']?.hint;
+  return <span>{typeof hint === 'string' ? hint : null}</span>;
 }

A child read by a key known only at runtime, as a custom object field reads one by its property name, has no data type to annotate with. Cast the entry, or read it with getByPath<UiSchema | undefined>(), as ObjectField does:

 function MyObjectField({ uiSchema, name }: FieldProps) {
-  const options = getUiOptions(uiSchema?.[name]);
+  // `name` is known only at runtime, so nothing types the entry under it
+  const options = getUiOptions(uiSchema?.[name] as UiSchema | undefined);
   return <span>{options.title}</span>;
 }

Spreading an entry of an untyped UiSchema fails with TS2698 (Spread types may only be created from object types), since the entry is unknown. Annotate the uiSchema it comes from with the data it describes:

-const base: UiSchema = { field: { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' } };
