+const base: UiSchema<{ field?: string }> = { field: { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' } };
 const uiSchema = { field: { ...base.field, 'ui:help': 'Shown below' } };

An entry read from a UiSchema<Record<string, unknown>> is unknown, so check it with isObject() before reading its keys.

An untyped UiSchema, or a UiSchema<GenericObjectType>, no longer fits a UiSchema<X> where X, or the element of an array X, has a string index signature of a type narrower than unknown, such as the uiSchema of a Form whose formData is a Record<string, string> or a Record<string, string>[]: each key of that signature holds a UiSchema for its value, which the unknown entries don't fit. A Record<string, unknown> target is fine, since its entries are as open as the untyped one's. Likewise a UiSchema<{ meta: any }> no longer fits a UiSchema<{ meta: string }>, or one with any other type for meta. Annotate the uiSchema with the data it describes:

-const uiSchema: UiSchema = { notes: { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' } };
+const uiSchema: UiSchema<Record<string, string>> = { notes: { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' } };

additionalProperties describes data of an unknown type in a UiSchema with no type argument, or whose T has no index signature, so a function written inside it, such as an items function or an inline ui:field, gets unknown for that data rather than any. Annotate its parameter:

 const uiSchema: UiSchema = {
   additionalProperties: {
-    items: (item) => ({ 'ui:title': item.label }),
+    items: (item: { label: string }) => ({ 'ui:title': item.label }),
   },
 };

Spreading the rest of a generic UiSchema<T, S, F> into a new object no longer gives back a UiSchema<T, S, F>, since the checker can't relate that rest to the type it came from. A generic custom field that strips keys this way needs a cast on the rest, which leaves the keys beside it checked:

 const { 'ui:title': _title, ...rest } = uiSchema;
-return { ...rest, 'ui:options': {} };
+return { ...(rest as UiSchema<T, S, F>), 'ui:options': {} };

A widget's value is unknown: a ui:widget can point any widget at data of any type, and some fields hand their widgets a value that isn't the field's data, such as the option index MultiSchemaField gives its selector. Narrow it before use. toInputValue() turns it into what an input's value prop takes:

-const MyWidget = ({ value, onChange }: WidgetProps) => <input value={value ?? ''} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)} />;
+const MyWidget = ({ value, onChange }: WidgetProps) => (
+  <input value={toInputValue(value)} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)} />
+);

Whatever a widget passes to onChange is unknown to it, since the field it reports to decides what the value means. A field's onChange takes an unknown value too, since a change reported from inside the field carries the value at the deeper FieldPath it names. A handler you pass as the onChange of a widget or a field can still declare the type it expects, while one you pass as onBlur or onFocus has to take an unknown value.

useAltDateWidgetProps() reads only a string, so the alt-date and alt-datetime widgets of every theme show a number or Date as empty: they write strings, so a field holding either couldn't keep it. Pass the date as the string the widget writes: a date-time such as date.toISOString() for alt-datetime, or a YYYY-MM-DD date for alt-date.

@rjsf/mantine's FileWidget hands FileInput an empty File for each stored file, where it handed the stored data URLs, which aren't Files. A ui:options.valueComponent that read the files' names or contents from its value gets neither: write your own FileWidget instead, whose useFileWidgetProps() gives each file's name, size, type and data URL in filesInfo.

A custom GridTemplate that reads a prop of its own from ui:layoutGrid declares it, as the themes now do:

-function MyGridTemplate({ gap, ...rest }: GridTemplateProps) {
+function MyGridTemplate({ gap, ...rest }: GridTemplateProps & { gap?: number }) {

GridTemplateProps is a type alias, not an interface, so neither an interface that extends it nor a declare module '@rjsf/utils' augmentation of it compiles. Build a props type of your own by intersection instead, and declare a prop an augmentation added on the template that reads it, as above:

-interface MyGridProps extends GridTemplateProps {
-  gap?: number;
-}
+type MyGridProps = GridTemplateProps & { gap?: number };

An Omit of GridTemplateProps keeps only its declared props, so it no longer takes the theme's other props. Intersect it with OpenProps, the open part of GridTemplateProps, to keep them:

-type MyRowProps = Omit<GridTemplateProps, 'style'> & { style?: MyStyle };
+type MyRowProps = OpenProps & Omit<GridTemplateProps, 'style'> & { style?: MyStyle };

GridTemplateProps.style is a CSSProperties, which has no key for a CSS custom property, so a style that sets one casts the object:

-const props: GridTemplateProps = { style: { '--my-gap': '8px' } };
+const props: GridTemplateProps = { style: { '--my-gap': '8px' } as CSSProperties };

A custom SubmitButton that reads a prop of its own from ui:submitButtonOptions.props checks for it, then narrows its unknown value. getSubmitButtonOptions() always returns props, the default ones when the uiSchema's are missing or aren't an object. Its return type is SubmitButtonOptions; annotated as UISchemaSubmitButtonOptions, its props are optional again:

-const variant = getSubmitButtonOptions(uiSchema).props?.variant;
+const { props } = getSubmitButtonOptions(uiSchema);
+const variant = 'variant' in props && typeof props.variant === 'string' ? props.variant : undefined;

A handler written inline for an undeclared key of ui:submitButtonOptions.props gets no type for its parameter from UiSchema, so annotate the parameter. onClick and onClickCapture are declared, so theirs still comes from the type:

-const uiSchema: UiSchema = { 'ui:submitButtonOptions': { props: { onMouseEnter: (event) => track(event) } } };
+const uiSchema: UiSchema = {
+  'ui:submitButtonOptions': { props: { onMouseEnter: (event: MouseEvent<HTMLElement>) => track(event) } },
+};

FieldProps and WidgetProps no longer accept props they don't declare. They declare the ones RJSF passes: on FieldProps the additional-property callbacks onKeyRename, onKeyRenameBlur and onRemoveProperty, propertyNamesEnum, an array item's index and a oneOf/anyOf field's options; on WidgetProps errorSchema, time and autocomplete. A field or widget that takes props of its own declares them, and passing one an undeclared prop is a type error:

-function MyField({ myProp }: FieldProps) {
+function MyField({ myProp }: FieldProps & { myProp?: string }) {

Give a prop of your own a name these props don't declare. The & intersects with a declared prop rather than replacing it, so FieldProps & { options: MyConfig } gives options: S[] & MyConfig, which can't be passed without a cast.

BaseInputTemplateProps declares the type, pattern and accept the widgets set on the input, so passing it another input attribute, such as maxLength, min or autoComplete, is a type error. A widget that passes a theme's own props to the registry's BaseInputTemplate reads it typed with them: @rjsf/core's CoreBaseInputTemplateProps (also for @rjsf/daisyui, which renders core's template) takes the <input> attributes, @rjsf/mui's MuiBaseInputTemplateProps the TextField props, and @rjsf/react-bootstrap's BootstrapBaseInputTemplateProps and @rjsf/shadcn's ShadcnBaseInputTemplateProps an extraProps, which also takes data-* attributes:

-const { BaseInputTemplate } = registry.templates;
+const BaseInputTemplate: SlotComponent<MuiBaseInputTemplateProps> = registry.templates.BaseInputTemplate;
 return <BaseInputTemplate {...props} multiline rows={3} />;

That annotation trusts the registered template rather than checking it: a BaseInputTemplate an app registers that ignores multiline still compiles, and renders a single-line input.

The onKeyRename, onKeyRenameBlur and onRemoveProperty a FieldTemplate or WrapIfAdditionalTemplate receives are undefined for a field ObjectField doesn't render, such as the root or an array item, which they always were at runtime. Every property ObjectField renders gets them, so they don't tell an additional property from a declared one:

-onKeyRename(newKey);
+onKeyRename?.(newKey);

An option a theme or custom component reads from ui:options that RJSF doesn't declare is unknown, so check its type before use:

-const { size = 'md' } = props.options;
+const size = typeof props.options.size === 'string' ? props.options.size : 'md';

FormContextType is object, so any object, an interface included, can be a form context. A component generic over the context, or left on the default object, names the keys it reads, each optional, since object promises none:

-const { locale } = registry.formContext;
+const { locale }: { locale?: string } = registry.formContext;

A dynamic uiSchema.items callback gets the context as F too, so one that reads a key passes its context type to UiSchema:

-const uiSchema: UiSchema = {
+const uiSchema: UiSchema<unknown, RJSFSchema, { isAdmin?: boolean }> = {
   items: (_itemData, _index, formContext) => (formContext?.isAdmin ? adminItem : userItem),
 };

A key computed at runtime, such as a field's id, is read from a member typed as a record:

-const label = registry.formContext.labels[id];
+const { labels = {} }: { labels?: Record<string, string> } = registry.formContext;
+const label = labels[id];

A context that is itself keyed that way can't be annotated as a record, since object isn't assignable to one; the component takes it as F:

-function IdField({ id, registry }: FieldProps) {
+function IdField({ id, registry }: FieldProps<unknown, RJSFSchema, Record<string, string>>) {
   const label = registry.formContext[id];

A component that knows the context type takes it as F, as in FieldProps<MyData, RJSFSchema, MyContext>, and reads its keys directly. The annotations above compile only for a context that is generic or the default object; on a known context they fail unless the two types share a key. Under @rjsf/antd, a component generic over the context, or on the default, can annotate with the exported AntdFormContext to read the theme's options, whose rowGutter is what antd's Row takes; a known context extends it, as in interface MyContext extends AntdFormContext, and its keys are read directly.

RJSFSchema is JSONSchema7, which @rjsf/utils augments with the keywords RJSF or its validators read beyond draft 7: $anchor, $dynamicAnchor, $dynamicRef, $recursiveAnchor, $recursiveRef, $vocabulary, contentSchema, dependentRequired, dependentSchemas, minContains, maxContains, prefixItems, unevaluatedItems and unevaluatedProperties from later drafts, OpenAPI's discriminator and components, Ajv's nullable, formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum, and ajv-errors' errorMessage. A schema with keywords of its own declares them the same way, so they type-check at every depth, a property's subschema included:

-const schema: RJSFSchema = { type: 'object', 'x-group': 'contact' };
+declare module 'json-schema' {
+  interface JSONSchema7 {
+    'x-group'?: string;
+  }
+}
+const schema: RJSFSchema = {
+  type: 'object',
+  'x-group': 'contact',
+  properties: { phone: { type: 'string', 'x-group': 'contact' } },
+};

If the declare module fails with TS2664, your project needs @types/json-schema of its own. If type and every other keyword then fail with TS2353, the file holding it needs an import or export. See Keywords of your own.

A type of your own, such as RJSFSchema & { 'x-group'?: string }, which Form infers as S or takes as its second type argument, declares a keyword on the root schema alone, since a subschema is a JSONSchema7Definition.

Since the augmentation is global, code that already augments JSONSchema7 with one of the keywords above under another type no longer compiles (TS2717: "Subsequent property declarations must have the same type"). Declare it with the type @rjsf/utils gives it.

OpenAPI's discriminator is the interface JSONSchema7Discriminator, which declares propertyName and mapping. A field of its own, such as defaultMapping, now fails with TS2353, so declare it by augmenting that interface:

declare module 'json-schema' {
  interface JSONSchema7Discriminator {
    defaultMapping?: string;
  }
}

RJSFSchema has no index signature any more, so schema[key] with a string key and passing a schema as a Record<string, unknown> are type errors. Type the key as keyof RJSFSchema, and the parameter as RJSFSchema.

An object that was only accepted through that index signature now fails with TS2353. A properties or $defs map isn't a schema itself, so type it as Record<string, RJSFSchema>. A schema that carries a marker such as ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG is an RJSFMarkedSchema:

-const properties: RJSFSchema = { name: { type: 'string' } };
+const properties: Record<string, RJSFSchema> = { name: { type: 'string' } };

-const schema: RJSFSchema = { type: 'string', [ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG]: true };
+const schema: RJSFMarkedSchema = { type: 'string', [ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG]: true };

A GenericObjectType, such as a value isObject() narrows, has unknown values, so read a schema through isSchemaObject() instead, and in a function generic over S, cast what mergeObjects() or mergeSchemas() return to S:

-if (isObject(schema)) { const { properties } = schema; … }
+if (isSchemaObject(schema)) { const { properties } = schema; … }
-const merged: S = mergeSchemas(a, b);
+const merged = mergeSchemas(a, b) as S;

A value of an interface type no longer fits a GenericObjectType, such as the mui option, since an interface has no implicit index signature. Spread it, or declare its type with type:

-const uiSchema: UiSchema = { 'ui:options': { mui: slotProps } };
+const uiSchema: UiSchema = { 'ui:options': { mui: { ...slotProps } } };

RJSFMarkedSchema has no index signature and its markers are unknown BREAKING CHANGE​

RJSFMarkedSchema no longer has an index signature for other keys, so marked['foo'] is a TS7053 error ("Element implicitly has an 'any' type"). A keyword of JSONSchema7 or one of the later-draft, OpenAPI and Ajv keywords @rjsf/utils declares, such as marked.$defs, still reads with its type; for a keyword of your own, such as marked['x-custom'], declare it on JSONSchema7 as any members of the public types are specific types shows for RJSFSchema. A marker's value is unknown, so const added: boolean | string = marked[ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG] is a TS2322 error. Read a marker with hasSchemaMarker(), which also returns false for a boolean subschema:

-const added: boolean | string = marked[ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG];
+const added = hasSchemaMarker(marked, ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG);

hasSchemaMarker() takes only the markers that hold a flag, and says whether one is set. Read the value of any other marker, such as the $ref RJSF_REF_KEY holds, by indexing an RJSFMarkedSchema: marked[RJSF_REF_KEY] is unknown, so it has to be narrowed before use. On a schema of another type, Reflect.get(schema, RJSF_REF_KEY), behind an object check, returns any, since the type doesn't declare the key, so give the result the type unknown. Write a marker with Reflect.set().

ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG counts only when set to a truthy value BREAKING CHANGE​

In 6.x, WrapIfAdditionalTemplate, in @rjsf/core and every theme, and the label SchemaField picked read ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG by its presence, while the rest of RJSF read it by its value. So a schema with the flag set to undefined or false, such as { ...schema, [ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG]: false }, drew a key input and remove button and was labelled by its key, but was otherwise a declared property. Those reads now take the flag's value too, so such a field renders as a plain declared field, with no key input or remove button, labelled by its title where it has one.

Setting the flag to true brings the key input back, but makes the field an additional property everywhere else as well: its uiSchema is read from uiSchema.additionalProperties rather than uiSchema[key], under constAsDefaults: 'always' the computed defaults drop it where the object's const doesn't name its key, omitExtraData drops it, and getDisplayLabel() gives an object or array field a label. Set it to true only for a field that is an additional property; otherwise leave it out:

-const extra = { ...schema, [ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG]: false };
+const extra = schema;

A custom template that tests ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG in schema still draws a key input and remove button for a field whose flag is falsy, unlike the templates RJSF ships. Read the flag with hasSchemaMarker() to match them:

-const additional = ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG in schema;
+const additional = hasSchemaMarker(schema, ADDITIONAL_PROPERTY_FLAG);

createPrecompiledValidator() returns its validator class BREAKING CHANGE​

createPrecompiledValidator() returns its class, AJV8PrecompiledValidator from @rjsf/validator-ajv8 or ATAPrecompiledValidator from @rjsf/validator-ata, where it returned ValidatorType. A variable or state it initializes takes that class as its type, so assigning it another validator, such as one from customizeValidator(), no longer type-checks: the other validator lacks the precompiled one's rootSchema, validateFns and other members. Annotate the variable as ValidatorType<S, F>, or pass it as useState<ValidatorType>()'s type argument. That types its rawValidation() errors as unknown[] again, rather than ErrorObject[]:

-let validator = createPrecompiledValidator(validateFns, schema);
+let validator: ValidatorType = createPrecompiledValidator(validateFns, schema);
 validator = customizeValidator();

A localizer gets quoted property names from a precompiled or ata validator BREAKING CHANGE​

A localizer handed to createPrecompiledValidator() from @rjsf/validator-ajv8, or to customizeValidator() or createPrecompiledValidator() from @rjsf/validator-ata, now gets each property name in the missingProperty and property params of an error quoted, such as 'foo' where it got foo, as customizeValidator() from @rjsf/validator-ajv8 already did; for @rjsf/validator-ajv8, so is each name in deps. The quotes let these validators replace the name in a localized message with the property's title or ui:title. A property with no title keeps its key, now quoted, so with ajv-i18n's Spanish messages a missing untitled foo reads debe tener la propiedad requerida 'foo' where it read debe tener la propiedad requerida foo; update the snapshots that hold such messages. A localizer that looks a property up by its param, such as in a map of labels, strips the quotes first:

-error.message = labels[error.params.missingProperty];
+error.message = labels[error.params.missingProperty.slice(1, -1)];

The localizer gets copies of the errors, and only the message it sets on each is kept. The errors that rawValidation() returns keep their params unquoted.

ValidatorType and customizeValidator() take the schema as their first type argument BREAKING CHANGE​

ValidatorType<S, F> puts the form data type on validateFormData<T>(), since a validator checks data of any shape against a schema. import validator from '@rjsf/validator-ajv8' (and the same export from @rjsf/validator-ata and @rjsf/validator-cfworker) fits every Form, and customizeValidator() takes only <S, F>:

-const validator = customizeValidator<MyData>();
+const validator = customizeValidator();

 <Form<MyData> schema={schema} validator={validator} />

The first type argument is now the schema type, so a leftover customizeValidator<MyData>() or ValidatorType<MyData> does not always fail where it is declared. If MyData shares no keys with JSONSchema7, the declaration is the error (TS2559: Type 'MyData' has no properties in common with type 'JSONSchema7'). A shared key of a conflicting type fails at the declaration too (TS2344: Type 'MyData' does not satisfy the constraint 'JSONSchema7'). Otherwise (a title: string, say) the declaration compiles with the schema typed as MyData: a Form that infers its types from it reports the mismatch on its schema prop (TS2322: Type 'RJSFSchema' is not assignable to type …, or TS2741: Property '…' is missing in type 'RJSFSchema' when MyData also has a required key that JSONSchema7 lacks), and a Form<MyData> may not report it at all, since the validator's methods are checked bivariantly. In every case, drop the type argument.

BaseInputTemplate puts multiple only on a file input BREAKING CHANGE​

ArrayField passes multiple to the widget of every multi-select, whatever widget ui:widget names, and a BaseInputTemplate can't tell that multiple from one a widget passes on purpose. Every theme's BaseInputTemplate now puts multiple on a file input only. Before, core and daisyui put it on any input, and react-bootstrap and shadcn put a multiple in extraProps on any input, so an email input took a comma-separated list of addresses.

A widget that wants an email input to take several addresses renders the <input> itself rather than the registry's BaseInputTemplate, and so carries what the template did for it: the name, the disabled, readonly and required state, ui:emptyValue for a cleared input, the onBlur and onFocus that drive blur validation, and the ARIA attributes of getControlAttributes():

-return <BaseInputTemplate {...props} type='email' multiple />;
+const { id, htmlName, value, disabled, readonly, required, autofocus, options, onChange, onBlur, onFocus } = props;
+return (
+  <input
+    id={id}
+    name={htmlName || id}
+    type='email'
+    multiple
+    value={toInputValue(value)}
+    disabled={disabled}
+    readOnly={readonly}
+    required={required}
+    autoFocus={autofocus}
+    onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value === '' ? options.emptyValue : e.target.value)}
+    onBlur={(e) => onBlur(id, e.target.value)}
+    onFocus={(e) => onFocus(id, e.target.value)}
+    {...getControlAttributes(props)}
+  />
+);

It leaves out the theme's styling, the examples list and the clear button, which a widget that needs them renders too.

@rjsf/daisyui ignores a size, color or colorGradient of another type BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/daisyui's RatingWidget and ToggleWidget read a size or color option only as a string, trimmed, and fall back to the default for any other or a blank one, so size: 5 no longer gives a toggle-5 or rating-5 class. RatingWidget draws its color gradient only for a colorGradient of true, where any truthy value, such as 1, 'true' or even 'false', drew it. Write the options with those types:

- 'ui:options': { size: 5, colorGradient: 'true' },
+ 'ui:options': { size: '5', colorGradient: true },

AltDateWidget uses the default years for a yearsRange reaching before 100 BREAKING CHANGE​

useAltDateWidgetProps(), and so the AltDateWidget of @rjsf/core (which most themes fall back to), @rjsf/antd, @rjsf/chakra-ui and @rjsf/mantine, show the default years, 1900 to two years from now, for a yearsRange whose years reach before 100 or after 9999, once a relative range is counted back from the current year. They offered such a range as given, but wrote a year before 100 as 19xx, since Date.UTC() reads 0-99 that way. A range such as [50, 2030] now loses its own years as a whole, so a stored year outside the default ones, such as 1500, shows as blank. Start the range at 100 or later to keep its years:

- 'ui:options': { yearsRange: [50, 2030] },
+ 'ui:options': { yearsRange: [100, 2030] },

withTheme() returns a ThemedForm BREAKING CHANGE​

withTheme() returns the new ThemedForm<T, S, F> rather than ComponentType<FormProps<T, S, F>>: a function component that is generic over the form data like Form, so a theme's default Form export infers T from formData or takes it as <Form<MyData> />. The Theme, Templates and Widgets exports keep each component's own generic type, so withTheme<MyData>(Theme) and { ...Templates, FieldTemplate: MyFieldTemplate } typecheck for any T. generateForm<T, S, F>() and generateTheme<T, S, F>() still exist for pinning the types up front. An existing ComponentType<FormProps<…>> annotation of the return value still compiles, but it fixes T again; drop it to keep the per-use inference. Since ThemedForm is a plain generic function type, setting or reading component statics such as displayName on the return value no longer type-checks.

ErrorSchema<T> and FormValidation<T> node shapes BREAKING CHANGE​

ErrorSchema<T> and FormValidation<T> now describe the tree that toErrorSchema() and createErrorHandler() actually build. Previously they resolved to the wrong shape for anything but a plain object: a leaf field's node resolved to that field's own type, an array's node to an array rather than a node keyed by index, and ErrorSchema<any> to an index signature that no concrete error schema was assignable to. In practice a typed error schema never type-checked.

There are two things to do.

Drop the casts you used to work around the old shapes. The value type-checks on its own now:

-const extraErrors = { name: { __errors: ['too short'] } } as unknown as ErrorSchema;
+const extraErrors: ErrorSchema<FormData> = { name: { __errors: ['too short'] } };

Reach into nodes with ?.. Every node is optional, because the tree only contains the fields that actually have errors:

-errors.address.city.addError('unknown city');
+errors.address?.city?.addError('unknown city');

For reference, this is the shape a typed error schema now accepts — a node per field, keyed by index for arrays, with no children below a leaf:

type FormData = { name: string; address?: { city: string }; tags: string[] };

const errors: ErrorSchema<FormData> = {
  __errors: ['form-level problem'],
  name: { __errors: ['too short'] },
  address: { city: { __errors: ['unknown city'] } },
  tags: { 0: { __errors: ['not allowed'] } },
};

A field whose type is a union — what a oneOf/anyOf property gives you — accepts the children of every member it can hold, since which one is present depends on the current value:

type FormData = { thing: string | { city: string } };

const errors: ErrorSchema<FormData> = { thing: { city: { __errors: ['unknown city'] } } };

FormValidation<T>, the tree a customValidate function receives, is the same tree with addError() on every node.

In full, the children a node accepts are decided by the type of the data it describes:

Field's typeChildren of its error node
An objectA node per property
An arrayA node per index, keyed as 0, 1, …
A tupleA node per position, each of that position's own type
A tuple with a rest elementIts declared positions as above, the rest as an array's are
A primitive (string, number, boolean)None — a leaf holds only __errors
Date or FileNone — an object holding no form fields
A unionThe children of every member
any or unknownUnconstrained

An optional property is described by the type it holds, so address?: { city: string } gets the same node as address: { city: string }. Any other class instance used as a field value (a Money or LatLng value object, say) is treated as an object, so its properties are accepted as children even though nothing produces errors for them.

If you leave T at its default (unknown) and never annotate an error schema, nothing changes for you.

An array field's node is never an array, which the numeric index signature used to let through, so a typed error schema keys the items by index:

-const extraErrors: ErrorSchema<FormData> = { tags: [{ __errors: ['not allowed'] }] };
+const extraErrors: ErrorSchema<FormData> = { tags: { 0: { __errors: ['not allowed'] } } };

A field typed as a union of an array and an object with its own length field, such as { length: number } | string[], still accepts an array as its node, since that length field can hold errors.

The array is rejected through a length key on an array field's node that can hold nothing, so that key shows through: keyof of such a node includes length, editors offer it in autocompletion, and Required<> of the node asks for a length no value can supply.

An array of item errors is keyed by index BREAKING CHANGE​

An extraErrors, a field's raise or a customValidate result that holds an array for the items of an array field, which an untyped error schema still accepts, is handled as the object keyed by index, so its errors are listed, block the submit and reach onError. The errorSchema passed to onChange, onSubmit and the templates keys those items by index as well, so code that reads such a node as an array (errorSchema.tags.map(...), .length) has to read it by index instead (#3827).

extraErrors now blocks submission by default BREAKING CHANGE​

FormProps.extraErrorsBlockSubmit has been replaced with FormProps.extraErrorsAreWarnings, and the default behavior is inverted: extraErrors now block form submission by default, the same as JSON Schema validation errors.

If you were relying on the old default (extraErrors displayed but non-blocking), set extraErrorsAreWarnings to true. If you were setting extraErrorsBlockSubmit to true to get blocking behavior, remove the prop entirely — that is now the default.

If your app sets extraErrors from a failed server response (the async validation pattern above) and leaves it populated afterward, resubmitting the form will now re-block on those same stale errors and call onError again, since every submit re-merges whatever extraErrors is currently set to. Clear extraErrors (e.g. back to {}) when the user edits the form or before they resubmit, the same way you'd clear a schema validation error.

Removal of the experimental_/Experimental_ prefix BREAKING CHANGE​

The features below were marked experimental while their API stabilized. They are no longer experimental in v7, and the prefix has been dropped from their names:

Old nameNew name
FormProps.experimental_defaultFormStateBehaviorFormProps.defaultFormStateBehavior
FormProps.experimental_customMergeAllOfFormProps.customMergeAllOf
Experimental_DefaultFormStateBehavior (type, @rjsf/utils)DefaultFormStateBehavior
Experimental_ArrayMinItems (type, @rjsf/utils)ArrayMinItems
Experimental_CustomMergeAllOf (type, @rjsf/utils)CustomMergeAllOf

The corresponding experimental_defaultFormStateBehavior/experimental_customMergeAllOf parameters on the @rjsf/utils schema functions (e.g. getDefaultFormState, retrieveSchema, createSchemaUtils, and others) were renamed the same way, and are now members of the SchemaContext those functions take; see @rjsf/utils schema functions take a SchemaContext in place of the validator. Update any code that names these props, types, or parameters explicitly.

time/date-time formats now require a timezone offset BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/validator-ajv8 now depends on ajv-formats 3.x instead of 2.x. Per RFC 3339, ajv-formats 3 requires the JSON Schema time format to include a timezone offset (Z, or +HH:MM/-HH:MM); previously the offset was optional for time alone. date-time already required an offset in ajv-formats 2.x, so it's unaffected by this change. This closes #3930, where format: "time" values produced by RJSF were not spec-compliant.

  • @rjsf/core's TimeWidget (used for format: "time", and the equivalent TimeWidget in @rjsf/daisyui and @rjsf/mantine) now appends the browser's local UTC offset to the value whenever it's changed, e.g. 14:30:00-04:00 instead of 14:30:00. The offset is stripped back off when displaying a value in the native time input. format: "date-time"/alt-datetime were already emitting Z-suffixed UTC strings and are unaffected.
  • If you have previously-stored formData for a format: "time" field that lacks a timezone offset, it will now fail validation. Options:
    • Let the widget resave the value the next time a user edits that field — it will pick up the offset automatically. Note this reinterprets the wall-clock value in the browser's current local offset, so if the stored value already carried a different offset (e.g. entered in another timezone), resaving it will represent a different instant rather than preserving the original one.
    • Backfill stored data with an explicit offset (e.g. treat legacy values as UTC and append Z).
    • If you need to keep accepting offset-less values for a given field, change that field's schema to format: "iso-time"/format: "iso-date-time" instead of format: "time"/format: "date-time" — ajv-formats 3 added these as an explicit, optional-timezone escape hatch for validation. RJSF maps both to the same widget used for time/date-time (TimeWidget/DateTimeWidget, including the dedicated DateTimeWidgets in @rjsf/antd and @rjsf/daisyui), and doesn't add a timezone offset for those formats, so committed values keep behaving like format: "time"/format: "date-time" did before this release. A stored value that happens to carry an offset anyway is still stripped for display, since the underlying date/time picker can't render one either way.

UiSchema<T> checks field names BREAKING CHANGE​

UiSchema<T> used to intersect GenericObjectType (Record<string, any>), so any string key was accepted. The per-field entries are now a mapped type over T, which means a field name that isn't in the form data is a compile error:

type FormData = { firstName: string; address: { city: string } };

const uiSchema: UiSchema<FormData> = {
  firstName: { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' },
  address: { city: { 'ui:placeholder': 'City' } },
  lastName: { 'ui:widget': 'text' }, // error: `lastName` is not a field of FormData
};

FormProps already infers T from formData, so a form with typed form data gets this without naming the type anywhere.

What has not changed:

  • Untyped uiSchemas. UiSchema with no type argument, or with any form data, accepts the same keys as before — arbitrary nesting included. Reading a nested entry back gives unknown, and with no type argument a function under additionalProperties gets unknown data; see any members of the public types are specific types.
  • The ui: namespace. Any ui:-prefixed key is still accepted at every level, so theme-specific and application-specific directives keep working, except on an object whose data is a Record<string, V> with a V that can't hold every value, such as Record<string, string>: its uiSchema reads every key as an entry of the data, so it rejects the ui: keys. Form infers T from initialFormData, so <Form initialFormData={data} uiSchema={{ 'ui:order': ['a'] }} /> with data: Record<string, string> is a TS2322 error. Give the form the wider type, <Form<Record<string, unknown>> initialFormData={data} uiSchema={{ 'ui:order': ['a'] }} />, or the same for that object in a larger T.
  • oneOf/anyOf fields. A union-typed field accepts the keys of every branch, since which branch is present depends on the current value.

What to fix, if any of it affects you:

  • A uiSchema that names a field absent from T — a property added by a dependencies subschema, or an additionalProperties key when T has no index signature. Declare the field in T, as an optional property where it isn't always there, or nest the entry under the additionalProperties key described below. An index signature of unknown values ({ [key: string]: unknown } on the relevant object) also compiles, but it turns off the checking of that object's entries, the declared fields included, so a typo such as name: { 'ui:wigdet': 'textarea' } is no longer caught.
  • Keys the old index signature accepted silently are now declared, with types: additionalProperties (a uiSchema for the data the index signature of T holds, or for unknown data when T has none), additionalItems (a uiSchema for the array's element type), anyOf and oneOf (positional lists, one uiSchema per subschema), and the legacy unprefixed classNames (a string; ui:classNames is the prefixed spelling of the same thing). If you passed an object where a positional list is expected — oneOf: { 'ui:title': '...' } — it was already ignored at runtime, with a console warning; it is now also a type error.
  • A form data field named classNames, anyOf or oneOf cannot be given a per-field entry, because the entry's type is intersected with the declared key's type and a string or a list has nothing in common with a uiSchema. This makes a runtime limitation visible rather than adding one: SchemaField consumes and deletes classNames from every uiSchema it receives, and anyOf/oneOf are read as positional lists wherever the schema has that keyword, so such a field's uiSchema was never reliably delivered. Rename the field, or configure it through ui:options on the parent. A field named items, additionalItems or additionalProperties is fine: those keys hold a uiSchema, so the intersection accepts the per-field entry.
  • A self-referential form data type (type TreeNode = { children: TreeNode[] }) nested far enough in one uiSchema literal can exhaust the type checker (Excessive stack depth comparing types), since the per-field entries recurse with the data. Annotate the deep sub-entry as plain UiSchema to stop the recursion there.
  • A uiSchema typed by an interface you declared is rejected, because an interface has no index signature and UiSchema requires one for its ui: keys. This is not new — the ui:${string} signature predates this change — but the field-name checking makes it easier to hit. Use a type alias, or annotate the literal with UiSchema<T> directly.

ui:options types the options RJSF's widgets read BREAKING CHANGE​

UiSchema and UIOptionsType now declare eight options that RJSF's widgets read, each with the type its readers use, in both the ui:options and ui:<name> spellings. They were any before.

OptionType
acceptstring
expandableboolean
format'DMY' | 'MDY' | 'YMD'
hideClearButton, hideNowButtonboolean
shape'star' | 'heart'
starsnumber
yearsRangereadonly [number, number]

Nothing changes at runtime. What to fix, if the compiler flags it:

  • A custom widget that uses one of these names with another type, such as ui:format: { ... }, no longer compiles, and reading options.format gives the type above. Rename your option:

    - 'ui:options': { format: { currency: 'USD' } },
    + 'ui:options': { moneyFormat: { currency: 'USD' } },

  • A uiSchema held in an unannotated variable infers yearsRange: [2000, 2030] as number[] and shape: 'heart' as string, which no longer fit. Annotate the variable, or mark those values as const. Marking the whole uiSchema as const also makes arrays such as ui:order and ui:enumNames read-only, which don't fit:

    - const uiSchema = { 'ui:options': { yearsRange: [2000, 2030] } };
    + const uiSchema: UiSchema = { 'ui:options': { yearsRange: [2000, 2030] } };

  • A custom alt-date widget that passes on a date element's range or options.yearsRange, both now readonly [number, number], no longer compiles against a parameter typed [number, number]. Mark the parameter readonly, or destructure the range as @rjsf/mantine's AltDateWidget does:

    - function yearOptions(range: [number, number]) {
    + function yearOptions(range: readonly [number, number]) {

RatingWidget stars run from minimum to maximum BREAKING CHANGE​

RatingWidget, in @rjsf/core, which every theme but daisyui renders, and in @rjsf/daisyui's own copy, read maximum as a count of stars and ignored stars when maximum was set. It now reads maximum as the last value a star can have, and stars, still 5 by default and at most 5, as the most stars it draws. Fields like these draw different stars:

Schema and optionsStars beforeStars now
maximum: 30, 1, 20, 1, 2, 3
minimum: 3, maximum: 53, 4, 5, 6, 73, 4, 5
maximum: 00, 1, 2, 3, 40
minimum: 1, maximum: 5, stars: 31, 2, 3, 4, 51, 2, 3

To keep the stars you had, set the bounds to the values you want drawn, and drop a stars option smaller than the range:

- { type: 'integer', maximum: 3 }
+ { type: 'integer', minimum: 0, maximum: 2 }
- 'ui:options': { stars: 3 },

For maximum: 3, lowering the bound also rejects a stored 3. To keep that value valid, leave the schema as it is and cap the stars instead:

+ 'ui:options': { stars: 3 },

UiSchemaDefinitions drops its T parameter BREAKING CHANGE​

UiSchemaDefinitions<S, F> no longer takes the form data type, and types every entry as UiSchema<unknown, S, F>. UiSchema's own ui:definitions key uses the same type. A definition applies to whichever field references it, so typing it by the root form's data rejected the nested keys of the field it describes.

-const definitions: UiSchemaDefinitions<MyFormData, RJSFSchema, MyContext> = { ... };
+const definitions: UiSchemaDefinitions<RJSFSchema, MyContext> = { ... };

A leftover three-argument UiSchemaDefinitions<MyFormData, RJSFSchema, MyContext> fails with TS2707 (too many type arguments). A one- or two-argument UiSchemaDefinitions<MyFormData> or UiSchemaDefinitions<MyFormData, RJSFSchema> binds MyFormData to the schema type S: it may compile, or fail with a TS2559 that doesn't mention the dropped parameter. Drop the form data argument in every case.

@rjsf/mantine's onChangeOverride now receives the change event BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/mantine's BaseInputTemplate routed onChange and onChangeOverride through a single variable and handed the value to both, so an onChangeOverride received the input's string value. Every other theme, and @rjsf/core's own BaseInputTemplate, pass it the raw ChangeEvent — which is also what WidgetProps['onChangeOverride'] has always declared.

onChangeOverride now receives the ChangeEvent with this theme too. If you pass one to a @rjsf/mantine widget, read the value off the event:

// Before
const onChangeOverride = (value: string) => setSomething(value);

// After
const onChangeOverride = (event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => setSomething(event.target.value);

A numeric field with an onChangeOverride now renders Mantine's TextInput rather than its NumberInput, which reports only the parsed value and never an event. The input keeps type="number" (@rjsf/core's <input> no longer does, see below); the override is what handles the input in that case, so the stepper controls and number formatting it replaces have nothing to drive.

Note that @rjsf/core applies ui:emptyValue for you when the input is cleared; an onChangeOverride bypasses onChange entirely, so handle an empty string yourself if you need that behaviour.

@rjsf/mantine's SelectWidget keeps its value under a schema default BREAKING CHANGE​

A single SelectWidget whose schema has a default no longer clears its value when its selected option is clicked again, as the other themes leave out their empty option under a default, so an anyOf/oneOf field's option selector can't be cleared to no option and drop the field's data (#5527). To let such a field be cleared, set allowDeselect or clearable in its ui:options.

@rjsf/mantine's ColorWidget reads colorFormat instead of format BREAKING CHANGE​

ColorWidget used to read ui:options.format for ColorInput's format, the name the alt-date widgets read for their order of date parts. It now reads colorFormat, and format has no effect on it. Without a colorFormat, ColorInput uses Mantine's default or your theme's.

A typed uiSchema stops compiling, since format only takes a date order. An untyped one, such as a uiSchema loaded as JSON, gives no error and the color silently goes back to that default, so search for it there too, in both its ui:options.format and ui:format spellings:

  color: {
-   'ui:options': { format: 'rgba' },
+   'ui:options': { colorFormat: 'rgba' },
  },

@rjsf/mantine's AltDateWidget renders its date parts through SelectWidget BREAKING CHANGE​

Each date part of @rjsf/mantine's AltDateWidget (and AltDateTimeWidget) is rendered by the registry's SelectWidget, through DateElement, as in the other themes, rather than by a Mantine Select of its own (#5503). A replacement SelectWidget now renders the date parts too, so it must name and describe them as the other themes' parts need. As in the other themes, a part is no longer required when its field is, since a native select that is required blocks the submit of a date picked only in part. Each part is handed the options of Mantine's Select, searchable, allowDeselect, size, success, inputContainer and wrapperProps, beside the part's enumOptions, so one that spreads its options onto an element should leave those out. Each part's hidden input, which a native form submission reads, holds the index of the picked option, as SelectWidget encodes it, rather than its number, as in the other themes: January submits root__month=0 rather than root__month=1. Read the date from rjsf's formData instead. A month, day, hour, minute or second shows two digits, as in the other themes, so a test that picks or reads a part's option by its text changes:

-await user.click(screen.getByRole('option', { name: '1' }));
+await user.click(screen.getByRole('option', { name: '01' }));

@rjsf/antd's onChangeOverride is now called for a numeric field BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/antd's BaseInputTemplate wired its InputNumber branch straight to onChange. InputNumber reports only the parsed value and never an event, so an onChangeOverride on a numeric field was never called at all.

A numeric field with an onChangeOverride now renders the Input branch (still type="number") so the override receives the ChangeEvent, as WidgetProps['onChangeOverride'] declares and as every other theme does. That field loses InputNumber's stepper controls and formatting, which the override replaces anyway; a numeric field without an onChangeOverride still renders InputNumber as before.

@rjsf/antd's GridTemplate reads a column's span as twelfths BREAKING CHANGE​

A layout grid's span now counts twelfths of a row in every theme, so @rjsf/antd's GridTemplate doubles a column's span into antd's 24 columns rather than handing it to Col as is. A ui:col or ui:columns written with antd's span now spans twice as much: span: 12, half a row before, is a whole row. Halve each span; an odd number becomes a half step, which antd's 24 columns still lay out exactly:

 'ui:row': {
   children: [
-    { 'ui:col': { span: 9, children: ['address'] } },
-    { 'ui:col': { span: 15, children: ['employment'] } },
+    { 'ui:col': { span: 4.5, children: ['address'] } },
+    { 'ui:col': { span: 7.5, children: ['employment'] } },
   ],
 },

A column whose span is more than 12, which only an unmigrated one can be, logs a warning saying to halve it. One of 12 or under can't be told apart from a migrated one, so check those yourself. A column with a flex prop or a flex, flexBasis or width style of its own now keeps that width and drops its span, logging a warning that the span is ignored, where before Col was handed both. antd's breakpoint props, such as xs or md, still take antd's 24ths. See span in each theme.

@rjsf/antd starts an object and an array heading, and labelAlign aligns field labels too BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects a form that renders an object or an array with a title through @rjsf/antd, and a form that sets formContext.labelAlign. ObjectFieldTemplate and ArrayFieldTemplate ended the heading of an object or an array by default, away from the fields it heads, whose labels sit above their controls at the start. The heading now starts its column, on the same side as those labels.

A form whose formContext.labelCol has a span and an xl that aren't 24, such as { span: 8 } for a horizontal form, and that sets no labelAlign, keeps its headings at the end: antd ends the labels of a column that narrow, and the headings follow them. On a screen up to screenXSMax wide, 575px by default, antd starts every field label whatever labelCol says, so there such a form keeps its headings at the end beside labels at the start.

labelAlign now reaches the labels too: the theme passes it to the Form.Item of every field and of an additional property's key, so 'start' and 'left' start them and 'end' and 'right' end them, where it used to move the headings only. It doesn't align the text of a CheckboxWidget, which the widget draws beside its box. In a standard horizontal form, where labelCol is narrower than 24 columns such as { span: 8 }, a labelAlign of 'start' or 'left' now starts the labels, which antd ends by default; 'end' and 'right' change nothing there. antd starts the label of a 24-column labelCol whatever labelAlign says, so under the default labelCol labelAlign moves the headings only. antd 6 logs a development warning for 'left' and 'right', which it deprecates for 'start' and 'end'. @rjsf/antd now needs antd 6.7 or newer, the first release to understand 'start' and 'end'. The theme reads labelAlign and labelCol from formContext for a heading, which can't see the labelAlign, labelCol or layout of an enclosing antd Form. A field's label gets the labelAlign and layout of an enclosing Form through antd's context, but not its labelCol, which the theme replaces with formContext.labelCol, { span: 24 } by default.

To keep a heading at the end in a form without such a labelCol, set labelAlign to 'end'. Under a labelCol of 24 columns this ends the headings but not the labels, which antd starts there, so it brings back the old mismatch between a heading and the label of its fields:

-<Form schema={schema} validator={validator} />
+<Form schema={schema} validator={validator} formContext={{ labelAlign: 'end' }} />

A heading's column also gains the ant-form-item-label-start and ant-form-item-label-left classes and loses antd's end alignment, so a test or stylesheet that expected text-align: end on it, or that selected the heading's column without those classes, needs the same labelAlign.

A layout grid row without a column template lays out on 12 tracks in chakra-ui, fluentui-rc and shadcn BREAKING CHANGE​

So that a column's span lays out the same in every theme, a ui:row in @rjsf/chakra-ui, @rjsf/fluentui-rc or @rjsf/shadcn that has no column template of its own (templateColumns, templateAreas, columns, a gridTemplateColumns, gridTemplateAreas, gridTemplate or grid style, the same keys in chakra-ui's css, or a grid-cols-* class) now lays out on 12 tracks, and each child is full width unless it spans fewer. A row that relied on the grid placing its children by itself, such as a chakra-ui row with autoFlow: 'column', a fluentui-rc row with rows but no columns, or a shadcn row with grid-flow-col, now stacks them. Give such a row its template to keep the old layout:

 'ui:row': {
+  templateColumns: 'repeat(3, 1fr)',
   autoFlow: 'column',
   children: ['first', 'middle', 'last'],
 },

A custom GridTemplate is handed a fieldId BREAKING CHANGE​

LayoutGridField now hands every GridTemplate a fieldId, so a theme can name the column in the warnings it logs about a span. A column gets the id of the first field it holds; a row, or a column holding no field of its own, gets the id of the field whose layout grid holds it. A custom GridTemplate that spreads its props onto an element would put fieldId on it, and React warns about the unknown prop. Take it off first:

 function GridTemplate(props: GridTemplateProps) {
-  const { children, column, ...rest } = props;
+  const { children, column, fieldId, ...rest } = props;
   return <div {...rest}>{children}</div>;
 }

To log the same span warnings as the built-in themes, hand fieldId to logGridSpanWarning() along with the column's span.

A row's span no longer reaches GridTemplate either: it only ever sized a column, and LayoutGridField now warns about it on a row and keeps it back.

Field identity is a FieldPath string instead of a FieldPathId object BREAKING CHANGE​

Every field, template and widget used to receive a fieldPathId prop, an object { $id, path, name? } rebuilt on every render. Because it was a new object each time, it defeated React.memo at every level and forced deep comparison of props to compensate. Field identity is now two primitive strings:

  • fieldPath: a FieldPath such as friends[0].firstName, telling where the data lives. It drives onChange writes. Property names are separated by ., array indexes are bracketed, and \ . [ ] inside a property name are backslash-escaped, so it stays unambiguous when property names contain dots or brackets. The root form is the empty string, exported as ROOT_FIELD_PATH.
  • id: the DOM id such as root_friends_0_firstName, telling what the element is called. It drives htmlFor, focus and accessibility attributes. Some ids differ from v6, as Ids can't collide or split an id list describes. The optional-data controls (enableOptionalDataFieldForType) of an object with properties of its own or room for more keys beside its oneOf/anyOf take the id of the component rendered beside the options, and the selected option draws none, where v6 drew a second set for it under the same DOM id.

FieldProps and FieldTemplateProps receive both. Every other template that received fieldPathId (ArrayFieldTemplate, ArrayFieldTitleTemplate, ArrayFieldDescriptionTemplate, ArrayFieldItemButtonsTemplate, CyclicSchemaExpandTemplate, FieldErrorTemplate, FieldHelpTemplate, ObjectFieldTemplate, UnsupportedFieldTemplate) now receives id instead. The childFieldPathId prop on ObjectField/ArrayField is gone, since fieldPath is always a truthful data address. IChangeEvent and FormState no longer carry fieldPathId either, so an onChange(e)/onSubmit(e) handler that read e.fieldPathId must derive what it needs some other way — the root form's id is idPrefix, and e.schemaUtils, e.formData and e.errorSchema are unchanged.

-const { fieldPathId } = props;
-<label htmlFor={fieldPathId.$id}>
-<h2 id={titleId(fieldPathId)}>
+const { id } = props;
+<label htmlFor={id}>
+<h2 id={titleId(id)}>

The id helpers titleId(), descriptionId(), helpId(), errorId(), examplesId(), buttonId() and optionalControlsId() accept only a string id.

FieldProps['onChange'] carries the FieldPath string instead of a FieldPathList; fields forward the fieldPath prop they already hold:

-onChange(newValue, fieldPathId.path, ownErrors, fieldPathId.$id);
+onChange(newValue, fieldPath, ownErrors, id);

ownErrors stands for the errors the field itself raises, not the errorSchema prop it was given: see "The errorSchema passed to onChange holds only the field's own errors" below.

toFieldPathId() and the FieldPathId type are removed. Build paths with toFieldPath(segment, parentPath?) and derive what you need from them:

WasNow
toFieldPathId(name, options, parent)toFieldPath(name, parentFieldPath)
fieldPathId.$idid prop, or fieldPathToId(fieldPath, options)
fieldPathId.pathfieldPathToList(fieldPath)
fieldPathId.namefieldPathToName(fieldPath, options, isMulti)

FieldPath is a branded string, so a plain string (a DOM id, for example) is rejected by the compiler where a FieldPath is expected. A FieldPath is still assignable wherever a string is accepted.

The useDeepCompareMemo() hook is removed. It existed to hand out a stable fieldPathId object across renders; with two primitive strings there is nothing to stabilize. A custom field or widget that used it for its own props can use useMemo(), or compare the values it cares about directly.

Ids can't collide or split an id list BREAKING CHANGE​

Every id RJSF renders is built by @rjsf/utils: a field's own id by fieldPathToId(), and the id of an element that is part of a field, such as its description, a date part or the key input of an additional property, by partId(), which joins the field's id and the part's name with __. fieldPathToId() never writes a __ into a field's own id, so the id of one field's part can't be another field's id, it writes no whitespace, so a field id stays one id in aria-describedby, aria-labelledby and aria-controls (#5558), and every id is a CSS identifier as it stands, by the CSS Syntax 3 rules browsers ship, so #${id} selects the element in querySelector() and in a stylesheet with no escaping.

A property name is written into an id as it is, except for an escape. A character is written as an escape, -_ followed by the two uppercase hex digits of its code, when it is an ASCII character other than a letter, a digit, - or _, such as a space, ., :, /, #, [ or %; when it is an _ that begins or ends the name, stands next to another _ or follows a -; or when it is a - that ends the name. An empty name is written -_FF. Every other character, an _ or - inside a name such as snake_case or kebab-case and any non-ASCII letter included, is written as it is. The encoder writes -_ nowhere else, so every -_ starts an escape and two names never write the same id. A name such as firstName, first-name, snake_case_name or prénom keeps its v6 id.

These ids change:

Elementv6v7
Field whose property name holds whitespace, such as first nameroot_first nameroot_first-_20name
Field whose property name holds another character a CSS identifier can't hold unescaped, such as a.b, a:b or 100%root_a.b, root_a:b, root_100%root_a-_2Eb, root_a-_3Ab, root_100-_25
Field whose property name begins or ends with _, holds __ or -_, or ends with -, such as _id, __typename or a-root__id, root___typename, root_a-root_-_5Fid, root_-_5F-_5Ftypename, root_a-_2D
Field whose property name is ''root_root_-_FF
Date part of an AltDateWidget (#5504)root_when_yearroot_when__year
Radio or checkboxes option, from optionId()root_color-0root_color__0
Key input of an additional property, from the new additionalKeyId()root_foo-keyroot_foo__key
Expand button of a cyclic schema, from expandButtonId()root_child-buttonroot_child__expand
Component rendered beside anyOf/oneOf options, from the new besideOptionsId()root_pet_XxxOfroot_pet__XxxOf, and root_pet__XxxOf2 beside the options of an option that is itself an anyOf/oneOf
Option selector of an anyOf/oneOf option that is itself an anyOf/oneOf, from the new optionSelectorId() (#5574)root_pet__anyof_select, the same id as the selector above itroot_pet__anyof_select2
Type selector of the fallback UI for an unsupported type, from the new fallbackTypeSelectorId()root_x___internal_type_selector, and root.x.__internal_type_selector under idSeparator: '.'root_x__internalTypeSelector, root_x__internalTypeSelector2 for an option offering types of its own, and root.x__internalTypeSelector under idSeparator: '.'
@rjsf/daisyui's time input in the date-time picker popuproot_when-pickerroot_when__time
@rjsf/mantine's success messageroot_when-successroot_when__success
@rjsf/mantine's label and description of an input, an additional property's key input includedroot_when-label, root_when-description, root_foo-key-labelroot_when__wrapperLabel, root_when__wrapperDescription, root_foo__key__wrapperLabel
@rjsf/mui's label of a text input, a select or an additional property's key inputroot_when-label, root_foo-key-labelroot_when__inputLabel, root_foo__key__inputLabel
@rjsf/mui's helper text of a text input or select, from helperText in ui:options.muiroot_when-helper-textroot_when__helperText

Every field's control takes its id as its name too, unless the form sets a nameGenerator, so a field in the first four rows above posts under its new id, such as root_first-_20name rather than root_first name, and FormData.get('root_first name'), or server code reading the v6 name, gets null. A date part's name is its id, and so is the name of an additional property's key input in @rjsf/antd, @rjsf/chakra-ui, @rjsf/mantine and @rjsf/mui (root_foo-key in v6) and of a nested option selector, so each posts under its new id too, and code reading it from FormData or form.elements.namedItem(), or a test finding it by [name=...], should use the new id. A selector or test aimed at one of the v6 ids should aim at the v7 id, which #${id} selects as it is, such as #root_first-_20name. A custom widget or template rendering an element of its own beside a field's control, such as a popup or a second input, should take its id from partId(id, '<name>') rather than appending a suffix of its own, so it can't take another field's id either. Focus-on-error relies on it too: where no element has a field's id, it focuses the first input or button whose id is a part of the field's, so a widget whose controls take ids such as ${id}-0 is no longer focused for its field's error. One id is still derived by a library rather than built by RJSF: @rjsf/mantine's Select and MultiSelect name their listbox by the ${id}-label id Mantine gives their label, so that label keeps it, and a sibling property named such as color-label writes the same id.

The idPrefix and idSeparator are written into ids as given, so to keep ids CSS identifiers holding no __, each should hold only letters, digits, - and _, with no __ in either or where they meet. A property name holding the idSeparator still writes the id a path of several names would, as the name a_b and the path a.b, a property b of a property a, both write root_a_b, as in v6; choose an idSeparator no property name holds to tell those apart.

IChangeEvent members are read-only BREAKING CHANGE​

IChangeEvent, the event onChange and onSubmit receive, is now declared on its own instead of as a Pick of the Form's internal state, and every member is readonly. The members and their types are unchanged, except two. formData is now EventFormData<T>; see Generic defaults are unknown instead of any. And edit is gone: it only restated whether you had passed data, so check your props instead. Readonly modifiers do not affect assignability, so a handler that reads the event or passes it on compiles as before; only code that assigns into the event breaks:

// Before: compiled, and wrote into data the form shares with its parent
onChange={(event) => { event.formData = normalize(event.formData); setData(event.formData); }}

// After: copy out of the event into your own state
onChange={(event) => setData(normalize(event.formData))}

The modifier is shallow: it stops event.formData = ..., not a write inside formData. Treat the whole event as immutable, as the guide says for received form data above.

IChangeEvent has required dirty, dirtyFields, touched, touchedFields and submitCount, and FormRef a required getStatus() BREAKING CHANGE​

IChangeEvent, the event onChange and onSubmit receive, has five new required members, the form's status: dirty, dirtyFields, touched, touchedFields and submitCount (see Unsaved changes and Touched fields). FormRef has a new required method, getStatus(), which returns the same five.

This is only a breaking change if you build an IChangeEvent or a FormRef yourself, such as a wrapper component calling an onChange prop, a test fixture or a test double; code that only reads events or calls the handle is unaffected. Such an object fails to compile until it adds them:

-const event: IChangeEvent<MyData> = { ...rest };
+const event: IChangeEvent<MyData> = {
+  ...rest,
+  dirty: false,
+  dirtyFields: {},
+  touched: false,
+  touchedFields: {},
+  submitCount: 0,
+};

A stand-in for a FormRef likewise needs a getStatus() method returning { dirty, dirtyFields, touched, touchedFields, submitCount }.

ui:emptyValue extended scope BREAKING CHANGE​

ui:emptyValue used to only supply a value when a user actively cleared a field's widget. It now applies whenever the field is blank for any reason — on initial render, after a form reset, or when cleared — since getDefaultFormState() threads uiSchema through its defaults pipeline (computeDefaults()/getObjectDefaults()) to pick it up.

If a field has no formData and no schema.default, and you set ui:emptyValue for it, that field's formData will now be populated with the ui:emptyValue on first render and after a reset, instead of staying undefined (and being omitted from formData entirely) until the user clears it once. See ui:emptyValue.

Shallow comparison replaces experimental_componentUpdateStrategy BREAKING CHANGE​

Form and SchemaField now compare their props shallowly, as React.memo does, and keep the references of unchanged data across changes so that comparison is enough. The experimental_componentUpdateStrategy prop is removed, and with it shouldRender(), shallowEquals() and the ComponentUpdateStrategy type from @rjsf/utils.

What to change:

  • Remove the experimental_componentUpdateStrategy prop from <Form> and from any globalFormOptions read of it.
  • Give Form stable references for props that hold functions: customValidate, transformErrors, translateString, nameGenerator, customMergeAllOf, validator, fields, widgets, templates, formContext, and a uiSchema carrying components such as ui:widget. A value recreated on every render re-derives the form's state on every render, so wrap it in useCallback or useMemo, or define it outside the render function. A changed one now takes effect at once, where v6 ignored it until another prop changed; with liveValidate: 'onChange', a changed validator, customValidate, transformErrors, customMergeAllOf or schema also re-validates the current data. That re-validation, and the one setFieldValue('', data) triggers, validates with the schema resolved for the data whenever the schema utilities are unchanged (the same schema, validator, defaultFormStateBehavior and customMergeAllOf), the way an edit is validated; a replaced value shows the same live errors typing it would, and a miss that only the root schema reports (if/then, oneOf) shows on submit, as it does for typed data. uiSchema and formContext take effect in rendering at once, but a change to either re-validates only on the next data change, blur or submit, which matters if ui:required depends on state outside the form.
  • Treat the formData you receive from onChange, onBlur, onSubmit and the other callbacks as immutable. It shares unchanged subtrees with the previous value, the formData you passed included, so mutating it in place corrupts your own state. Copy before changing, as with any reducer.
  • Treat schemas returned by retrieveSchema() as immutable; it may return the same instance across calls.
  • Replace shouldRender(this, nextProps, nextState) in a class component's shouldComponentUpdate by extending PureComponent, which is the same comparison.
  • Replace shallowEquals with shallowEqual from fast-equals.

A type list follows its ui:widget to the field and class it renders BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects a schema whose type is a list and whose ui:widget belongs to another type it lists.

A list resolving to object or array used to ignore a ui:widget such as textarea: ['null', 'object', 'string'] rendered ObjectField, and ['array', 'string'] threw No widget 'textarea' for type 'array'. It now renders the field of the type that has the widget, here StringField, and fills in no defaults for the object's properties. A value that is already an object or an array stays in its own field, which ignores the widget. To keep the object or array field, remove the ui:widget:

 const uiSchema = {
-  note: { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' },
 };

resolveWidget() follows the same rule, so it returns TextareaWidget for those schemas rather than throwing.

The rjsf-field-<type> class now names the field rendered rather than the type the list resolves to: a textarea on a ['null', 'number', 'string'] is rjsf-field-string and a select over ['null', 'boolean', 'string'] is rjsf-field-string, where both were named for their first non-null type. Update a CSS rule or test that matches the old class.

A typeless oneOf/anyOf of constants now renders as a select BREAKING CHANGE​

A oneOf/anyOf whose options are all constants (const or a single-value enum) used to render as an unsupported field when the schema omitted type, because neither a field nor a widget could be resolved without one. SchemaField now infers the type from the constant values, so the select these schemas always described actually renders (#4666):

{
  "oneOf": [
    { "const": "gpl", "title": "GPL" },
    { "const": "mit", "title": "MIT" }
  ]
}

That includes object and array constants, which render through a select whose options are labelled with their title, or with their JSON when they have none, whether the schema omits type or declares type: 'object'/'array' (#5317). Object and array constants are given the type object/array, and a declared type is kept as declared, so custom fields, templates and widgets see the type of the value they choose. The select is rendered by StringField, which renders every other select, rather than by ObjectField/ArrayField, which edit a value's contents. An empty oneOf: []/anyOf: [] offers nothing to choose, so a typed object or array with one is still edited through ObjectField/ArrayField. getDefaultFormState() fills such a select as a whole too, the way it fills a primitive select: a required oneOf/anyOf select defaults to the constant its own default names, or else its first, honoring constAsDefaults (including skipOneOf), a required enum select is left unfilled, and a value already picked is kept as it is. An ancestor's default naming one of its constants picks that one, and ui:initialValue/ui:emptyValue apply to it as they do to a primitive select. Both used to get an empty {}/[] that no option allows, and a picked object could be blended with the select's default. A typed object/array whose constants are spelled as an enum ({ "type": "object", "enum": [{ "a": 1 }, { "a": 2 }] }) renders the same select, where it used to render an ObjectField with no control or an ArrayField list editor. omitExtraData(), sanitizeDataForNewSchema() and the ui:required check treat such a select's value as one constant rather than a container, so omitExtraData/liveOmit keep the picked object or array whole instead of pruning it to nothing, and switching to a schema whose select doesn't offer it clears it. Picking one sanitizes the data a condition on it controls, as picking a primitive option does, where it used to leave data only the old branch allowed. An array select offers the radio alias as well as select and hidden, and no longer the checkboxes or files aliases, which read the picked array as a list of selections; a multi-select array still has no radio. A select, spelled as an enum or a oneOf/anyOf of constants, whose type list names more than one non-null type renders through StringField, which keeps each option's value as it is, instead of through the field for the first listed type, which rendered NullField for a list starting with null and cast every option's value to a number for a list starting with number (so a true option wrote 1).

Most forms only gain the field they were already asking for. Three narrower shapes change behavior, and each is worth checking:

A schema with both anyOf and oneOf. optionsList() and the option selector read anyOf before oneOf, but isSelect(), sanitizeDataForNewSchema(), BooleanField, the LayoutGridField path (findFieldInSchema(), LayoutMultiSchemaField), the defaults getDefaultFormState() computes, the ui:required check, retrieveSchema()'s option resolution and getClosestMatchingOption()'s scoring of nested properties read oneOf first, so a schema carrying both keywords could render one list while deciding it was a select from the other — or throw schema cannot be inferred as a constant during render (#5309). Every one of them now reads anyOf first, through the new getXxxOfKey() utility (an empty anyOf: [] gives way to a non-empty oneOf), so a constant default comes from the anyOf options on screen and a ui:required field inside the rendered anyOf option is reported. The option selector follows: its id suffix is __anyof_select, where it used to say __oneof_select whenever a oneOf was present, and its options take their labels and per-option uiSchema from uiSchema.anyOf, where they used to come from uiSchema.oneOf. A schema with constant options under both keywords renders the anyOf options, and one whose anyOf options aren't all constants renders that anyOf's option selector, where it used to render a select of the oneOf constants. A schema with only one of the two keywords is unaffected.

What to change: give the two keywords the same options, or drop the redundant one.

A type: 'boolean' with labelled constant options. A checkbox shows no option labels, so a boolean whose oneOf/anyOf has more than one constant option, at least one of them labelled by its title or a ui:title in the matching uiSchema.oneOf/uiSchema.anyOf entry, now defaults to a select, the same widget its typeless spelling gets (#5309):

{
  "type": "boolean",
  "oneOf": [
    { "const": true, "title": "Yes" },
    { "const": false, "title": "No" }
  ]
}

The same goes for a nullable boolean ("type": ["boolean", "null"]) whose options include a null constant, which a checkbox has no state for, labelled or not. A single option, the usual way to spell a checkbox that must be checked, and unlabelled true/false options keep the checkbox. A custom field chosen by ui:field isn't handed that default: the uiSchema it receives has no ui:widget unless the caller set one. ui:field: 'BooleanField' still gets the select, and so does a field registered under the schema's $id, which keeps its label that way.

What to change: set "ui:widget": "checkbox" to keep the checkbox.

A typeless falsy const with constAsDefaults: 'never'. getSchemaType() returned undefined for a typeless schema whose const was falsy (0, false, '' or null), which is what rendered those as unsupported fields. A typeless { "const": null } now resolves to null and renders through NullField, exactly like an explicit { "type": "null" }.

At the default constAsDefaults setting nothing changes in the emitted data: such a property already contributed its constant as its own default. With defaultFormStateBehavior.constAsDefaults set to 'never', which suppresses that default, a typeless { "const": null } and a required typeless { "const": false } now write null and false into the form data on mount where nothing was written before — the first as the null default the form fills in for a type: 'null' value, the second from the required-boolean default. Each matches what the explicit type spelling already did. Required { "const": 0 } and { "const": "" } are unaffected.

What to change: nothing, if you want the two spellings to agree. If a form relied on those keys staying absent, drop the property from the schema instead of relying on it not rendering.

A boolean enum labels its values Yes/No BREAKING CHANGE​

A type: 'boolean' field labels every true and false in its enum that ui:enumNames doesn't name with the translated Yes/No, as it already labels untitled boolean constants (#5319). The labels are in the enumOptions it passes to whatever widget renders it, so a select, radios or a custom widget that reads options.enumOptions shows them. Only an unnamed two-value enum of true and false read Yes/No before, so "enum": [true] and a nullable "enum": [true, false, null] now read Yes, No and null where they read true, false and null. ui:enumOrder now orders a boolean's Yes/No options, those of a two-value enum and the implicit true and false of a plain { "type": "boolean" }, where it used to ignore them unless ui:enumNames was also set. As it does for any enum, the order drops a value it doesn't list unless it has '*', so "ui:enumOrder": [true] now leaves only Yes where it showed Yes and No, and an empty "ui:enumOrder": [] leaves no options at all. A constant option whose title is empty ("title": "") now has an empty label where it read Yes or No, since BooleanField reads its options through optionsList(), which keeps an empty title for every other type (#4448).

What to change: name the values with ui:enumNames to keep other labels, list both values or add '*' to a ui:enumOrder meant only to put one first, drop an empty ui:enumOrder, and drop an empty title to keep Yes or No. Update tests or DOM snapshots that match the option text true/false.

ui:enumOrder orders constant anyOf/oneOf options BREAKING CHANGE​

ui:enumOrder now orders the options of an anyOf or oneOf made entirely of constants, as it orders enum values, where 6.x ignored it there (#4298). As it does for an enum, the order drops a value it doesn't list unless it has '*', so a "ui:enumOrder": ["b"] left beside a constant oneOf of a, b and c now leaves only b. Options keep their schema order when any of them is read through a discriminator or ui:optionsSchemaSelector.

What to change: list every value, or add '*', to a ui:enumOrder beside constant options, or remove one that was never meant to apply.

EnumValue includes null, objects and arrays BREAKING CHANGE​

EnumValue, the type of the entries of ui:enumOrder, ui:enumDisabled and optgroups, is now string | number | boolean | null | object, where it was string | number | boolean (#5392). Code that writes those lists still compiles. Code that reads them, such as a custom widget reading options.enumDisabled, can now fail to compile where it treats an entry as a primitive.

What to change: handle null, objects and arrays where you read an EnumValue, or narrow it first. Remove a cast you added to list one of those values.

- const disabled = options.enumDisabled?.map((value) => value.toString());
+ const disabled = options.enumDisabled?.map((value) => enumOptionValueLabel(value));

enumOptionValueLabel() spells an object or array out as JSON, where String() would give [object Object] or join an array's items.

number/integer fields no longer render a native <input type="number"> by default BREAKING CHANGE​

A BaseInputTemplate now renders a number/integer field as <input type="text" inputMode="decimal|numeric" pattern="..."> instead of <input type="number">, avoiding the cross-browser keystroke-filtering, scroll-wheel, and locale decimal-separator quirks of a native number input. The pattern still blocks a non-numeric submission the same way required already does, and accepts the exponent notation JavaScript renders very small and very large numbers with. A number accepts either sign of exponent (1e-7, 1e+21); an integer is only ever rendered that way from 1e21 up and always with a +, so a negative exponent is rejected there rather than admitting 1e-7 where 0.0000001 is refused. The integer pattern accepts every spelling of a whole number the field itself produces while you type — a trailing separator and zeros (5., 5.00), and the fractional mantissa of the exponent form (String(2 ** 70) is 1.1805916207174113e+21) — while still refusing an actual fraction such as 1.5. Set ui:options.inputType: 'number', or use the updown widget, to keep a native number input for a field. See #4038.

A schema whose type is an array counts as a number/integer field when exactly one of its entries isn't "null", so ["number", "null"] and ["number"] both render the numeric text input — SchemaField already rendered them through NumberField, and they used to come back as a plain text input carrying min/max/step. A union of more than one non-null type, such as ["number", "string"], keeps the plain text input it had before. A schema with no type at all but a numeric const counts the same way, since that is the type SchemaField picks its field by.

step, min and max only constrain a native number input, so these fields no longer get them, and the browser no longer range- or step-checks the value before submit. minimum, maximum and multipleOf are still enforced by RJSF's own validation, which reports them as form errors. They are still returned when the field renders a native number input, through ui:options.inputType: 'number' or the updown widget, along with step="any" for a number field with no multipleOf so decimals are accepted (the updown widget did not get that step before).

Because the value lives in a text input with a pattern, native constraint validation can now block a submit whose value doesn't match, such as legacy server data like 'yo' loaded into a number field. When that happens onSubmit and onError never fire, and the browser shows its own message on the field instead of an RJSF error. If you want RJSF's validation to be the only validator, set noHtml5Validate on the Form.
