A pattern the value fails is reported by the browser as a bare "Please match the requested format", which says nothing on a field that now looks like a plain text box, so RJSF sets a title on the input for the browser to append to that message. The two strings go through translateString as TranslatableString.NumberInputTitle ("Enter a number") and TranslatableString.IntegerInputTitle ("Enter a whole number"); translate them as you do the rest. A BaseInputTemplate of your own that renders a plain <input> takes that title from getBaseInputProps(), which returns it beside the input props, and puts it before them. A pattern of your own replaces the derived one and takes the derived title with it, since that title describes a rule no longer in force: pass it as the pattern prop of BaseInputTemplate from a widget in any theme, through extraProps in shadcn and react-bootstrap, or through slotProps.htmlInput in mui. A title of your own reaches the input as a widget prop in core and daisyui, through extraProps in shadcn and react-bootstrap, or through slotProps.htmlInput in mui; the other themes render a fixed set of props, so it doesn't reach the input in those.

That title is set whenever the pattern is, not only when the value fails it, which has two visible consequences. The browser shows it as a tooltip when the pointer rests on any number/integer field, and because title is the last fallback in accessible-name computation, a numeric field rendered with no label at all (ui:options: { label: false }, or a layout that hides it) is now announced by that title instead of going unnamed — the same name for every such field on the page. Give those fields a ui:title or an aria-label if either matters, or your own pattern, or your own title in the themes listed above that forward it.

A text input also lets a value that isn't a number reach formData: asNumber() keeps the raw string when Number() can't parse it, so a half-typed 1.2.3 or a lone - stays in the number slot, where a native number input reported an empty value instead. Code reading formData from onChange, from getFormData(), or through liveValidate errors should expect a string there while a field is being edited. RJSF's validation reports it as a type error, and the pattern blocks submitting it.

The numeric virtual keyboards that inputMode="decimal" and "numeric" request are also digit-only on some platforms: the iOS ones have no minus key, so a field that accepts negative values can't have one typed on an iPhone or iPad. RJSF doesn't switch inputMode by the schema's minimum, because most number fields have none and would lose the numeric keyboard. For a field that needs negative values on iOS, set ui:options.inputType: 'number' (or use the updown widget), whose keyboard does have a minus key.

Accessibility changes with the element. A native <input type="number"> is exposed as a spinbutton, and min and max give it aria-valuemin/aria-valuemax, so a screen reader announces a { "type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 10 } field as "spin button, 1 to 10". A text input with inputMode is a textbox, and inputMode is only a virtual-keyboard hint that assistive technology doesn't see, so the range is no longer announced. RJSF doesn't add role="spinbutton" or aria-valuemin/aria-valuemax to compensate: the role promises arrow-key stepping that a text input doesn't implement, and those attributes aren't valid on a textbox. For a field where the range matters to the user, state it in ui:description or ui:help, which the input is already linked to through aria-describedby, or set ui:options.inputType: 'number' (or use the updown widget) to keep the native semantics.

This only affects themes whose BaseInputTemplate renders a plain native <input>; @rjsf/antd and @rjsf/mantine already render their own InputNumber/NumberInput component and are unaffected, except that the plain input they fall back to when a widget supplies an onChangeOverride is still type="number". If your code selects the widget by its DOM type (input[type="number"], getByRole('spinbutton')), select on inputMode (input[inputmode="decimal"]) or your own field/id instead.

A BaseInputTemplate of your own forwards inputMode and pattern BREAKING CHANGE​

InputPropsType gained optional inputMode and pattern members. If your own BaseInputTemplate spreads the result of getBaseInputProps() onto an <input>, they reach it automatically. If it hands them to a component that doesn't forward unknown props to the native <input>, pull inputMode and pattern out and pass them to it explicitly, as @rjsf/mui does through slotProps.htmlInput; without them the field renders as a plain text input with no numeric keyboard or pattern.

@rjsf/mui now applies the derived input attributes before slotProps.htmlInput, so a step, min, max or accept you pass through slotProps.htmlInput or ui:options.mui.slotProps.htmlInput takes precedence instead of being overwritten by the derived value. If you added one of those to work around the old clobbering — a { "type": "integer", "multipleOf": 5 } field given slotProps={{ htmlInput: { step: 1 } }}, say — it now takes effect, and the browser step-checks against your value rather than the schema's. BaseInputTemplateMuiProps['slotProps']['htmlInput'] is typed as InputHTMLAttributes<HTMLInputElement | HTMLTextAreaElement>, or MUI's (ownerState) => props returning them, so those <input>-only attributes are accepted.

FieldTemplateProps gains a required keyName BREAKING CHANGE​

FieldTemplateProps has a new required keyName: string member, the name of the field's property in its parent object, and WrapIfAdditionalTemplateProps picks it up too. It carries none of the decoration label may have picked up — a ui:title, or the (deprecated) marker the default deprecatedHandling appends — so an additionalProperties key is read and renamed from the real key rather than from what is displayed. Rendering a FieldTemplate does not change; only code that constructs FieldTemplateProps itself is affected, and that code fails to compile with TS2741 until it supplies keyName.

A custom WrapIfAdditionalTemplate should take the key control's value from keyName instead of label, keeping label for the control's own label:

const keyLabel = translateString(TranslatableString.KeyLabel, [label]);
// ...
<input type='text' id={additionalKeyId(id)} onBlur={onKeyRenameBlur} defaultValue={keyName} />;

Without it, a deprecated additional property keyed foo shows foo (deprecated) in its key input and renames itself to that string on blur.

ui:hideError now suppresses the theme's error styling BREAKING CHANGE​

ui:hideError was only ever half honored by the themes. It suppressed the error messages RJSF renders, but the input underneath kept whatever the theme uses to signal invalid — MUI's Mui-error, Bootstrap's is-invalid, Chakra's invalid flag, Fluent's validationState, shadcn's border-destructive — so a field with hidden errors still rendered a red outline with nothing explaining it (#3684). @rjsf/mantine went further: its widgets handed the messages to Mantine's own error prop, and its AltDateWidget and RangeWidget rendered an Input.Error apiece, so a Mantine user saw the error text itself under a directive asking for it to be hidden. Every theme's widgets now respect the directive, so a form using ui:hideError loses that outline — and, on Mantine, the error text that came with it. A field's ui:hideError is resolved as its own, then the one its parent resolved to, so a parent's directive reaches its children; ui:globalOptions holds no hideError, so a ui:hideError at the root of the uiSchema hides every field's errors. The directive also reaches components that were never handed it: the oneOf/anyOf selector MultiSchemaField renders, the widget ArrayField renders for a multi-select array or an array of files, and the ArrayFieldTemplate and ObjectFieldTemplate, whose hideError prop was declared but never set.

@rjsf/chakra-ui's CheckboxesWidget changes in two more ways, since it had a second, unrelated source of error styling:

  • It no longer flags a required field while it is still empty. Its inner CheckboxGroup was marked invalid whenever the field was required and had nothing selected, before validation had found anything wrong and whatever ui:hideError said, so every checkbox carried aria-invalid="true" and data-invalid from the first render. That state is now derived from the field's visible errors like every other error state, and there is no option to bring the old behavior back; a required checkboxes field is flagged once validation reports an error for it, as any other field is.
  • Once the field does have visible errors, every checkbox is marked invalid (aria-invalid="true" and data-invalid), where a field that was not required used to mark only the surrounding fieldset.

This changes nothing about what rawErrors contains. Fields and widgets are still handed the full list while errors are hidden, which is what lets a custom widget render them its own way — that is the whole point of the directive. What changed is that the built-in widgets no longer treat a non-empty rawErrors as reason enough to style themselves as invalid.

If you maintain a custom theme or widget, derive your error state from its field's plan rather than reading rawErrors directly: hasWidgetErrors() reads the aria-invalid the plan gives a widget's control, with ui:hideError applied, falling back to rawErrors with hideError only for a widget rendered without a plan, and a template reads its field's own errors, with ui:hideError applied, from its hasErrors prop:

// Before: renders an error state even when `ui:hideError` is set
const hasError = rawErrors.length > 0;

// After
const hasError = hasWidgetErrors(props);

hasVisibleErrors(), added in this release for the same purpose, is deprecated in favor of the plan, as is VisibleErrorsProps, its parameter type; a widget or container template that draws its own messages reads them from getErrorsToDraw(). See A field's label, description, help and errors are drawn where its plan says.

A custom FieldTemplate needs no such change to its own error state. One that lists the props it forwards to WrapIfAdditionalTemplate one by one, rather than spreading them, adds hasErrors to that list, as it does propertyNamesEnum and keyName: WrapIfAdditionalTemplateProps picks it as a required prop, and core's WrapIfAdditionalTemplate takes its has-error class from it alone, so a list without it fails to type-check, and in plain JavaScript an extra key's wrapper loses its error class. SchemaField withholds rawErrors from the FieldTemplate while the errors are hidden, as it always has, and now does so for a layout grid's discriminated cell too. A template's rawErrors is deprecated, though: take the error state from its hasErrors prop, the field's own errors with ui:hideError applied. A custom field that renders the theme's FieldTemplate itself, rather than through SchemaField, passes hasErrors, a required prop, alongside the errors it hands over: the built-in templates take their error state only from it, so a field passing rawErrors with hasErrors={false} keeps its messages but has no red outline or invalid status. In @rjsf/antd it also decides whether the messages are shown; a field passing just rawErrors still has them shown through v7, without the form item's error status. v7 requires hasErrors rather than falling back to rawErrors the way 6.x templates did: TypeScript reports a template rendered without it, and from plain JavaScript, where nothing checks the type, such a template has no error state in any theme, and neither does the WrapIfAdditionalTemplate it hands its props to. ArrayFieldTemplate and ObjectFieldTemplate are handed their own errors as rawErrors whatever hideError says, as a widget is; that rawErrors is deprecated too. They take their error state from their own hasErrors, as a FieldTemplate does, and the messages they draw from getErrorsToDraw(), which gives presentation.errors.messages only where presentation.errors.by is 'self', since the FieldTemplate draws them under 'template'. hasWidgetErrors() follows the aria-invalid its field's plan gives its control, so an anyOf/oneOf option's control is styled invalid while the field above draws the errors. That cell's template is also handed the classNames and style it never was, so its wrapper now carries rjsf-field-error while the field has errors to show; see A discriminated cell of a layout grid renders through SchemaField. What a FieldTemplate gains is errorSchema, which ArrayFieldTemplateProps and ObjectFieldTemplateProps already declared: it carries every error whatever hideError says, so a template that renders the errors itself can reach the ones the directive withholds, which blanking rawErrors had left it no way to do. A template that spreads its leftover props onto a DOM node should destructure errorSchema out along with the rest, or React will warn about an unknown errorschema attribute.

The form-level error list is unaffected; it is controlled separately by showErrorList.

A ui:field component that renders SchemaField for its own data, and hands that field a ui:hideError of false while its own hides the errors, now has the field's own errors drawn by that inner field, which is styled in error and has its control marked aria-invalid. In 6.x the inner field drew nothing for them, since only the field naming the component had them, and while it hid them, nothing showed. A component that wants them hidden throughout leaves ui:hideError alone in the uiSchema it hands on, or sets it to true.

A discriminated cell of a layout grid renders through SchemaField BREAKING CHANGE​

A discriminated oneOf/anyOf that a LayoutGridField lays out renders its option selector alone, while the grid lays out the selected option's properties in cells of their own. LayoutMultiSchemaField rendered that cell outside any SchemaField, building its FieldTemplate's props itself, so each prop it left out was missing for that one field: no rjsf-field* rule and no ui:classNames ever reached it, for one (#5327). The grid now renders the cell through SchemaField, as it renders every other cell, and LayoutMultiSchemaField renders only the selector widget, in place of the options, so the cell's template is handed what every other field's is, resolved the same way (#5419).

What changes for a form that already renders one of these cells:

  • A CSS rule matching .rjsf-field, .rjsf-field-<type> or .rjsf-field-error now matches the cell's wrapper, where it never did. A rule written to style every field will start applying to these cells; a rule written to exclude them has to say so.
  • ui:classNames and ui:style on the cell are applied by the FieldTemplate wrapper, and are kept out of both the options and the uiSchema handed to the selector widget, the way SchemaField has always kept them from its children (see #439). A custom selector widget that styled itself from options.classNames/options.style, or from getUiOptions(props.uiSchema), no longer receives them. Read them from ui:options under a name of your own if the widget, rather than the wrapper, is what should carry them.
  • The template is handed the hidden, formData, description, rawDescription, help and rawHelp props it never was. A ui:widget: 'hidden' on such a cell now hides it, where the widget used to render inside the full wrapper, and a ui:description, schema.description or ui:help on it now renders.
  • ui:disabled and a deprecated schema are resolved as for any other field, where the cell ignored both. ui:disabled now disables the cell and its selector widget, and re-enables them when it is false on a form or a grid that disables everything. A deprecated cell is hidden by ui:deprecatedHandling: 'hide', disabled by 'disable', and by the 'label' default has the deprecation marker appended to its label, which its FieldTemplate and its selector widget both receive.
  • A cell with no title is labelled by the name the grid gives it, as every other cell is, where it was left unlabelled: its property name (see A layout grid cell is named by its property name). Give it a ui:title, or set ui:label: false to hide the label; the selector is still named by its text.
  • A field of your own registered as LayoutMultiSchemaField is rendered within the FieldTemplate that SchemaField renders, so one that rendered its own FieldTemplate now renders two. Render only the selector, and take disabled, readonly, required, hideError and presentation from its props, which SchemaField has resolved from the cell's uiSchema. The grid names the field in the cell's ui:field, in place of any field the cell or its ui:definitions entry names, which a discriminated cell has never rendered and the console now warns once about, and sets ui:fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf beside it, so the options give way to the selector as they do to any field that renders them. The field keeps both out of the uiSchema it hands its selector widget, so a custom selector widget reading getUiOptions(props.uiSchema) doesn't see them. The cell's FieldTemplate, DescriptionFieldTemplate, FieldHelpTemplate and FieldErrorTemplate still do, in the uiSchema SchemaField hands them. A template that decides whether to draw the label with the deprecated getDisplayLabel() now draws none for a cell with no type, since that turns the label off for any uiSchema with a ui:field, and a RadioWidget selector's aria-labelledby then names nothing; read presentation.label.by, or templateDrawsLabel(), instead.
  • A $ref cell takes its ui:definitions entry, which it ignored, so a definition shared between a grid cell and a field elsewhere now gives the cell its ui:widget, ui:title and the rest too.
  • ui:autofocus on the cell focuses its selector, where the widget was handed autofocus: false and nothing took focus.
  • LayoutMultiSchemaField reads its options from the schema's oneOf/anyOf, and no longer reads an options prop, which only the grid passed, or the undeclared baseType. The grid no longer passes options to any cell, so a custom ui:field in a oneOf/anyOf cell without a discriminator, which received it through SchemaField, has to read the options from schema.oneOf/schema.anyOf instead. Named outside a grid it no longer throws, but it is still meant for one: without ui:fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf: true the options render beside it with a selector of their own, and with it nothing renders the selected option's properties.
  • A selector property with no type, nor one its const or enum implies, takes the type of the first option that isn't a boolean schema, declared or inferred, where it took the selected option's, so its widget no longer depends on the data, and a selector with no option selected renders, where it threw. With no option to take a type from, as when every option is a boolean schema, it is typed as an object, with its default widget or one the cell names by an alias an object takes: select, radio or hidden.
  • computeEnumOptions() and getSelectedOption() can no longer be imported, since deep imports are removed.
  • A cell whose oneOf/anyOf is empty has no option to select, so it renders the field its schema would without the keyword, as a cell with no union does, where it threw.

The rjsf-field-<type> class is rjsf-field-undefined for the usual discriminated schema — { discriminator, oneOf: [{ $ref }, ...] } declares no top-level type, and getSchemaType() has nothing to infer one from. That is what SchemaField has spelled for any typeless schema since 6.x, which is the only thing this change promises about it. It is not a spelling to key a rule off: a later release may drop the type class for a schema it cannot type, or derive it from the selected option, in getFieldClassNames() for every field at once. Key off .rjsf-field, which every field carries whatever its schema says.

A custom field that renders its own FieldTemplate should build these props with the three new @rjsf/utils helpers rather than by hand, so it keeps carrying whatever the contract gains next:

import { ERRORS_KEY, getDeprecatedHandling, getFieldClassNames, getUiOptions, omitConsumedStyling } from '@rjsf/utils';

const uiOptions = getUiOptions(uiSchema, registry.globalUiOptions);
// A field resolves `ui:hideError` itself, in either direction, falling back to the prop, which carries the parent's
// value rather than this field's; and its errors arrive in `errorSchema`, not in the `rawErrors` a widget is handed,
// so `hasWidgetErrors(props)` is not the answer here the way it is inside a widget. A field that plans itself with
// `resolveFieldPresentation()` reads this from its plan's `errors.messages` instead
const hideError = uiOptions.hideError === undefined ? props.hideError : Boolean(uiOptions.hideError);
const hasErrors = !hideError && (errorSchema?.[ERRORS_KEY]?.length ?? 0) > 0;
const classNames = getFieldClassNames(schema, hasErrors, uiOptions.classNames);
// `hide` means the `hidden` prop, `disable` means the `disabled` one, and `label` decorates the label handed to the
// template — but not the one handed to the widget below it
const deprecatedHandling = getDeprecatedHandling(schema, uiOptions);
// What to hand the children, with the styling this template consumed removed
const childUiSchema = omitConsumedStyling(uiSchema);

Pass rawErrors on the same terms SchemaField does — the full list while the errors are shown, undefined while they are hidden — and pass errorSchema through unchanged, so a template rendering the errors itself can still reach the hidden ones.

A LayoutGridField with no layout, or a cell or condition naming no field, renders nothing BREAKING CHANGE​

A LayoutGridField with no ui:layoutGrid object, because it is missing, misspelled or not an object, rendered every field of its schema, as a plain object field does. It now renders nothing, as the ui:layoutGrid reference says, and logs a warning naming the field. A cell that names no field and whose render doesn't resolve, such as {}, { name: '' } or { render: 'Misspelled' }, rendered every field of the grid's schema again inside the grid, under the same ids, and now renders nothing too, logging a warning unless the cell is null. In a ui:columns, which renders a GridTemplate around each cell, its column is left empty.

A ui:condition with no field, or a field of '', read no value, so a none condition such as { "ui:condition": { "operator": "none", "value": "x", "children": ["a"] } } rendered its children. It is now never met, so it renders nothing and logs a warning.

To keep those fields, give the LayoutGridField its ui:layoutGrid, or drop its ui:field so it renders as a plain object field. Remove a cell that names no field, give it the name of the field it should render, or fix its render. Give a ui:condition the field it tests, or replace a condition that should always render with its children.

A layout grid cell is named by its property name, not its dotted path BREAKING CHANGE​

A LayoutGridField cell that names a nested field, such as person.address.city, handed that full dotted path to the cell's SchemaField as its name, so a cell with no title was labelled person.address.city. It now hands over the property name, city, so the cell is labelled by it, as the same field is outside a grid. A cell that names an array item, such as person.list.0, is named list-0, as ArrayField names that item. Ids, htmlName, form data and errors come from the full path, so they don't change.

A grid shows its cells side by side without the headings of the objects that hold them, so two untitled cells with the same property name, such as person.name and company.name, are now both labelled name. Give each one a ui:title to tell them apart.

The name reaches more than the label: it is the name prop of the cell's field, including one the cell names by ui:field, and of its widget, and the keyName of its WrapIfAdditionalTemplate. A custom field, widget or template inside a grid that read the dotted path from name now gets the property name. A field or FieldTemplate reads the full path from fieldPath instead, which is unchanged. A widget or WrapIfAdditionalTemplate is handed no fieldPath; one that needs the path takes it from the custom field or FieldTemplate that renders it, which reads fieldPath. A cell with a render component still hands it the dotted path as name.

A nested cell with no title that you want to keep the old label gives it a ui:title:

 {
   "ui:field": "LayoutGridField",
   "ui:layoutGrid": { "ui:row": [{ "ui:col": ["person.address.city"] }] },
+  "person": { "address": { "city": { "ui:title": "person.address.city" } } }
 }

EnumOptionsType.value is unknown BREAKING CHANGE​

An enum option's value is typed unknown instead of any, since it can be any JSON value an enum, const or examples entry holds. The helpers typed by it follow: enumOptionsSelectValue(), enumOptionsDeselectValue() and enumOptionsValueForIndex() return unknown values, and enumOptionSelectedValue() takes value as unknown and returns a string (a string[] when multiple) or its emptyValue (undefined when it is omitted) instead of any. Its second type parameter is the type of emptyValue and defaults to undefined, so a call that passes <S> explicitly along with an emptyValue, as the v6 themes did, no longer compiles: drop the type arguments and let them be inferred, or pass <S, typeof emptyValue>. UIOptionsType.emptyValue is unknown as well, as is every ui:options value read through the type's index signature, so an emptyValue taken from options and returned by enumOptionSelectedValue() is unknown until it is narrowed. Nothing changes at runtime; only code that used a value as a narrower type stops compiling. Compare values with === (or deepEquals() from @rjsf/utils for object and array values) rather than includes(), which no longer accepts an unknown argument (for ui:enumDisabled, use enumOptionsIsDisabled() from @rjsf/utils, which also matches object and array values by deep equality), and render an option's label rather than its value. An unknown value no longer fits a value attribute either, and String() would turn every object or array value into "[object Object]" or a comma-joined list. Encode the options with enumOptionsDomValues() instead, reading each option's DOM value at its index, and decode the attribute in the change handler with enumOptionValueDecoder(), which is what the built-in select widgets do; the two must use the same format, which getOptionValueFormat(options) reads from ui:optionValueFormat:

// Before
<select value={value} onChange={(event) => onChange(event.target.value)}>
  {enumOptions.map((option) => (
    <option key={option.value} value={option.value} disabled={enumDisabled.includes(option.value)}>
      {option.value}
    </option>
  ))}
</select>

// After
import {
  enumOptionSelectedValue,
  enumOptionsDomValues,
  enumOptionsIsDisabled,
  enumOptionValueDecoder,
  getOptionValueFormat,
} from '@rjsf/utils';

const { enumOptions = [], enumDisabled, emptyValue } = options;
const optionValueFormat = getOptionValueFormat(options);
const domValues = enumOptionsDomValues(enumOptions, optionValueFormat);
<select
  value={enumOptionSelectedValue(value, enumOptions, false, optionValueFormat, '')}
  onChange={(event) => onChange(enumOptionValueDecoder(event.target.value, enumOptions, optionValueFormat, emptyValue))}
>
  {enumOptions.map((option, index) => (
    <option
      key={domValues[index]}
      value={domValues[index]}
      disabled={enumOptionsIsDisabled(option.value, enumDisabled)}
    >
      {option.label}
    </option>
  ))}
</select>

AnyOfField and OneOfField take their options already retrieved BREAKING CHANGE​

SchemaField retrieves each anyOf/oneOf option for the field's data and hands the retrieved schemas to AnyOfField/OneOfField as options, which used to retrieve them a second time. A custom field that rendered one of them itself with the raw option schemas, say <AnyOfField {...props} options={schema.anyOf} />, now retrieves them first. An option may be a boolean schema, which SchemaField retrieves as an empty one:

const options = (schema.anyOf ?? []).map((option) =>
  registry.schemaUtils.retrieveSchema(typeof option === 'object' ? option : {}, formData),
);
return <AnyOfField {...props} options={options} />;

A custom field that passed the options prop it received from SchemaField on is unaffected.

FieldTemplateProps.rawHelp carries an element ui:help BREAKING CHANGE​

rawHelp is string | ReactElement and carries whatever ui:help resolved to, where it used to be string and silently undefined for a ui:help given as a React element. It is now a reliable answer to whether a field has any help at all, which is what a FieldTemplate gating on it wants:

// Before: renders nothing for `'ui:help': <strong>…</strong>`, since `rawHelp` was `undefined`
{rawHelp && help}

// After: renders the element too, with no change to the code
{rawHelp && help}

A string ui:help is unaffected: rawHelp already carried it. Only the element form was lost. @rjsf/antd's FieldTemplate gated on rawHelp this way and so dropped an element ui:help along with the field's errors; every theme and every custom FieldTemplate doing the same is fixed by this change.

Two things to check in code that reads rawHelp as a string:

  • A template using it where a string is required — rawHelp.length, a template literal, or a string-typed prop — no longer compiles. Narrow it first (typeof rawHelp === 'string' ? rawHelp : undefined) to recover exactly the old value.
  • A template that spreads its leftover props onto a DOM node should destructure rawHelp out along with the rest. React warns about the unrecognized prop either way, but an element value renders as rawhelp="[object Object]" where a string used to render as itself.

Clearing a custom error now also clears it from the error list BREAKING CHANGE​

A field, widget or template can raise its own error by passing an errorSchema as the third argument of onChange:

onChange(value, fieldPath, { __errors: ['must be a company address'] });

Clearing it again — calling onChange for the same path with no errorSchema — used to remove the message from the field but leave it in the list the ErrorListTemplate renders, until the next validation replaced the list wholesale. Both now drop the entry at the same time.

This was an aliasing accident rather than a design: when the validator's own error schema is empty, validationDataMerge() returns the additional schema by reference, so the form's committed errorSchema and the custom-error builder were the same object. Clearing mutated it in place, which the field saw when it re-rendered, while the top-level errors array was never rebuilt. The form no longer mutates committed state, so the list is recomputed instead.

If you have a test asserting that a cleared custom error is still listed at the top of the form, it will now fail; the error is gone from both places.

An error a field raises is kept apart from the validator's BREAKING CHANGE​

An error raised through onChange at a path the validator had already reported an error for used to be written into the validator's result, in place of that error. The form now keeps what a field raises to itself, whether or not the validator reported anything there. The raise still takes the validator's errors at its path off the display, so onChange(value, fieldPath, { __errors: [] }) clears them as before.

Three things follow:

  • A parent that passes formData and stores what onChange reports no longer loses the raise when it renders the edit back.
  • The raise is still shown after the next validation, beside whatever the validator reports for the new value, the way a raise at a path without a validator error always was. It used to be replaced by that validation. Like any error a field raises, it keeps the form from submitting for as long as it stands. A field clears its own error by raising again, or by calling onChange with no errorSchema. The latter clears the error at the field's own path only: errors the field raised for paths below its own stay until it raises again, and raising {} takes all of them off.
  • In errors, and so in the ErrorListTemplate, the raise is listed after the validator's errors and extraErrors, where it used to take the place of the validator error it replaced.

Raising an empty errorSchema now clears the field's earlier raise at that path too, where it used to clear only the validator's error and leave the field's own standing.

The errorSchema passed to onChange holds only the field's own errors BREAKING CHANGE​

The errorSchema a field, widget or template passes to onChange is now read as the errors that field itself raises at its path, and nothing else. The form used to accept the errorSchema prop handed back, with the validator's errors and extraErrors in it, and worked out by comparing messages which entries were the field's own. An error of the field's own that read the same as an extraErrors message at the same path was therefore taken for the parent's, and disappeared when the parent cleared extraErrors.

A widget or field that raises the messages it computes needs no change:

onChange(value, value === 'test' ? undefined : { __errors: ['Value must be "test"'] }, id);

A field that passes its errorSchema prop back, or a copy of it with entries added, now claims every error in it as its own. They stay on display after the validator stops reporting them and after the parent clears extraErrors, until the field raises again. Pass only what the field raises:

// Before
onChange(newValue, fieldPath, errorSchema);
onChange(newValue, fieldPath, { ...errorSchema, __errors: [...(errorSchema?.__errors ?? []), 'Bad value'] });

// After
onChange(newValue, fieldPath);
onChange(newValue, fieldPath, { __errors: ['Bad value'] });

A raise still takes the validator's errors at and below its path off the display until the form validates again, so raise at the narrowest path the error belongs to: a raise at an object's path removes the validator's errors of the properties below it. It also replaces the errors the fields below it raised themselves, since a raise is everything the field has to say about its path. A raise at the root therefore replaces those of every field in the form.

ArrayField no longer passes an errorSchema when it adds, copies, removes or reorders items; the form moves the errors it holds for the items itself. Three things to check:

  • A custom field or template that wraps ArrayField and passes its onChange on in the same call is unaffected. One that passes it on later, from a debounce or after an await, sends a change the form no longer knows the move of, so the errors do not move with the items, as for a field written from scratch below. One that listened for the remapped errorSchema in the third argument of that onChange no longer receives it. One that adds an error of its own to the changes it passes on raises at the array's path, and so replaces the errors the items' fields raised themselves: there is no remapped errorSchema left to merge it into.
  • A custom field that hands ArrayField a copy of the array it sorted or filtered itself is not supported: ArrayField adds, copies, removes and reorders by reading the form's value at its fieldPath, so those operations, and the errors they move, act on the form's indexes and not on the copy's. Pass formData through unchanged, see Form data has one owner.
  • A custom array field written from scratch has no way to tell the form where an item went, so the errors of its items do not move with them. Without live validation, the validator's errors of the items whose values changed are cleared. Validating again, with liveValidate or validateForm(), puts the validator's errors in place, but not the errors the items' fields raised themselves: those stay at the old indexes, and one left at the index of an item that was removed keeps the form from submitting. Raise at the array's path with the change, onChange(newItems, fieldPath, {}) to clear them or an errorSchema holding them where their items went.

The optional data controls no longer pass the field's errorSchema back either. Adding data passes none. Removing it passes an empty one, which clears the errors at and below the removed value, the validator's and the fields' own: they describe fields that are no longer shown, and an own error left standing would keep the form from submitting. Removing an additional property clears the errors at and below its key the same way.

Two more changes take the errors of the fields they affect along, without an errorSchema. Renaming an additional property moves the errors under its key to the new name, where they used to stay under the old one. Switching the option of a oneOf or anyOf drops the errors the fields raised under every key the option that was left declared or the data held, and at the field's own path: the option's fields are rendered anew under the new option's schema, so a raise of the old option's widget would stand on a field that never made it. The validator's errors go only under the keys the new option does not declare, whose fields are gone; under a key it declares too they may describe a constraint it shares, and stay until the form validates again, as does one on the switched field itself. A property the schema declares beside its options is still the same field and keeps its errors.

A custom ArraySchemaField is handed each item's own errors as rawErrors BREAKING CHANGE​

ArrayField hands the field component it renders for each item, a custom ArraySchemaField or SchemaField, the item's own errors as the deprecated rawErrors. It used to hand every item the array's errors, so the docs told a custom ArraySchemaField to read its own from its errorSchema. Nothing warns about the change, so check a custom ArraySchemaField that reads rawErrors:

  • One that drew rawErrors next to each item as the array's errors now draws that item's own there. Draw the array's errors in the ArrayFieldTemplate, which is handed them, instead.
  • One that drew rawErrors and also hands its errorSchema to a SchemaField, which draws the __errors it holds, now draws the item's errors twice. Draw only one of them:
// Before: rawErrors held the array's errors
const CustomArraySchemaField = (props: FieldProps) => {
  const { rawErrors, registry } = props;
  const { SchemaField } = registry.fields;
  return (
    <>
      <SchemaField {...props} />
      {rawErrors?.map((error) => <p key={error}>{error}</p>)}
    </>
  );
};

// After: rawErrors holds the item's own errors, which the SchemaField already draws
const CustomArraySchemaField = (props: FieldProps) => {
  const { SchemaField } = props.registry.fields;
  return <SchemaField {...props} />;
};

noValidate now turns off live validation on blur BREAKING CHANGE​

noValidate disables validation everywhere else — on change, on submit, and when props change — but liveValidate='onBlur' ran and displayed schema errors regardless of it. It is now honored there too.

If you combined noValidate with liveValidate='onBlur' and depended on blurring a field to produce errors, drop noValidate:

-<Form noValidate liveValidate='onBlur' ... />
+<Form liveValidate='onBlur' ... />

FormRef.validate() takes only the data BREAKING CHANGE​

validate() now takes only the data to validate: validate(formData). Its schema, altSchemaUtils and retrievedSchema parameters are gone. They existed for the form's own validation passes, which call the internal pipeline directly. Nothing on the handle is typed by the schema or the form context any more, so the type is FormRef<T> rather than FormRef<T, S, F>.

To validate against another schema or validator, build the utilities for it and call its validator yourself, passing the form's customValidate, transformErrors and uiSchema as validate() did:

-const { errors } = formRef.current.validate(data, otherSchema, otherSchemaUtils);
+const { errors } = otherSchemaUtils
+  .getValidator()
+  .validateFormData(data, otherSchema, customValidate, transformErrors, uiSchema);

To hand customValidate the same defaults the form would, pass the trailing getCustomValidateFormData: () => otherSchemaUtils.getDefaultFormState(otherSchema, data, true, undefined, uiSchema).

validate() also added the errors of ui:required fields on top. For those, merge otherSchemaUtils.getUiRequiredErrorSchema(uiSchema, data) into the result with validationDataMerge().

@rjsf/daisyui applies ui:classNames and ui:style on the field wrapper BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/daisyui's FieldTemplate applied ui:classNames twice — once on the WrapIfAdditionalTemplate wrapper it renders every field in, and again on its own inner field-template div — while applying ui:style to that inner div alone (#5327). A ui:classNames declaring a border or padding drew it twice, one nested inside the other, and a ui:style written to go with those classes landed on a different element than they did. Both now go to the wrapper, the way @rjsf/core and every other theme applies them.

ui:options.daisy's own className, style and theme are unaffected. They are this theme's per-field theming of that inner div, which is what they are for.

Two things to check:

  • A CSS rule or a test that reached ui:classNames on .field-template, or read ui:style off it, has to look at the wrapper above it instead.
  • A custom WrapIfAdditionalTemplate registered for this theme is now what applies both, so one that renders <div className={classNames}> and ignores style silently drops every ui:style on upgrading, where ignoring it was harmless before. Apply style alongside classNames on the element you return, in the plain branch as well as the additional-property one.

@rjsf/mantine widgets reference rjsf's ids for labels and descriptions BREAKING CHANGE​

Most @rjsf/mantine widgets passed aria-describedby to a Mantine component that discarded it, and the checkbox and radio groups pointed aria-labelledby at a Mantine label that was never rendered (#5332). Every widget now references the ids the other themes use: an input is described by the field's error, description and help ids (root__error root__description root__help), and a checkbox or radio group is labelled by the field's title id (root__title). Accessibility is all that changes, apart from a few places where the markup your code or tests may select on is different:

  • RadioWidget's label has the field's title id (root__title) instead of the id Mantine generated for it (root-label). CheckboxesWidget's label keeps that id, but Checkbox.Group now renders it, as a <div class="mantine-CheckboxGroup-label"> inside the group's wrapper, where it used to be a <label> before the group. Both groups are labelled by it, where before the checkbox group had no accessible name. When the label is hidden (ui:label: false) or left out of inputWrapperOrder, it is still rendered with that id, hidden, so the group keeps its name; when the field has no label, a RadioWidget's group is named by a hidden title holding its fallback name, and a CheckboxesWidget's has no aria-labelledby. An aria-label in ui:options names either group the same way, over a hidden label, and no longer lands on Mantine's wrapper; a label on screen still names the group. Select the label by #root__title, or better, the group by its accessible name:

    -container.querySelector('#root-label');
    +screen.getByRole('radiogroup', { name: 'My field' });

  • CheckboxesWidget and RadioWidget apply labelProps to their label, except an id, since the label's id has to match the group's aria-labelledby. As in Mantine's groups, labelProps comes from ui:options or the Mantine theme's CheckboxGroup/RadioGroup defaultProps, then ui:options.wrapperProps, then the theme's InputWrapper defaultProps, so a theme group default wins over ui:options.wrapperProps. CheckboxesWidget used to ignore labelProps entirely.

  • RangeWidget and AltDateWidget render their title, description and errors inside Mantine's Input.Wrapper (.mantine-InputWrapper-root), where they used to render them as siblings of the slider or the date parts. The InputWrapper options apply to them as to Mantine's inputs: an option in wrapperProps, from ui:options or else the Mantine theme's Input and InputWrapper defaultProps, wins over the same option set top-level, from ui:options or else the theme. So a theme's wrapperProps value beats a top-level ui:options one, and an option set to undefined in wrapperProps falls back to the theme's InputWrapper defaultProps. inputWrapperOrder orders or leaves out the title, description and errors, and labelProps, descriptionProps, errorProps, withAsterisk, labelElement and size style them; the slider and the date parts take that size too, unless the Mantine theme's Slider or Select defaultProps give them one and the field sets none of its own. A field that sets both size and wrapperProps.size sizes its inputs by size and its wrapper by wrapperProps.size, as a Mantine input does. The theme's Input styling props (classNames, styles, className, style, variant and the like) reach the wrapper too, as they do an input's. On AltDateWidget, the root element props from the theme's Input and InputWrapper defaultProps (className, style, mod, style props such as mt, and the root entry of classNames, styles and attributes), and the theme's Input wrapperProps other than the InputWrapper options and the Styles API props (classNames, styles, attributes, variant and the like, less their root entry), stay on each date part's own wrapper and aren't applied again around them all; set them in ui:options.wrapperProps to style the field's wrapper. The title keeps the field's title id (root__title) whatever labelProps says, has no for, and when it is hidden or left out of inputWrapperOrder it is rendered hidden, so the inputs keep their name. Their errors render in Mantine's single error element instead of one element per message. AltDateWidget applies an inputContainer around each date part rather than around them all, resolved as for a Select. Only the inputContainer of a ui:options.wrapperProps reaches the parts, over the theme's Select wrapperProps rather than replacing them, since the field's own wrapper applies the rest. Set these options on InputWrapper in the theme, not on Slider: Mantine's Slider spreads its own defaultProps on its root element.

  • RangeWidget renders its description by the same rules as the other widgets: it shows schema.description, which it used to leave out, and hides the description under ui:label: false, where it used to show ui:options.description regardless.

  • RangeWidget no longer passes Mantine input props that Slider doesn't take (leftSection, withErrorStyles, loading and the like) or the InputWrapper options from ui:options on to the slider's root element, where they became unknown attributes.

  • RangeWidget, PasswordWidget, TimeWidget, ColorWidget, FileWidget and DateTimeInput name their input by the nameGenerator, which they ignored. Without one, they, TextareaWidget and CheckboxWidget name their input by the field's id (root_address_city), as the other widgets do, where they used the bare property name (city, or "" at the root). Update any selector or form-data parsing that relied on the old name.

  • Every widget that renders a description, except CheckboxWidget, applies descriptionProps from ui:options, ui:options.wrapperProps or the Mantine theme's defaultProps, resolved as Mantine resolves them, where only ui:options.wrapperProps.descriptionProps used to reach it. The description is always rendered in a div, including under a wrapperProps.descriptionProps, which used to turn it back into Mantine's default <p>.

  • Mantine's error element has the field's error id (root__error) instead of the id Mantine generated for it (root-error), whatever errorProps.id says. FieldErrorTemplate shows, in Mantine's error element with that id, the errors no widget shows: those of a custom widget or ui:field, of @rjsf/core's RatingWidget, which has no Mantine counterpart, of a field of an unsupported type, of an array rendered item by item and of a oneOf/anyOf field, below its option. It used to render a hidden copy of every field's errors, so those were announced but never shown (#5490). ObjectFieldTemplate shows the object's own errors with that id, below its fields, where they used to be hidden; a custom ObjectFieldTemplate renders them only if it reads presentation.errors.messages itself. Inputs are now described by the error they show, including a oneOf/anyOf selector, which had no error to reference, and a checkbox's error is read once rather than twice. A oneOf/anyOf field's errors show once, below its option, and describe both the option selector and the option's control, each marked invalid, where the selector and the option's widget each showed them. CheckboxWidget renders its error below the checkbox, where Mantine's Checkbox rendered it below the label, and ignores errorProps, as before. A widget whose inputWrapperOrder leaves out 'error' shows its errors through FieldErrorTemplate instead, so a custom FieldErrorTemplate renders only errors Mantine's own element doesn't, and can give its element the field's errorId(id), as @rjsf/core's does. A widget of your own takes the declaration of the key it is registered under: under one of the theme's widget keys, such as TextWidget, it is declared to draw its own errors, so it should render presentation.errors.messages; under any other, or given directly as ui:widget, its errors are shown by FieldErrorTemplate. One registered as RangeWidget, AltDateWidget or AltDateTimeWidget is also declared labelledBy: 'aria-labelledby', so a label the template draws for it has no for, and it is named only through the aria-labelledby it spreads from getControlAttributes(). A BaseInputTemplate of your own draws the errors of @rjsf/core's TextWidget, EmailWidget, URLWidget and UpDownWidget, which the theme declares errors: 'self' because its own BaseInputTemplate draws them, so it should render presentation.errors.messages as well, or they aren't shown. Select an error by #root__error, or better, the input by its accessible description:

    -container.querySelector('#root-error');
    +expect(screen.getByRole('textbox')).toHaveAccessibleDescription(/must be string/);

  • Mantine's success message, rendered for a success option, has the id from successProps.id, else root__success, even when wrapperProps has an id, and inputs are described by it when it is shown. RangeWidget and AltDateWidget render it once, on the field's wrapper, and describe the slider thumb or each date part by it; a date part no longer renders one of its own, even from the theme's Select defaultProps. CheckboxesWidget and RadioWidget describe each option by it, rather than the group, like the field's other ids.

  • Each AltDateWidget date part is labelled by the field's label followed by the part, so a query by the part alone no longer matches when the field has a label, which falls back to its property name when there is no title:

    -screen.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'year' });
    +screen.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'My field year' });

Snapshot tests of Mantine forms will change too, as inputs gain the rjsf ids of the parts that render in aria-describedby and the hidden copy of the errors is gone. An assertion on an input's accessible description (toHaveAccessibleDescription()) now includes the field's help text and errors along with its description. RangeWidget's aria-describedby moves from the slider's root element to its focusable role="slider" thumb, and so does the field's id (root_x), so focusOnFirstError reaches the thumb; select the slider's root by .mantine-Slider-root. The field's id replaces an id given in thumbProps.

getDisplayLabel() reads a boolean's widget from the reduced ui options BREAKING CHANGE​

A boolean field left to its default widget is a checkbox, which draws its own label, so getDisplayLabel() reports false for it and the theme's FieldTemplate renders none. It decided that from the ui:widget key alone, and ui:options: { widget: 'radio' } is the same choice spelled the other way, so a boolean naming its widget that way was treated as having no widget at all: the template suppressed the label, leaving a radio group or a select with nothing above it (#5318).

FieldTemplateProps.displayLabel is now true for that spelling, in every theme. A FieldTemplate of your own needs no change; a snapshot of a form with a boolean field whose widget is set through ui:options.widget gains that field's label.

Naming the checkbox a boolean already resolves to, by the CheckboxWidget key it is registered under, now counts as naming no other widget and reports false. A checkbox renders the field's label itself after its input, so ui:widget: 'CheckboxWidget' had every theme render a second label beside the widget's own; that field now carries one label again. The checkbox alias still reports true, since that is the spelling a FieldTemplate matches to lay a checkbox field out itself, taking over the field's description along with its label. getDisplayLabel() itself still recognizes a widget only by name, so one registered under some other key, or passed to ui:widget as a component, reports true. SchemaField no longer asks it whether a field's own widget draws its label (see below): it looks the widget up by its alias, the key it is registered under or the component itself, and draws the label where that widget's declaration, from the theme or the Form's presentation prop, says, so a self-labelling widget registered under another key and declared label: 'self' draws one label however ui:widget names it (#5389). A component passed to ui:widget that is registered under no key has no declaration of its own and is planned by the theme's default. Where that default leaves the label to the template, as in @rjsf/core, @rjsf/antd, @rjsf/daisyui, @rjsf/react-bootstrap and @rjsf/shadcn, one that draws its own label anyway, ignoring both its presentation and hideLabel, renders a label twice. Where it has the widget draw the label, as in @rjsf/chakra-ui, @rjsf/fluentui-rc, @rjsf/mantine and @rjsf/mui, one that draws no label renders none. Register it under a key and declare it in presentation to give it one label.

@rjsf/daisyui's date and label markup changed BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/daisyui rendered its field label from the schema type rather than from the widget, and rendered it whether or not the field had a title, so several kinds of field were labelled wrongly or not at all; its DateWidget mangled a format: 'date' value at both ends (#5318). The theme's API only gained exports, so the migration is limited to snapshot tests of a daisyui form, stylesheets targeting these elements, and anything that stored what its date widget committed.

What a format: 'date' field commits is now YYYY-MM-DD, the shape @rjsf/core's native date input and every other theme produce, where it was a full UTC date-time such as 2020-05-03T00:00:00.000Z — not a date, so ajv-formats rejected the value the user had just picked. Closing the picker with no day chosen commits ui:emptyValue (undefined by default) rather than '', which failed that format the same way. A stored value carrying a time names the day its own text spells, whatever separator, time and zone follow it, so a 2020-05-03T00:00:00.000Z or a 2020-05-03T12:00:00+02:00 reads as 3 May. The exception is what v6 stored, toISOString() of the local midnight beginning the day the user picked: a value that spells that instant in UTC, however a backend writes it back (with or without the seconds and zero fraction, a space for the T, and Z, +00:00, +0000 or +00 for the zone), and lands on local midnight names that local day. A value with an offset of its own, or a lowercase t, came from somewhere else and is read as its text reads.

DateWidget reads an iso-date-time field as the day its text names, as DateTimeWidget does (#5395). v6's exception doesn't apply to that format, so a value v6 stored in an iso-date-time field under ui:widget: 'date' reads as the day before the one picked, for anyone ahead of UTC, until the day is picked again. DateTimeWidget reads a field by its format the same way, so in a format: 'date' field it shows the day a stored date-time names, at the start of that day, rather than the instant, which behind UTC is the evening before. Anything asserting on the committed shape sees 2020-05-03 where it saw a date-time. A value the widget cannot read at all is now left alone when the picker is dismissed, where it used to be replaced by the empty value.

Neither picker stores anything unless the user chose a date. Opening a picker and dismissing it used to commit whatever it was holding, so a format: 'date' field holding a date-time had the day the widget read out of it written back over the value — data the user never touched, rewritten by a glance at the calendar. A format: 'date-time' or iso-date-time field is left alone the same way, including the seconds neither picker can set. Picking a day is still the request to store one, and still rewrites a date-time in a date field as the date that field's format requires.

Either picker commits the shape the field's format declares, rather than the one its own name suggests: a date for format: 'date', a UTC ISO string for date-time, and a naive local date-time for iso-date-time. widgetMap resolves ui:widget: 'date' and ui:widget: 'date-time' on any string schema, whatever format it declares, so { 'ui:widget': 'date' } on a format: 'date-time' field used to commit a value that field's own format rejects, and { 'ui:widget': 'date-time' } on a format: 'date' field likewise.

What the markup looks like:

  • A field with no title renders no <label> at all, where an empty one used to take up space — every root field and array item, along with the lone required * on an untitled array item.
  • A boolean rendered through anything other than a checkbox or toggle now has a label, where it had none. Those two widgets render their own after the input, and so does the description. Which widget renders the label is decided from the registry, so a widget you register as CheckboxWidget or toggle — a wrapper around the theme's own, or a replacement — is the one that renders it. A widget registered under any other key gets the template's label as well as its own.
  • A widget rendering a group of controls marks it with role='radiogroup'/role='group', carries the field's id, and names itself from the label through aria-labelledby (a __label id suffix, since TitleFieldTemplate claims titleId()).
  • A hidden field renders only its children, as in @rjsf/core. An additionalProperties entry hidden with ui:widget: 'hidden' therefore loses its key input and remove button, and a field hidden by deprecatedHandling: 'hide' — the other thing SchemaField reports through that prop — is hidden rather than rendered in full.
  • ToggleWidget renders the field's label beside the switch, where it rendered ui:options.label — a flag, not text, so that label was always empty. It shares one input component with CheckboxWidget, which wraps the input in a <span> where both used a <div> a <label> does not permit, and makes the checkbox honor ui:autofocus. Both take the input's required attribute from schemaRequiresTrueValue(), as the * beside it already did: HTML5 constraint validation refuses an unchecked required box, so a boolean a parent merely lists as required — whose false the schema accepts, and which RJSF fills in as false — could not be submitted at all: the browser stopped the submit with its own prompt, before RJSF validated it or called onSubmit or onError.
  • BaseInputTemplate no longer renders a second, display: none label for its input, and the date widgets' triggers show ui:placeholder rather than schema.title.
  • Both date widgets open their picker from a <button type='button'> where they used a <div role='button' tabindex='0'>, so the field's label reaches the control it names. A stylesheet or snapshot targeting that div, or its role/tabindex, needs updating. That label names the button through its own htmlFor, whichever FieldTemplate rendered it. The button has the combobox role, as SelectWidget's trigger does, so it holds the date it displays as its value and is aria-invalid while its errors show; a query for either trigger by the button role should use combobox.
  • Both date widgets honor ui:disabled and ui:readonly, which neither read before: the picker opened from a disabled field and committed a new value over it. A second press on the trigger, or on the label pointing at it, now closes the picker and commits, where it closed and reopened in one gesture. Escape discards the date it was closed on, where the calendar kept it and the next close committed it.
  • CheckboxesWidget no longer puts required on every option box, which HTML5 constraint validation read as "check all of them" and which blocked the submit of a required array outright. RadioWidget keeps the attribute, where the browser does read same-named inputs as one group.
  • CheckboxWidget, ToggleWidget and both date widgets' triggers set aria-describedby, so the description, errors and help around them are announced with the control.
  • CheckboxWidget and ToggleWidget render the * for a required field whose schema is not a boolean, which ui:widget: 'toggle' can be pointed at: the template's label used to carry that marker, and the widget draws one of its own only for a boolean that has to be true.
  • Both date widgets' triggers show the translated AriaDateLabel string, "Select a date", for a field with no value, no ui:placeholder and no title, where the button rendered empty — blank on the screen and nameless to a screen reader. Escape also restores the month the stored value names, where the calendar reopened on the month the user had navigated away to and discarded.
  • Both date pickers' Done button and the DateTimeWidget's time input label go through translateString, as TranslatableString.DoneLabel ("Done") and TranslatableString.TimeLabel ("Time"), where they were hard-coded English; a translateString that maps every key needs the two new ones (#5482)
  • Both date widgets' popup is one element with the date-picker-popup class, and that element is the dialog the trigger controls: DateWidget's was a role='presentation' wrapper, and DateTimeWidget's had no class. Where the browser has native popovers it is a manual popover in the top layer, fixed below or above its trigger; elsewhere it is position: absolute just below the trigger at z-index: 100, as DateTimeWidget's was. For DateWidget that is a regression in Safari before 17 and Chrome before 114: an ancestor with overflow: hidden that doesn't scroll, such as a card or a collapse, now cuts off the calendar and its Done button, where the fixed popup at z-index: 99999 escaped it. Give that ancestor overflow: visible, or override .date-picker-popup's position and z-index with !important. Its position, size, margin, padding, overflow, overscroll behavior and text color, and that z-index, are inline styles, so a stylesheet changing any of them on .date-picker-popup needs !important, and a selector or query for its presentation role, or for a dialog inside it, should target .date-picker-popup or the dialog role itself (#5633)
  • getGroupProps() is exported from @rjsf/daisyui, which also re-exports @rjsf/utils' new fieldLabelId(). A group widget of your own that renders its controls itself should use getGroupAndOptionProps(), also exported, whose option gives each control the aria-describedby and aria-invalid its field's plan describes it by. A group of checkboxes also hands it the registry, and renders the requiredCue it returns inside the group, so a required one is named as required. A custom group widget takes its role and aria-labelledby from getGroupProps(), handed the field's presentation. Under a plan the label's id is the plan's, which getLabelId() reads, and beneath a label drawn above with the same id it differs from fieldLabelId()'s, so a widget pointing at fieldLabelId() itself can be named by the wrong label. A widget or FieldTemplate of your own can name itself the way the built-in ones do rather than hard-coding the id suffixes; fieldLabelId() is the label's id for a field rendered without a plan.

@rjsf/daisyui's useTheme() reads the stored theme, and ThemeContext is removed BREAKING CHANGE​

useTheme() read ThemeContext, which each ThemeProvider filled with the theme stored in localStorage under daisyui-theme when it mounted, or cupcake where none was stored. Outside a provider it got the context's default: night, which nothing on the page shows, and a setTheme() that did nothing.

useTheme() now reads the stored theme itself, as an external store, wherever it is called, and its setTheme() stores one. Inside DaisyUIFrameProvider it names the theme that frame shows: the frame's chosen dataTheme where it has one, which a stored theme doesn't change, and the stored theme where it has none. Everywhere but inside a DaisyUIFrameProvider with a chosen dataTheme, every caller names the same theme, and follows one that another caller, DaisyUIFrameProvider or another tab stores. Where nothing is stored, or the storage can't be read, it names cupcake. The server has no storage, so it renders a frame's chosen dataTheme there, or cupcake where no dataTheme is chosen. A hydrating client starts from the same theme, and then shows the stored theme where no dataTheme is chosen. ThemeProvider holds no theme of its own and renders its children as they are; it is kept so that an app that wraps its forms in it needs no change. ThemeContext is gone. It was never exported from the package root, only from lib/theme/Theme.js and lib/theme/index.js.

What an app has to change:

  • An import of ThemeContext through @rjsf/daisyui/lib/theme/Theme.js or @rjsf/daisyui/lib/theme/index.js no longer resolves. Read the theme with useTheme():

    -import { ThemeContext } from '@rjsf/daisyui/lib/theme/Theme.js';
    -const { theme, setTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext);
    +import { useTheme } from '@rjsf/daisyui';
    +const { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();

  • A ThemeContext.Provider that gave part of a page a theme of its own no longer reaches useTheme(), which names the stored theme everywhere but inside a DaisyUIFrameProvider with a chosen dataTheme. Keep that theme in your own state, and give it to DaisyUI through data-theme on an element around that part:

    -<ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme: 'dark', setTheme }}>
    +<div data-theme='dark'>
       <Form schema={schema} validator={validator} />
    -</ThemeContext.Provider>
    +</div>

  • Code that relied on useTheme() returning night outside a provider, such as a data-theme={useTheme().theme} with no ThemeProvider around it, now gets the stored theme, or cupcake, a light theme, where nothing is stored. To keep showing night there, write data-theme='night' rather than reading it from useTheme().

  • ThemeProvider no longer holds its own theme. Two providers on one page each kept the theme stored when they mounted, and changed it only through their own setTheme(). Now a setTheme() called under either one changes the theme every useTheme() names, inside both providers and outside them, and so does a theme that DaisyUIFrameProvider or another tab stores. The one exception is a useTheme() inside a DaisyUIFrameProvider with a chosen dataTheme, which keeps naming that theme. Give providers that should show different themes their own data-theme, as above. A ThemeProvider can be removed; leaving it in place changes nothing.

@rjsf/daisyui no longer ships src/styles.css or depends on tailwindcss BREAKING CHANGE​

@rjsf/daisyui published src/styles.css, which imported Tailwind's preflight and utilities layers and set --color-primary and --color-secondary on :root. No documentation mentioned it and the package's exports never let it be imported by name, so it is removed, along with the tailwindcss dependency only it used.

An app that loaded the file through its path in node_modules loads Tailwind and daisyUI from its own stylesheet, as daisyUI's setup already asks. Don't carry the two variables over: they were Tailwind 3 style RGB triplets, which daisyUI 5 reads as invalid colors, so btn-primary and bg-primary lose their color. Set a daisyUI theme's colors instead.

-@import '../node_modules/@rjsf/daisyui/src/styles.css';
+@import 'tailwindcss';
+@plugin 'daisyui';

An app that relied on @rjsf/daisyui to install tailwindcss adds it to its own dependencies.

@rjsf/daisyui's SelectWidget names its open list of options by the field's label BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects tests that find a daisyUI SelectWidget by its field's label while its list is open, which it is whenever the select has focus, as after a click, ui:autofocus or focusOnFirstError.

The list had no name. While it is open, it is now named by the field's label, else its ui:placeholder, else TranslatableString.SelectPlaceholder ("Select ..."), so getByLabelText with the field's label finds both the combobox and the list, and throws. On a required field, whose label reads "Color*", it doesn't throw: the combobox is named "Color*", so getByLabelText('Color') matches only the open list, through the label's text, and returns it, and a test then clicks or types into the list rather than the combobox.

Find the combobox by its role and its whole name, "Color*" on a required field, which matches it alone, open or closed:

-screen.getByLabelText('Color');
+screen.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Color' });

@rjsf/shadcn's SelectWidget names its combobox and fills empty placeholders BREAKING CHANGE​

The multiple SelectWidget rendered its cmdk search combobox with no accessible name, and its search input always showed a hardcoded, untranslated "Select ..." that ignored ui:placeholder; the single SelectWidget rendered a blank trigger where no ui:placeholder was given (#5458). The combobox is now named from the field's resolved label: the schema title or a ui:title override, falling back to ui:placeholder and then to the new TranslatableString.SelectPlaceholder ("Select ...") for an untitled field. The same fallback replaces the search input's hardcoded placeholder, and the field's description and aria-required reach the focusable combobox input. The single SelectWidget fills its empty trigger from the same fallback, so a single select without ui:placeholder now shows the translated placeholder where it used to render blank. Its trigger has the combobox role, so it holds the option it displays as its value and is aria-invalid and aria-required as its field is; with no label drawn for it, it is named by the field's label or, for an untitled field, by its ui:placeholder, else TranslatableString.SelectPlaceholder. A query for the trigger by the button role should use combobox.

The migration touches two kinds of code: visual snapshots of a shadcn form, where a single select without ui:placeholder goes from blank to "Select ..." and a multiple select with one shows it in place of "Select ..."; and a translateString table of your own, which gains the TranslatableString.SelectPlaceholder key to translate.

@rjsf/shadcn's multiple SelectWidget takes its field's id and opens only on user action BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects snapshots, selectors and tests that reach the search input of a shadcn multiple SelectWidget.

The input was cmdk's, with an id cmdk generated, such as radix-_r_3h_, and a cmdk-input attribute, and its list opened as soon as it took focus. The input now has the field's id, such as root_color, and no cmdk-input attribute, so the field's label and focusOnFirstError focus it. Its list opens on a click, typing, Down Arrow, Up Arrow or Enter, not on focus, so ui:autofocus and focusOnFirstError leave it closed.

Update snapshots of a form with a multiple select, find the input by the field's id or its role, and open the list before choosing an option:

-const input = container.querySelector('[cmdk-input]');
-input.focus();
+const input = screen.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Color' });
+await user.click(input);
 await user.click(screen.getByRole('option', { name: 'red' }));

@rjsf/shadcn's SelectWidget names its list of options by the field's label BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects tests that find an open shadcn SelectWidget's list of options by its name, or that find the select by its field's label while its list is open.

The list was always named "Suggestions", cmdk's default. It is now named by the field's label, else its ui:placeholder, else TranslatableString.SelectPlaceholder ("Select ..."), in the single and the multiple select. While the list is open, getByLabelText with the field's label finds both the combobox and the list, so it throws. On a required field, whose label reads "Color*", it doesn't throw: the combobox is named "Color*", so getByLabelText('Color') matches only the open list, through the label's text, and returns it, and a test then clicks or types into the list rather than the combobox.

Find the list by the field's label, or by its role alone, and the combobox by its role and its whole name, "Color*" on a required field, which matches it alone, open or closed:

-screen.getByRole('listbox', { name: 'Suggestions' });
+screen.getByRole('listbox', { name: 'Color' });
-screen.getByLabelText('Color');
+screen.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Color' });

@rjsf/shadcn's RangeWidget ignores name, disabled, value and defaultValue from ui:options.props BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects a shadcn range that sets any of these in ui:options.props. The value replaced the form's value on the slider, so its thumbs stayed where it put them, and only the first thumb's value could reach the form. A name changed what the range submits under, and disabled: false let a user edit a range on a disabled or read-only form. RangeWidget now drops all four keys, so the form's data always sets the slider, and it draws one thumb. Other ui:options.props keys, such as min, orientation and onValueChange, still apply.

Set the starting value through the form's data, or the schema's default, instead:

 const uiSchema = {
   volume: {
     'ui:widget': 'range',
-    'ui:options': { props: { value: [2] } },
   },
 };
+const formData = { volume: 2 };

For name, use the Form's nameGenerator. For disabled, use ui:disabled.

@rjsf/mantine ignores id, name, value, defaultValue, readOnly, autoFocus, data, multiple, error, onChange, onBlur and onFocus in ui:options BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects a Mantine field that sets any of these in ui:options. Options reach Mantine's components as props, so these could replace what the form passes: an onChange stopped the form seeing any edits, a name changed what the field submits under, a defaultValue showed an empty field with a value the form didn't have, a readOnly locked a field the form treated as editable, a data replaced a select's options so that picking one lost the value, and an error: false stopped marking an invalid field as invalid. They're now dropped as invalid options. Other options that Mantine's components take as props still apply.

  • For value and defaultValue, set the form's data or the schema's default.
  • For id, use the Form's idPrefix.
  • For name, use the Form's nameGenerator.
  • For readOnly, use ui:readonly, which renders the field disabled rather than read-only.
  • For autoFocus, use ui:autofocus.
  • For data, set the options in the schema, with enum or oneOf.
  • For multiple, make the field's schema an array of files.
  • For error, add the message with the Form's extraErrors or customValidate, and hide messages with ui:hideError.
  • For onChange, onBlur and onFocus, use the Form's props of the same name.

@rjsf/mui's widgets keep the form's value, disabled state and handlers over ui:options.mui BREAKING CHANGE​

This affects a field that sets disabled, onChange, onBlur, onFocus, value or checked in ui:options.mui or ui:globalOptions.mui. They replaced what the form sets on MUI's controls: an onChange was called in place of the form's, so editing the field never changed the form's data, and a disabled: false let a user edit a disabled or read-only field.

All four are now ignored where MUI uses them in place of the form's:

  • a field drawn by BaseInputTemplate, such as a text, number or date input: the top level of ui:options.mui, and slotProps.input
  • SelectWidget: the top level, rjsfSlotProps.select and rjsfSlotProps.input, an input element in rjsfSlotProps.select, which is ignored whole as it would replace the input the field draws, and the SelectDisplayProps inside rjsfSlotProps.select, rjsfSlotProps.htmlInput and the inputProps and slotProps.input of rjsfSlotProps.select and rjsfSlotProps.input, which also keeps the field's id on the combobox
  • CheckboxWidget: rjsfSlotProps.checkbox
  • RangeWidget: the top level and rjsfSlotProps.slider, and the onBlur and onFocus of rjsfSlotProps.slider.slotProps.root

Only disabled is ignored where MUI calls an onChange, onBlur or onFocus beside the form's, so those keep working:

  • BaseInputTemplate: slotProps.root, slotProps.htmlInput, and the inputProps and slotProps.input inside slotProps.input
  • SelectWidget: rjsfSlotProps.root, rjsfSlotProps.htmlInput, and the inputProps and slotProps.input inside rjsfSlotProps.select and rjsfSlotProps.input
  • CheckboxWidget: the top level and rjsfSlotProps.formControlLabel, which go on the <label>, so its onBlur and onFocus run as focus moves through the box (MUI already ignored an onChange there), and rjsfSlotProps.checkbox.slotProps.input
  • CheckboxesWidget: rjsfSlotProps.formControlLabel, as on CheckboxWidget, and rjsfSlotProps.checkbox.slotProps.input
  • RadioWidget: rjsfSlotProps.radio.slotProps.input
  • RangeWidget: rjsfSlotProps.slider.slotProps.input

The widgets also ignore a value or checked there that would replace the form's data, which left the field showing a value the form didn't hold:

  • BaseInputTemplate: a value at the top level, in slotProps.input and slotProps.htmlInput, and in the inputProps and slotProps.input inside slotProps.input
  • SelectWidget: a value at the top level, in rjsfSlotProps.select, rjsfSlotProps.input and rjsfSlotProps.htmlInput, and in the inputProps and slotProps.input of rjsfSlotProps.select and rjsfSlotProps.input
  • CheckboxWidget: a checked in rjsfSlotProps.checkbox and rjsfSlotProps.checkbox.slotProps.input
  • CheckboxesWidget: a checked or value in rjsfSlotProps.checkbox.slotProps.input
  • RadioWidget: a checked or value in rjsfSlotProps.radio and rjsfSlotProps.radio.slotProps.input, and a checked in rjsfSlotProps.formControlLabel
  • RangeWidget: a value in rjsfSlotProps.slider.slotProps.input

An inputProps inside the input slot still replaces the whole htmlInput slot, as MUI does, so the <input> loses the attributes the field gives it there, such as aria-describedby, required, min and max; give the <input>'s props through htmlInput instead.

A disabled or read-only SelectWidget also ignores an open or defaultOpen in rjsfSlotProps.select, rjsfSlotProps.htmlInput or the inputProps or slotProps.input of either slot, and an open in their MenuProps, since MUI lets a user pick an option from a menu held open. It ignores a tabIndex there, or in a SelectDisplayProps inside them, too, since MUI lets a user open a focused select's menu from the keyboard even while disabled.

  • For disabled, use ui:disabled or ui:readonly.
  • For onChange, onBlur and onFocus, use the Form's props of the same name.
  • For value and checked, give the field's value through the Form's initialFormData.
 const uiSchema = {
   pet: {
-    'ui:options': { mui: { disabled: true, onChange: logChange } },
+    'ui:disabled': true,
   },
 };
+
