It terminates on every recursive schema, including the ones that overflowed the stack: the shapes of #5500, #5452 a and c, and definitions whose dependencies refer to one another. Five definitions that all refer to one another took about 18 s per call, and now take a fraction of a second.

These overflowed the stack, and now give:

  • A recursion behind an allOf under allOf: 'populateDefaults' is filled one level further, as every other recursion is. With outer = { allOf: [{ $ref: inner }, { properties: { extra: { default: 'e' } } }] }, inner = { properties: { name: { default: 'n' }, back: { $ref: outer } } } and properties: { a: { $ref: outer } }: { a: { name: 'n', extra: 'e', back: { name: 'n', extra: 'e' } } }. With tags = { type: 'array', minItems: 1, items: { $ref: tags }, allOf: [{ minItems: 1 }] }, required: ['t'] and properties: { t: { $ref: tags } }: { t: [[undefined]] }.
  • A schema at the root that refers back to itself through a then fills the property it recurses through, as under a property. With Pet = { properties: { petType: { default: 'cat' }, friend: { $ref: Pet } }, if: { properties: { petType: { const: 'cat' } } }, then: { $ref: Cat } }, Cat = { allOf: [{ $ref: Pet }, { properties: { hunts: { default: 'h' } } }] } and a root $ref to Pet: { petType: 'cat', hunts: 'h', friend: { petType: 'cat', hunts: 'h' } }.
  • A property that a patternProperties pattern matches and that refers back to its definition is filled one level further, as a property without the pattern is, and keeps the pattern's defaults where it stops. With node = { type: 'object', properties: { child: { $ref: node } }, patternProperties: { '^c': { type: 'object', properties: { tag: { oneOf: [{ const: 'p' }] } } } } } and a root $ref to node: { child: { tag: 'p', child: { tag: 'p' } } }.
  • Chains through several cycles of definitions stop at a fixed depth. With cycles of two and three definitions, each holding a property k: { allOf: [{ $ref: Leaf }, { $ref: next }] }, under one root allOf and allOf: 'populateDefaults', the defaults stop after a few levels rather than following the least common multiple of the cycle lengths.

These defaults change:

  • An array whose minItems sits in an allOf is filled to the depth the same array with minItems beside its items is. With pl = { properties: { a: { default: 'x' }, child: { $ref: pl } } } and arr: { type: 'array', items: { $ref: pl }, allOf: [{ minItems: 1 }] } under allOf: 'populateDefaults': before { arr: [{ a: 'x', child: { a: 'x', child: { a: 'x' } } }] }, after { arr: [{ a: 'x', child: { a: 'x' } }] }.
  • Extra keys of the data are filled down to where the schema stops recursing. With map = { type: 'object', properties: { name: { default: 'm' } }, additionalProperties: { $ref: map } }, a root $ref to map and the data { k: { j: { i: {} } } }: before { name: 'm', k: { name: 'm', j: { name: 'm', i: { name: 'm' } } } }, after { name: 'm', k: { name: 'm', j: { i: {} } } }. The data below is kept as it is, and the form still renders every level. Keys a patternProperties pattern matches stop the same way: with node = { type: 'object', properties: { n: { default: 'n' } }, patternProperties: { '^c': { $ref: node } } }, a root $ref to node and the data { c1: { c2: { c3: { c4: {} } } } }: before { n: 'n', c1: { n: 'n', c2: { n: 'n', c3: { n: 'n', c4: { n: 'n' } } } } }, after { n: 'n', c1: { n: 'n', c2: { c3: { c4: {} } } } }.
  • The keys a default object names no longer grow on every call. With the same map and default: { k: {} }: the first call gives { name: 'm', k: { name: 'm' } }, as before. Before, each further call on that result added one more level. After, every call gives the same result.
  • A then gives a property without a type the default its branch declares, as the form renders it. With p: { if: {}, then: { $ref: S, default: 'sib' } } and S = { type: 'string', default: 'def' }: before {}, after { p: 'sib' }. With p: { if: {}, then: { $ref: O, required: ['a'] } } and O = { type: 'object', properties: { a, b }, default: { a: 'da', b: 'db' } }: before {}, after { p: { a: 'da', b: 'db' } }.
  • A chain of dependencies is filled in one call. With k0 having a default and each k(i-1) a dependency adding k(i) with a default, nine keys long: before, the first call gave { k0, k1 } and each further call added one key. After, the first call gives k0 to k8.
  • The keywords beside a $ref apply at every level, as they do in the form. With node = { properties: { name: { default: 'n' }, child: { $ref: node, properties: { own: { default: 'o' } } } } } and a root $ref to node: before { name: 'n', child: { name: 'n', child: { own: 'o' } } }, after { name: 'n', child: { own: 'o', name: 'n', child: { own: 'o' } } }.
  • A default beside a $ref overrides the referenced schema's wherever it stands, as it already did on a property, an array's items or the root: { properties: { status: { $ref: Status, default: 'active' } } } with Status = { type: 'string', default: 'draft' } gives { status: 'active' } before and after. With s = { type: 'string', default: 'target' }, node = { properties: { v: { $ref: s, default: 'beside' }, child: { $ref: node } } } and a root $ref to node: before { v: 'beside', child: { v: 'target' } }, after { v: 'beside', child: { v: 'beside' } }. Along a chain of aliases, with alias = { $ref: s, default: 'alias' } and inner: { $ref: alias }: before { inner: 'target' }, after { inner: 'alias' }. computeDefaults() on { $ref: s, default: 'beside' }: before 'target', after 'beside'. In a draft-07 tuple position, arr: { type: 'array', items: [{ $ref: s, default: 'beside' }, { $ref: s }] }: before { arr: ['target', 'target'] }, after { arr: ['beside', 'target'] }, and the form's first input shows beside. In additionalItems, arr: { type: 'array', minItems: 2, items: [{ type: 'string' }], additionalItems: { $ref: s, default: 'beside' } }: before { arr: [undefined, 'target'] }, after { arr: [undefined, 'beside'] }.
  • An anyOf/oneOf option written as a $ref is merged with its field's default as an option written in place is. With O = { type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'number' }, b: { type: 'number' } } }, o: { default: { a: 1 }, anyOf: [{ $ref: O }] } and the data { o: { b: 2 } }: before { o: { b: 2 } }, after { o: { a: 1, b: 2 } }, which the option written in place already gave. With S = { type: 'string', default: 'child' } and s: { default: 'parent', anyOf: [{ $ref: S }] } under nestedDefaultsPrecedence: 'ancestorWins': before { s: 'parent' }, after { s: 'child' }, as for S written in place. An option { $ref: s, default: 'beside' } gives 'beside' where it gave 'target'.
  • An allOf behind the $ref of an extra key of the data follows the allOf defaults behavior, as one behind a property's $ref does. With A = { allOf: [{ type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string', default: 'a' } } }] }, { type: 'object', additionalProperties: { $ref: A } } and the data { k: {} }, under the default allOf: 'skipDefaults': before { k: { a: 'a' } }, and a showed in the form, after { k: {} }. A key a patternProperties pattern matches changes the same way. The keywords beside a $ref are no such allOf: under 2019-09 and 2020-12, with M = { $ref: O, properties: { b: { default: 'b' } } } used as additionalProperties: { $ref: M }, the defaults are { k: { b: 'b', a: 'a' } } before and after. Before, only an additionalProperties of the root schema was filled: under a property, p: { type: 'object', additionalProperties: { $ref: A } } with { p: { k: {} } } gave { p: { k: {} } } before and after. Set allOf: 'populateDefaults' to fill it: { k: { a: 'a' } } before and after.
  • Under allOf: 'populateDefaults', a dependencies entry inside an allOf is filled when a default qualifies it, as one beside properties is. With p: { allOf: [{ dependencies: { a: { properties: { c: { type: 'string', default: 'c' } } } } }, { type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string', default: 'x' } } }] } and no data: before { p: { a: 'x' } }, after { p: { a: 'x', c: 'c' } }, and the form's c input shows c. The same allOf at the root already gave c.
  • A $ref spelled #/definitions/%41 is the same recursion as #/definitions/A. With the A above: before { name: 'n', child: { name: 'n', child: { name: 'n' } } }, after { name: 'n', child: { name: 'n' } }. A chain of aliases stops at its first alias the same way: with node = { properties: { n: { default: 'n' }, c: { $ref: A1 } } }, A1 = { $ref: A2 }, A2 = { $ref: node } and a root $ref to node: before { n: 'n', c: { n: 'n', c: { n: 'n' } } }, after { n: 'n', c: { n: 'n' } }.
  • Without a rootSchema, the schema is its own root whatever the data. A $ref resolved against the schema only while the form data was empty. With { definitions: { a: { type: 'string', default: 'x' } }, properties: { p: { $ref: '#/definitions/a' }, q: { type: 'string' } } }: before, every call threw Could not find a definition for #/definitions/a.. After, it gives { p: 'x' }, and { p: 'x', q: '1' } for the data { q: '1' }. A $ref in a dependencies entry that the data qualifies resolves too, where it threw.
  • A definition that merges a schema which merges it back in, taken as the root schema with no data, gives {} where it gave undefined. With Pet = { type: 'object', properties: { petType: { type: 'string' } }, if: { properties: { petType: { const: 'cat' } } }, then: { $ref: Cat } }, Cat = { allOf: [{ $ref: Pet }, { type: 'object', properties: { hunts: { type: 'boolean' } } }] } and a root $ref to Cat: before undefined, after {}.
  • Under allOf: 'populateDefaults', the option an allOf entry chooses gives its defaults over an earlier entry's, nested as at the root. With o: { type: 'object', allOf: [{ properties: { c: { type: 'string', default: 'm0' } } }, { oneOf: [{ properties: { c: { type: 'string', default: 'opt' } } }, { properties: { z: { type: 'number' } } }] }] }: before { o: { c: 'm0' } }, after { o: { c: 'opt' } }. The same object at the root already gave { c: 'opt' }, and the form renders c from the chosen option. A field's schemas are merged in a fixed order (its own, its $ref, its allOf, the then/else, dependencies, patterns, then the option), and a later one's default wins, as a matching then's already does. Where the option declares no default for the key, the earlier entry's still applies. In such shapes the option's keys can also come first in the defaults object; the values are the same.
  • Under allOf: 'skipDefaults', a deep customMergeAllOf no longer fills a property's allOf defaults. Each field's defaults are computed from the field as the schema declares it, so a merger that also flattens the allOf of the properties inside the allOf it merges, such as createDeepAllOfMerge from @x0k/json-schema-merge, no longer exempts those properties from skipDefaults. With animalInfo: { properties: { animal: { default: 'Cat' } }, allOf: [{ if: { properties: { animal: { const: 'Cat' } } }, then: { properties: { food: { default: 'meat' } } } }] } and an allOf beside it at the root: before { animalInfo: { animal: 'Cat', food: 'meat' } }, after { animalInfo: { animal: 'Cat' } }, as without that merger. allOf: 'populateDefaults' fills it.
  • A root dependencies entry counts a default as its property's value whatever else the form data holds, as a nested one already did. With properties: { animal: { default: 'Cat' }, other: { type: 'string' } } and dependencies: { animal: { properties: { food: { default: 'meat' } } } }, for the form data { other: 'x' }: before { animal: 'Cat', other: 'x' }, after { animal: 'Cat', other: 'x', food: 'meat' }.

These stay as they were:

  • A recursion through an anyOf/oneOf option stops where the same recursion written as a property does, however deep the data goes below it, also when the property reaches the option list through a $ref of its own. With node = { properties: { name: { default: 'n' }, c: { anyOf: [{ $ref: node }, { type: 'null' }] } } }, a root $ref to node and the data { c: { c: { c: {} } } }: { name: 'n', c: { name: 'n', c: { c: {} } } }.
  • getDefaultFormState(pl) fills three levels, and getDefaultFormState({ $ref: pl }) two.
  • A default that satisfies an if, or a choice of anyOf/oneOf option, can switch the branch on the next call, so calling getDefaultFormState() on its own result can add more defaults. With { properties: { a: { default: 'x' } }, if: { required: ['a'] }, then: { properties: { b: { default: 'b' } } } }: the first call gives { a: 'x' }, and the second { a: 'x', b: 'b' }.

The root schema is treated as immutable BREAKING CHANGE​

The graph is parsed once per root schema object and kept while that object lives, and the plans and resolved schemas are kept against it. A change made to the root schema in place is therefore not seen, not even by a new createSchemaUtils() or by Form rendering it again. Before, the next retrieveSchema() read the schema as it then stood. To change a schema, pass a new object, as you would for any other React prop:

const schema = { type: 'object', properties: { color: { type: 'string', enum: ['red'] } } };
createSchemaUtils({ validator }, schema).retrieveSchema(schema);
schema.properties.color.enum = ['red', 'green'];
createSchemaUtils({ validator }, schema).retrieveSchema(schema).properties.color.enum;
// Before: ['red', 'green']
// After: ['red'], since `schema` is the object already parsed

const changed = { ...schema, properties: { color: { type: 'string', enum: ['red', 'green'] } } };
createSchemaUtils({ validator }, changed).retrieveSchema(changed).properties.color.enum;
// Before and after: ['red', 'green']

A schema you hand retrieveSchema() that the root does not hold, such as one a custom field builds from scratch, is parsed once per content and kept for as long as the root, and so is one you hand any other schema utility that resolves it, such as getDefaultFormState(), isSelect() or getClosestMatchingOption(). Calls handed the same content share its result, so do not change such a schema once handed in either. Build it from the schema rather than from form data: one built from form data keeps an entry for each distinct value until the root changes.

createSchemaUtils() no longer rewrites the root's $refs BREAKING CHANGE​

createSchemaUtils() used to rewrite every $ref of a draft 2020-12 root against the root's $id and keep that copy as its root schema. It now keeps the root schema it is given, and each $ref is resolved once, against the $ids around it, where it is looked up (#5529). getRootSchema(), and with it a form's registry.rootSchema, is the schema you passed:

const schema = {
  $schema: 'https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema',
  $id: 'https://example.com/root.json',
  $defs: { s: { type: 'string' } },
  type: 'object',
  properties: { a: { $ref: '#/$defs/s' } },
};
const schemaUtils = createSchemaUtils({ validator }, schema);
schemaUtils.getRootSchema().properties.a;
// Before: { $ref: 'https://example.com/root.json#/$defs/s' }
// After: { $ref: '#/$defs/s' }, since getRootSchema() returns `schema` itself
  • A ui:definitions entry is keyed by the $ref as the schema writes it. With the schema above, 'ui:definitions': { '#/$defs/s': { 'ui:widget': 'textarea' } } renders root_a as a textarea. Before, it rendered a text input, and only an entry keyed https://example.com/root.json#/$defs/s applied. Rename such keys to the $ref as written.
  • A $ref the rewrite left as written, because a validator would resolve the rewritten one again to somewhere else, resolves against the resource it sits in wherever it is looked up. Under $id: 'schemas/root.json', with $defs: { x: { type: 'number' }, child: { $id: 'nested/child.json', $defs: { x: { type: 'string' } }, additionalProperties: { $ref: '#/$defs/x' } } }: before, schemaUtils.retrieveSchema() of the additionalProperties that getRootSchema() holds gave the root's { type: 'number' }. After, it gives the child's { type: 'string' }.
  • makeAllReferencesAbsolute() is removed. A schema it rewrote before it was handed to Form or createSchemaUtils() can be handed over as it is.

Option matching and precompiled validators BREAKING CHANGE​

  • getClosestMatchingOption() and omitExtraData() resolve only an option's own $ref and leave the ones below it to the validator.
  • getClosestMatchingOption() scores a property written as a $ref as the definition it names, as far as the form data reaches, whether or not the $ref is recursive, resolving each $ref it follows in the resource of the declaration holding it. With Node = { type: 'object', properties: { next: { $ref: Node } } }, the options [{ type: 'object', properties: { a: { $ref: Node } } }, { type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'object', properties: { next: { type: 'object' }, z: { type: 'string' } } } } }] and the data { a: { next: { next: {} } } }: before, it overflowed the stack. After, it picks the first option.
  • Precompiled validator code must be regenerated; see Validators are handed pointers into the root schema.
  • getDefaultFormState() scores a field's options as the schema declares them, so a parent's customMergeAllOf no longer reaches the option its children choose for their defaults.

Validators are handed pointers into the root schema BREAKING CHANGE​

The form checks a condition or an option by handing the validator a $ref to where it sits in the root schema, rather than a copy of it. The rootSchema passed beside it is what the $ref resolves against, so a subschema means what JSON Schema says it means wherever the form reads it, and the schemas a precompiled validator compiles are named by the schema graph rather than enumerated.

A ValidatorType of your own has to resolve the $ref. isValid(schema, formData, rootSchema) is handed { $ref: '#/<pointer>' } for each if a field's resolution checks, the property an anyOf/oneOf option names as its discriminator, an option scoring has no required to drop from, the option MultiSchemaField keeps after a parent declines a switch, and, inside { type: 'object', properties: { <key>: { $ref } } }, the property a dependency's oneOf option is matched on. A property an option declares more than once where it applies whatever the data, as allOf: [{ $ref: Base }, { properties: { petType: { const: 'cat' } } }] does when Base declares petType too, is handed as an allOf of a $ref to each declaration. With this schema, retrieveSchema() for the data { a: 'x' } makes one call:

const schema: RJSFSchema = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { a: { type: 'string' } },
  if: { properties: { a: { const: 'x' } }, required: ['a'] },
  then: { properties: { extra: { type: 'string' } } },
};
// before: isValid({ properties: { a: { const: 'x' } }, required: ['a'] }, { a: 'x' }, schema)
// after:  isValid({ $ref: '#/if' }, { a: 'x' }, schema)

@rjsf/validator-ajv8, @rjsf/validator-ata and @rjsf/validator-cfworker register the root under its $id less any fragment, or under ROOT_SCHEMA_PREFIX when that leaves nothing, as rootSchemaIdOf() returns it, and prefix a local $ref with that id through withRootIdRefPrefix(schema, rootSchema); @rjsf/validator-ajv8 uses the id as its uriResolver normalizes it, http://example.com/a%20b.json for http://example.com/a b.json and http://example.com/a.json for http://example.com:80/a.json, which is what Ajv looks a $ref up by. A validator that ignores rootSchema finds nothing for the $ref, so every condition and option it checks fails.

A root carrying an $id. @rjsf/validator-ajv8 and @rjsf/validator-ata named the root by ROOT_SCHEMA_PREFIX in every local $ref, which a root with an $id is not registered under, so a condition holding such a $ref never held. With { $id: 'http://example.com/root.json', definitions: { I: { properties: { k: { const: 'x' } } } }, properties: { k: { type: 'string', default: 'x' } }, if: { $ref: '#/definitions/I' }, then: { properties: { t: { type: 'string', default: 't' } } }, else: { properties: { e: { type: 'string', default: 'e' } } } }, getDefaultFormState() gives { k: 'x', t: 't' } where it gave { k: 'x', e: 'e' }. An $id ending in an empty fragment, as http://example.com/root.json# and the $ids of the draft-06 and draft-07 meta-schemas do, names the same root, so rootSchemaIdOf() leaves that # out of the prefix rather than writing http://example.com/root.json##/if. @rjsf/validator-ajv8 registers such a root under its $id without the # too, which is how Ajv keys it, so a root edited under the same $id replaces the one before it: with a customizeValidator() instance that has validated against { $id: 'http://example.com/root.json#', type: 'object', properties: { k: { type: 'string', default: 'x' } }, if: { properties: { k: { const: 'x' } } }, then: { properties: { t: { type: 'string', default: 't' } } }, else: { properties: { e: { type: 'string', default: 'e' } } } }, the same root with a title added gives the defaults { k: 'x', t: 't' } where it gave { k: 'x', e: 'e' } and logged schema with key or id "http://example.com/root.json" already exists.

@rjsf/validator-cfworker registered a root carrying an $id under ROOT_SCHEMA_PREFIX in its place, so the $refs of a 2020-12 root with an $id, which resolve against that $id, resolved to nothing, and a condition holding one never held. With { $schema: 'https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema', $id: 'https://example.com/root.json', $defs: { isB: { properties: { k: { const: 'b' } }, required: ['k'] } }, type: 'object', properties: { k: { type: 'string' } }, if: { $ref: '#/$defs/isB' }, then: { properties: { t: { type: 'string', default: 'THEN' } } }, else: { properties: { e: { type: 'string', default: 'ELSE' } } } } and the data { k: 'b' }, getDefaultFormState() gives { k: 'b', t: 'THEN' } where it gave { k: 'b', e: 'ELSE' }. Options read from that root match the same way: with $defs: { isA: { type: 'object', properties: { k: { const: 'a' } }, required: ['k'] }, isB: { type: 'object', properties: { k: { const: 'b' } }, required: ['k'] } } and oneOf: [{ $ref: '#/$defs/isA' }, { $ref: '#/$defs/isB' }] in such a root, getFirstMatchingOption({ k: 'b' }, schemaUtils.getRootSchema().oneOf) gives 1 where it gave 0.

One validator, several roots. A validator caches what it compiles for a schema, and { $ref: '#/definitions/X' } means something else under every root. isValid({ $ref: '#/definitions/X' }, 's', { definitions: { X: { type: 'number' } } }) after the same call with a root whose X is a string gives false where it gave true: replacing the root drops what was compiled against it.

Option scoring. getFirstMatchingOption() and getClosestMatchingOption() match an option as JSON Schema reads it, and check in JavaScript that the data holds a key the option declares: a key named by its properties or patternProperties, or by those of its $ref target, its allOf entries, its then/else and its dependencies schemas. Where something in that scope declares properties, scoring drops every required in the scope, and every dependencies entry listing names, so a user who has yet to fill in a required key is still matched to the option; before, it dropped only the option's own required, and only when the option itself declared properties. An option whose scope declares no properties, as in the "at least one of" pattern, is matched by its required as before:

const rootSchema: RJSFSchema = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { email: { type: 'string' }, phone: { type: 'string' } },
  oneOf: [{ title: 'By email', required: ['email'] }, { title: 'By phone', required: ['phone'] }],
};
getFirstMatchingOption(context, { phone: '1' }, rootSchema.oneOf, rootSchema);
// before and after: 1

An option written as a $ref, or composed with allOf, is now matched as one written out in place is:

const rootSchema: RJSFSchema = {
  definitions: {
    A: { type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'number' } } },
    B: { type: 'object', properties: { b: { type: 'number' } } },
    Base: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['id'] },
  },
};
getFirstMatchingOption(context, { b: 1 }, [{ $ref: '#/definitions/A' }, { $ref: '#/definitions/B' }], rootSchema);
// before: 0, the first option matching any object; after: 1
getFirstMatchingOption(
  context,
  { kind: 'x' },
  [
    { type: 'object', properties: { kind: { const: 'y' } } },
    { allOf: [{ $ref: '#/definitions/Base' }], properties: { kind: { const: 'x' } } },
  ],
  rootSchema,
);
// before: 0, since Base's `required` failed the second option; after: 1

Where an option's own then overrides a keyword when the form renders it, scoring now holds the data to both, as validating the whole form on submit already did. When transformChange rewrites an option switch, MultiSchemaField checks the data against the option it keeps, read the same way. getOptionMatchingSimpleDiscriminator() and relaxOptionsForScoring() are removed, since option scoring no longer calls them; see Changes to existing utility functions.

Dependency oneOf options. A dependencies schema's oneOf option is applied when the property the dependency names fits what the option declares for it, and that declaration is now found in the same scope: the option's own properties, or those of its $ref target, its allOf entries, its then/else and its dependencies schemas. Before, only its own properties or its $ref target's counted, so an option declaring the property only in an allOf entry never applied:

const schema: RJSFSchema = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { k: { type: 'string', enum: ['a', 'b'] } },
  dependencies: {
    k: {
      oneOf: [
        { allOf: [{ properties: { k: { enum: ['a'] } } }], properties: { ka: { type: 'string', default: 'A' } } },
        { allOf: [{ properties: { k: { enum: ['b'] } } }], properties: { kb: { type: 'string', default: 'B' } } },
      ],
    },
  },
};
getDefaultFormState(context, { schema, rootSchema: schema, formData: { k: 'b' } });
// before: { k: 'b' }, the form shows `k` alone and warns "ignoring oneOf in dependencies"
// after:  { k: 'b', kb: 'B' }, the form shows `k` and `kb`

The same reading can make a second option apply where one did, and the dependency then applies neither, since exactly one option has to match:

const schema: RJSFSchema = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { k: { type: 'string', enum: ['a', 'b'] } },
  dependencies: {
    k: {
      oneOf: [
        { allOf: [{ properties: { k: { enum: ['a', 'b'] } } }], properties: { ka: { type: 'string', default: 'A' } } },
        { properties: { k: { enum: ['b'] }, kb: { type: 'string', default: 'B' } } },
      ],
    },
  },
};
getDefaultFormState(context, { schema, rootSchema: schema, formData: { k: 'b' } });
// before: { k: 'b', kb: 'B' }, the form shows `k` and `kb`
// after:  { k: 'b' }, the form shows `k` alone and warns "ignoring oneOf in dependencies"

Precompiled validators. Regenerate precompiled validator code with compileSchemaValidators() or compileSchemaValidatorsCode(): code generated by an earlier version throws No precompiled validator function was found. The new getValidationSchemas(rootSchema) lists what is compiled: the root, a $ref to each if and option, to the property each option declares under any discriminator.propertyName in the root, the copy of an option scoring derives where it drops a required, each dependency condition, and, where an option is a boolean, {}, the schema SchemaField retrieves it as, with { not: {} }, the schema a false option reads as. schemaParser(), its 6.x name, is gone; call getValidationSchemas() in its place. The list depends on the root alone and grows with its size, so schemas that failed to compile or failed in the form now work:

Schema6.11.07.0.0
definitions.node recursing through u: { anyOf: [{ $ref: node }, { type: 'string' }] }, used as v: { oneOf: [{ $ref: node }, { type: 'number' }] }the compile throws can't resolve reference #/definitions/nodecompiles; v matches { n: 'a', u: { n: 'b' } } to option 0 and 5 to option 1
a root with dependencies: { a: ['b'] } and oneOf: [{ $ref: '#' }, { properties: { c } }] (#5452 c)the compile overflows the stackcompiles
an option with properties: { id } and patternProperties: { '^s_': ..., '^s_n': ... }, data { id: 'a', s_na: 'xx' } (#5454)scoring the retrieved options throws No precompiled validator function was foundoption 0
an option { $id: 'myOption', properties: { id }, additionalProperties: { type: 'string' } }, data { id: 'a', extra: 'x' } (#5455)the compile throws schema with key or id "myOption" already existsoption 0
s: { allOf: [{ discriminator: { propertyName: 'kind' } }], oneOf: [A, B] }, or s: { discriminator, allOf: [{ oneOf: [A, B] }] }, where A and B declare kind as const 'a' and 'b', data { b: 'q' }scoring the options throws No precompiled validator function was foundoption 1

A schema a merge makes has no place in the root and is not compiled, as in 6.11.0: an option a customMergeAllOf rewrites, or one made by merging the oneOfs of two patternProperties matching the same key, throws No precompiled validator function was found when the form scores it. The error names the subschema when the schema it has no function for is a $ref. A subschema the root holds in several places, as a schema module that reuses one object holds it, is compiled at each place, so code compiled from the module serves an equal copy of it, such as its JSON, and the other way round, as in 6.11.0.

@rjsf/validator-ata compiles each schema as a document of its own, and ata-validator resolves a $ref only to an entry of the definitions or $defs in it. So each document carries what it reaches of the root: every subschema of the root it names through a $ref, such as a definition, a property, an option or the root itself, as an entry of its own in one container, the $ref renamed to it, since ata-validator compiles nothing for a document holding both definitions and $defs, and does not percent-decode a $ref such as #/definitions/c%20d. A $ref beside other keywords is compiled as an allOf entry beside them, as 2019-09, 2020-12 and Ajv read it, since ata-validator compiles no $ref beside keywords that assert something. A property that refers back to itself, tree: { type: 'object', properties: { name: { type: 'string' }, kids: { type: 'array', items: { $ref: '#/properties/tree' } } } }, now validates, reporting .tree.kids.0.kids.0.name for { tree: { kids: [{ kids: [{ name: 5 }] }] } }, where 6.11.0 overflowed the stack. A $ref that names nothing in the root, or one into another document, leaves ata-validator nothing to compile, which throws was not compiled to a standalone validator when the form validates against it. ata-validator compiles no function for a schema holding only annotations either, so each schema without a not or a $ref is compiled with not: { not: {} }, which always holds: a precompiled validator for the root { title: 'Anything' } returns true from isValid() where it threw was not compiled to a standalone validator.

JUNK_OPTION_ID is removed from @rjsf/utils: nothing read it any more.

Option selection and cycle expansion are form state​

The anyOf/oneOf option a field shows and which collapsed $ref cycles are expanded are kept by the form, by field path, rather than by the AnyOfField/OneOfField and CyclicSchemaField components. They survive the field unmounting and mounting again and follow the moves the form makes, of array items and of additional properties renamed or removed. The sections below list what changes; "before" is what 6.11.0 gives.

The selected option no longer follows the data while you type BREAKING CHANGE​

With no selection, a field shows the option getClosestMatchingOption() picks for its data, as before. A selection, the user's or that pick once an edit is made inside the option, holds for the data the form last rendered under it and for the data the form's own changes inside the option leave at the field, whatever those edits made of it, so a switch or an edit transformChange refuses keeps it too. Other data, such as setFieldValue()'s, a reset, a transformChange that rewrites a switch to data the chosen option does not fit, or an edit to a property the object declares beside its options that the options can disagree about, one an option names under properties, such as with a const that tells the options apart, or under required, or any such property where an option carries a keyword that reads the object whole, such as minProperties, not or additionalProperties, is shown under the option getClosestMatchingOption() picks for it, the selection winning a tie, as on 6.11.0, even when it is the data the field showed before the switch. An edit to a property every option is silent about, where each carries only type, annotations such as title, and properties and required that leave the property out, holds the option shown, as an edit inside the option does: every option says the same of that property, so the edit cannot be a choice between them. That pick does not replace the selection, and the selection is kept by field path, so it outlives the data it was made for. A field whose data holds a value for the discriminator.propertyName its schema declares is always shown under the option that value names, as before: the discriminator is the selector, so an edit to it is a switch.

  • With o: { anyOf: [{ title: 'A', type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string', default: 'd' } } }, { title: 'B', type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string' }, b: { type: 'string' } } }] }, select B, clear root_o_a and type d. Before: the selector went back to A, whose default the data now matched, and root_o_b disappeared. After: it stays on B, with root_o_b.
  • With { type: 'object', properties: { name: { type: 'string' } }, oneOf: [{ title: 'A', properties: { a: { type: 'string' } } }, { title: 'B', properties: { a: { type: 'string', maxLength: 2 }, b: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['b'] }] }, select B, type z into root_b, abc into root_a and then n into root_name. Before: the selector went to A at abc, which B rejects, and root_b disappeared; with omitExtraData and liveOmit, b: 'z' was dropped there. After: it stays on B through both edits, with { a: 'abc', b: 'z', name: 'n' }.
  • With { type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string' }, b: { type: 'string' } }, oneOf: [{ title: 'A', required: ['a'] }, { title: 'B', required: ['b'] }] } and {}, type x into root_b: the selector goes to B, before and after, since B's required names b. So does anyOf: [{ title: 'Few', maxProperties: 1 }, { title: 'Many', minProperties: 2 }] with { a: 'x' } when y is typed into root_b: Many, before and after.
  • A condition that swaps the option list a field offers starts the choice over. With kind: { enum: ['a', 'b'], default: 'a' }, if: { properties: { kind: { const: 'a' } } }, then: { properties: { x: { anyOf: [A1, A2] } } } and else: { properties: { x: { anyOf: [B1, B2] } } }, select A2, then b for kind. Before: B2, the index carried over. After: B1, the option the data matches; selecting a again shows A2 before and after.
  • A field that mounts again shows the option selected before. With the o above, select B, then render the form with o: { 'ui:field': Nothing, 'ui:fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf': true } and again without it. Before: A. After: B.
  • Data setFieldValue() sets that every option fits shows the selection, rather than the option an earlier call matched. With the root oneOf: [{ title: 'A', type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string' } } }, { title: 'B', type: 'object', properties: { b: { type: 'string' } } }], select B and type y into root_b; setFieldValue('', { a: 'x' }) then shows A before and after, and setFieldValue('', {}) shows, before, A, and after, B.
  • A selection outlives the array item it was made for. With { type: 'array', items: ...that oneOf } and [{}, {}], select B on the second item; setFieldValue('', [{}]) and later setFieldValue('', [{}, {}]). Before: the new second item shows A. After: B, the selection made at that index, which the new item's data fits. An item a field removes or moves takes its selection with it.

AnyOfField and OneOfField read and write the selection with useOptionSelection(), which @rjsf/core exports, and SchemaField reads it to stub an object's extra keys with the selected option (below). A custom AnyOfField or OneOfField that keeps the selection in its own state shows one option while the object beside it is stubbed for another, so read and write it through the hook instead; the options prop stays:

import { useOptionSelection } from '@rjsf/core';

const { selectedOption, selectOption } = useOptionSelection(registry, fieldPath, options, formData, discriminator);
// on a pick: selectOption(index), then onChange(dataForTheNewOption, fieldPath)

An object's extra keys are stubbed once, with the selected option BREAKING CHANGE​

An object field whose anyOf/oneOf options are rendered beside it stubs the extra keys of its data once, for itself and the selected option together. A key the selected option declares is left to the option, which renders it, and the object takes the option's additionalProperties, unevaluatedProperties and patternProperties beside its own: a key either describes is described by both, and a key either forbids is forbidden. The option's own field no longer stubs keys a second time. Where the selected option offers options of its own, the field it renders beside them takes the extra keys in the object's place, for the object, the option and the option it selects together, since only that field knows which of its options declares a key.

  • additionalProperties: { type: 'object', properties: { host: { type: 'string' }, port: { type: 'number' } } } beside anyOf: [{ patternProperties: { '^x-': { type: 'string' } } }], with the data { db: { host: 'h', port: 1 } } (#5462). Before: db rendered twice, as the object's root_db_host and root_db_port and as a second key row the option stubbed. After: once, with root_db_host and root_db_port.
  • properties: { name: { type: 'string' } } beside oneOf: [{ additionalProperties: { type: 'number' } }], with the data { name: 'n', k: 1 }. Before: root_name rendered twice, the second time as a key row the option stubbed. After: once, with k as a number row and the add button beside it.
  • additionalProperties: true beside oneOf: [{ oneOf: [{ properties: { x: { type: 'string' } }, additionalProperties: { type: 'string' } }] }], with the data { x: 'a', extra: 'e' }. Before: x and extra rendered twice, as the object's key rows and the nested option's, with an add button in each of the two object fields. After: once, in the nested option's field, with one add button.
  • additionalProperties: { type: 'string' } beside oneOf: [{ properties: { a: { type: 'string' } }, additionalProperties: false }], with the data { a: 'v', other: 'o' }. Before: root_a rendered twice, once as a string row of the object, and other as a string row. After: root_a once, the option's, and other gets no field, since the option forbids it.
  • additionalProperties: { type: 'string' } beside anyOf: [{ properties: { count: { type: 'number' } } }, { properties: { count: { type: 'number' }, b: { type: 'string' } } }]: add a property and rename newKey to count (#5461). Before: the data was { count: 'New Value' }, the string the add button wrote for a key the object describes, shown in the option's number field and, on 6.11.0, in a second key row as well. After: the data is { count: 0 }, seeded from the option's declaration, with root_count once. The option is the one SchemaField shows, so where a ui:field with ui:fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf keeps the options from rendering, the key is an extra key and the rename gives { count: 'New Value' }, before and after.
  • retrieveSchema() takes the selected option as a new last argument, selectedOption. Without it, the extra keys are stubbed for the object alone, a key an option declares included, as on 6.11.0.
  • getRenderedOptionSchema() renders the option of an object without its additionalProperties, patternProperties and unevaluatedProperties.
  • ObjectField renders the schema it is handed as it stands, where it retrieved it again for the data: SchemaField hands it the schema already retrieved, its extra keys stubbed with the selected option. A custom field that renders ObjectField itself with a schema it did not receive from SchemaField, such as a definition looked up in the root schema, retrieves it first, or the properties its $ref, allOf and conditions bring in, and the extra keys of the data, get no field: <ObjectField {...props} schema={registry.schemaUtils.retrieveSchema(schema, formData)} />. One that passes on the schema prop it received is unaffected.

getClosestMatchingOption() picks among the candidates BREAKING CHANGE​

getClosestMatchingOption() returns an option the data matches whenever one does, and some option whenever there are options: a tie goes to the selectedOption only where the data matches it, or where no option matches the data, and to the first candidate otherwise. A property holding an anyOf/oneOf of its own adds the score of the option picked among those, plus one where the data matches it, rather than that option's index.

getClosestMatchingOption(context, rootSchema, undefined, [{ type: 'string' }, { type: 'number' }]);
// Before: -1. After: 0
getClosestMatchingOption(context, rootSchema, undefined, [{ type: 'string' }, { type: 'number' }], 2);
// Before: 2, an index past the options. After: 0

A field opens on such a pick, so a field whose first option is { type: 'null', title: 'None' } and whose data several other options match opens on one of those: with five definitions A to E, each { type: 'object', properties: { child: { oneOf: [{ type: 'null', title: 'None' }, ...a $ref to each of the four others] } } }, the root oneOf: [{ type: 'null', title: 'None' }, ...a $ref to each definition] and the formData { child: { child: { child: null } } }, before, the form opened on None and rendered the root selector alone; after, it opens on A and renders a selector at each of the four levels.

The pick is remembered per option list and data object, so a form whose definitions refer to each other through oneOf options matches each level of its data once (#4990): rendering a form of five such definitions with the formData four levels deep validated 2124 times before, four times as many per level, and 122 times after, 35 more per level. Within one call a remembered pick is reused without looking at the data again, since a validator's isValid() must not change the data it checks (see below). A later call reuses it only while the data still holds what a copy kept with it holds, so data you mutate in place between calls is matched for what it holds now; that comparison costs time in proportion to the data below the option list, once per call. An object other than an array or a plain object, such as a Date, a File or a class instance, can't be copied, so a pick for data holding one is reused only within the call that made it: each call matches that data again, still once per level of it, and sees a change made in place since the last call.

A validator's isValid() must leave the data as it is BREAKING CHANGE​

ValidatorType.isValid() must not change the data it is handed, at any depth, since getClosestMatchingOption() reuses a pick it made for some data during the same call without comparing the data again. @rjsf/validator-ajv8 validates a copy of the data in isValid() under Ajv's useDefaults, coerceTypes and removeAdditional options and with a keyword registered with modifying: true, where Ajv wrote defaults and coerced values into the form's data and deleted properties from it while the form checked a condition or an option; validateFormData() and rawValidation() still validate the data itself. @rjsf/validator-ata already validated a copy, and @rjsf/validator-cfworker doesn't change the data. A ValidatorType of your own whose engine fills in defaults, coerces values or removes properties as it validates has to hand it a copy of the data in isValid().

const validator = customizeValidator({ ajvOptionsOverrides: { useDefaults: true } });
const schema: RJSFSchema = { type: 'object', properties: { flag: { type: 'string', default: 'on' } } };
const formData = {};
validator.isValid(schema, formData, schema);
// Before: formData is { flag: 'on' }. After: formData is {}, and isValid() still returns true

Switching from a null option restores the field's default​

A field that held nothing, as after a null option, and switches to an option whose defaults are an object gets the defaults of the field with that option alone, so a default the field declares comes back with the option's own (#5368). Those defaults hold no key set to undefined, so a default an ancestor declares for the field fills the keys they leave, as the form fills any other. With { type: 'object', oneOf: [{ title: 'Obj', type: 'object', required: ['kind'], properties: { kind: { const: 'obj' }, note: { type: 'string', default: 'from-option' }, extra: { type: 'string' } } }, { title: 'None', type: 'null' }], default: { kind: 'obj', extra: 'from-root' } }, select None, then Obj. Before: { note: 'from-option' }. After: { kind: 'obj', note: 'from-option', extra: 'from-root' }, the data the form mounted with. With the same oneOf as properties.w.properties.p and the default declared on the root as { w: { p: { kind: 'obj', extra: 'from-root' } } }, the round trip gave { w: { p: { note: 'from-option' } } } and gives { w: { p: { kind: 'obj', note: 'from-option', extra: 'from-root' } } }. The form mounts with { w: { p: { kind: 'obj', extra: 'from-root' } } }, before and after: on mount the ancestor's default object stands in for the option's own leaf defaults, while the switch writes the option's defaults and the ancestor's fill the keys they leave. An object property of the option gets the empty object a switch from another object option gives it, as before: with meta: { type: 'object', properties: { a: { type: 'string' } } } in Obj, the switch from None writes meta: {} before and after.

Cycle expansion is form state BREAKING CHANGE​

CyclicSchemaField reads which fields are expanded from the form and renders an expanded one from expandRefCycle(schema, rootSchema), which @rjsf/utils exports. retrieveSchema() no longer reads RJSF_REF_CYCLE_KEY: false on a copy of a flagged schema as an expansion: the copy is resolved like any other copy of the field it was made from, keeping its $ref path, so its recursion collapses where the field's would. A custom field that wrote { ...schema, [RJSF_REF_CYCLE_KEY]: false } to expand a field calls expandRefCycle() instead.

  • With t: { $ref: node } and node = { type: 'object', properties: { name: { type: 'string' }, child: { $ref: node } } }, click #root_t_child__expand, then render the form with t: { 'ui:field': Nothing } and again without it. Before: #root_t_child__expand again. After: root_t_child_name and #root_t_child_child__expand, as before the remount.

Sanitize is a diff of the field trees BREAKING CHANGE​

Form sanitizes its data by comparing the field tree the data before a change builds with the one the data after it builds, field by field, as each is rendered: the option the form selects and the $ref cycles the user expanded. A field that left the tree loses its value, unless the object still holds it as an extra key that constrains nothing, as under additionalProperties: true, and that extra key renders it: a scalar, or an object whose keys the extra key takes as its own, stays and renders as an extra key. An array, whose items such an extra key renders none of, is dropped, and so is a value equal to what the form fills the old field with from data without it, such as its default, its const, an empty object or its ui:initialValue or ui:emptyValue, even one the user chose. A kept value is judged by the extra key alone, so a limit the new branch puts on the object's keys, such as propertyNames or maxProperties, can reject it, which validation reports. For the form to drop the value instead, give that branch additionalProperties: false, with the keys it keeps declared in its own properties. Switching an anyOf/oneOf option through its selector leaves a property only the old option declares for this same diff, which judges it against the old option and the whole form's defaults, so a switch keeps and drops what a branch does. The object's extra keys are described by the new option's additionalProperties joined to its own, so an option with additionalProperties: false drops the property, and one whose extra keys have a schema of their own, as { type: 'string' }, keeps a value that schema's constraints take, as a branch does. A switch to an option declaring no properties no longer clears the object: it keeps the object's own fields and extra keys, whether or not the object takes extra keys and whether or not such a property stays. The kept key can make the data match the old option again: data loaded through initialFormData, formData or reset() opens on the first option it matches, so with options told apart only by the properties they declare it can open on the old one. Give the options a const property, or a discriminator, for the data to open on the option the user chose. A field whose constraints changed (its type, const, enum or constant options, maxItems, or the default its own schema or its parent's default object declares) has its value judged again: a value still holding the old default takes the new one, written in place, and a value of another type, or one the new const or enum rejects, is replaced or dropped as sanitizeDataForNewSchema() does it. An array's items are judged by the schema their position declares: a prefixItems or tuple items entry, and past them items, or additionalItems beside a tuple. An item is of another type only where its position's new type leaves out one the old schema declared there, a number counting as naming integer, and a position the old schema declared true, false or nothing at judges the item by the new schema alone. Where an item reaches a position the new schema closes with false, or the new schema rejects a prefix item, whose removal would move the items after it, the whole array is removed instead, for the defaults to fill, as sanitizeDataForNewSchema() clears it. The array keeps its items where the old schema closed that position with false too, and where both schemas declare a schema for a rejected prefix item's position and constrain it alike, its default aside, so the item already failed the old one. It keeps them too where the item is an unfilled prefix item or is at or past the new maxItems, where the user is editing the array or a field in it, and where the array is an item of another array. A field whose constraints did not change keeps its value, whatever else the change did. "Before" is what 6.11.0 gives.

  • A condition inside the selected option replaces its old default (#5465). With cfgFor = (name) => ({ type: 'object', default: { name }, properties: { name: { type: 'string' } } }), thing: { oneOf: [X, Y] } where X is { type: 'object', properties: { mode: { enum: ['a', 'b'], default: 'a' } }, dependencies: { mode: { oneOf: [{ properties: { mode: { const: 'a' }, cfg: cfgFor('a') } }, { properties: { mode: { const: 'b' }, cfg: cfgFor('b') } }] } } }, and the data { thing: { mode: 'a', cfg: { name: 'a' } } }, select b for mode. Before: cfg: { name: 'a' }. After: cfg: { name: 'b' }.
  • A default declared by a branch that requires the key is replaced too. With cfg declared plainly and allOf: [{ if: { properties: { mode: { const: 'a' } }, required: ['mode', 'cfg'] }, then: { properties: { cfg: cfgFor('a') } } }, ...the same for 'b'], select b for mode with the data { mode: 'a', cfg: { name: 'a' } }. Before: cfg: { name: 'a' }. After: cfg: { name: 'b' }.
  • An array or object write is sanitized like any other edit. With list: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } }, color: { enum: ['r', 'g'] } and allOf: [{ if: { properties: { list: { minItems: 2 } } }, then: { properties: { color: { enum: ['r'] } } } }], add a row to list with the data { color: 'g', list: ['x'] }. Before: color: 'g' until the next edit replaced it. After: color: 'r' as the row is added.
  • A schema change of a form that owns its data is sanitized as it arrives, unless the form is disabled or readonly, whose data no edit sanitizes either. With color: { $ref: '#/definitions/Color' } and Color narrowed from enum: ['a', 'b'] to enum: ['a'], and initialFormData { color: 'b' }. Before: color: 'b', kept until an edit sanitized and, with no conditional in the schema, for good. After: color: 'a' at once. Whether 6.11.0 ever replaced the value turned on a conditional elsewhere in the schema, so the form now applies one rule, the one an edit follows, to the schema change itself.
  • A value setFieldValue('', data) sets is taken as written, and no edit judges it unless the edit changes that field's constraints. With mode: { enum: ['basic', 'advanced'] }, color: { type: 'string' }, note: { type: 'string' } and allOf: [{ if: { properties: { mode: { const: 'advanced' } } }, then: { properties: { color: { enum: ['r', 'c'] } } }, else: { properties: { color: { enum: ['r'] } } } }], set { mode: 'basic', color: 'c' } and type into note: color: 'c' stays, which validation reports. An array setFieldValue() writes whole at its own path pairs each item that holds what an item of the array held with that item, so a reorder set back keeps the constraints its rows had.
  • An extra key holding the old branch's additionalProperties default takes the new one, as a declared property does. With mode: { enum: ['a', 'b'], default: 'a' } and dependencies: { mode: { oneOf: [{ properties: { mode: { const: 'a' } }, additionalProperties: tagFor('a') }, { properties: { mode: { const: 'b' } }, additionalProperties: tagFor('b') }] } }, where tagFor = (tag) => ({ type: 'object', default: { tag }, properties: { tag: { type: 'string' } } }), and the data { mode: 'a', extra: { tag: 'a' } }, select b for mode. Before: the form threw Cannot use 'in' operator to search for 'tag' in a as it rendered. After: extra: { tag: 'b' }.

sanitizeDataForNewSchema() takes newSchema, oldSchema and data alone, as on 6.11.0: the oldData, resolvedOldSchema and oldDataForPairing parameters earlier v7 builds added are removed. An object property whose data holds a value other than an object is sanitized to an empty object, or left out where its schema declares no properties, and one the data doesn't hold is left out (see sanitizeDataForNewSchema() removes the keys it discards), rather than sanitized as an empty object, which filled the new defaults of its own properties and descended into their object properties in turn, without end behind a recursive $ref. The defaults the form computes fill those properties in.

ui:required and omitting extra data read the option on screen​

The ui:required check and omitting extra data read the option a field shows and the cycles the user expanded, through a new optional fieldState argument of getUiRequiredErrorSchema() and omitExtraData(), which Form passes. With thing: { anyOf: [{ properties: { aField } }, { properties: { bField } }] }, ui:required on bField and the data { thing: { aField: 'a' } }, a field showing the second option now blocks the submit for the missing bField, where the check read the first option, which the data matches best. With a recursive node whose child is { $ref: node }, ui:required on child.name blocks the submit once the user expands child, and not before. Omitting keeps the data of the option shown: with thing: { anyOf: [{ properties: { a } }, { properties: { b } }] }, the data { thing: { b: 'v' } } and the first option shown, submitting with omitExtraData drops b, which the option on screen has no field for; it kept b while the option was read from the data. An edit reads the option the field shows while it is made, so live omitting and live validation agree with the screen: with the root oneOf: [{ title: 'A', properties: { a: { type: 'string' } } }, { title: 'B', properties: { a: { type: 'string', maxLength: 2 }, b: { type: 'string' } } }], omitExtraData and liveOmit: 'onChange', select B, type z into root_b and abc into root_a. Before: the selector went to A, which the data now matches, and b was dropped with root_b. After: B stays on screen with root_b, and the data is { a: 'abc', b: 'z' }. With ui:required on b and liveValidate: 'onChange' in place of the omit, the same steps report .b must have required property 'b' under B, where the form showed A and no error. Omitting keeps its two policies, as on 6.11.0: an optional object whose filtered content is all empty is pruned, and an anyOf over empty data applies every branch.

A field is named once per data path BREAKING CHANGE​

A field's own ui:field and the schema's $id name a custom field through one slot, read in that order, so a field named by $id renders the way one named by ui:field does (#5391). A named field is applied once per data path (#5377): a SchemaField rendered for the same data below it, and the selected anyOf/oneOf option, render as though no field were named. "Before" is what 6.11.0 gives. With fields={{ MyField }} and anyOf = { type: 'string', anyOf: [{ minLength: 2 }, { maxLength: 5 }] }:

  • schema: { $id: 'MyField', ...anyOf }. Before: MyField is not rendered; the option selector and the selected option's input render. After: MyField renders beside the option selector, above the selected option's input.
  • schema: { $id: 'MyField', ...anyOf } with uiSchema: { 'ui:fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf': true }. Before: as above. After: MyField renders alone, in place of the options.
  • schema: anyOf with uiSchema: { 'ui:field': 'MyField' }. Before: MyField renders twice, beside the option selector and again in place of the selected option's input. After: once beside the option selector, and the selected option renders its own input (#5358). The field's own label is still left to MyField, as a ui:field always left it.
  • schema: anyOf with uiSchema: { 'ui:field': 'MyField', anyOf: [{ 'ui:field': 'OptionField' }, {}] } and OptionField registered too. Before: MyField beside the option selector, and OptionField for the selected option. After: MyField beside the option selector, and the selected option's own input: the option renders at the data path MyField was named for, so its own ui:field is not applied, and the console warns once that it is ignored. A ui:field from a ui:definitions entry for the option's $ref is ignored the same way, and the warning names uiSchema.anyOf[0], the entry the definition is copied into. The same holds for an option naming OptionField by $id (anyOf: [{ $id: 'OptionField', minLength: 2 }, { maxLength: 5 }]), which 6.11.0 rendered as MyField a second time, though a $id, an identifier first, is not warned about. Without the ui:field on the union, the option's own field renders, as before.
  • schema: { type: 'object', properties: { val: { type: 'string' } } } with uiSchema: { val: { 'ui:field': 'SchemaField' } }. Before: the page runs out of memory. After: the field renders exactly as though no field were named, whichever of ui:field or a $id names it: one input, root_val, labelled by the field's title, with one description, help and option selector. A field named FallbackField likewise renders as it does for a schema whose type sends it there, labelled as though no field were named.

A custom field that renders registry.fields.SchemaField for its own data gets the default field for the schema, whatever the uiSchema it passes names. That field draws the label, description and help the custom field's plan hands down to it, as the plan section describes, and the extra key's input and remove button and the anyOf/oneOf option selector stay with the field's own SchemaField, so each renders once. To render another custom field for the same data, render that field's component directly; to render a different custom field for an option, name it on the option alone, rather than beside a field named for the union. Each Form starts with no field named, so a Form rendered inside a custom field applies its own root ui:field or $id.

getUiOptions() returns a field's options alone BREAKING CHANGE​

getUiOptions(uiSchema, globalOptions) leaves a required in globalOptions out, and no longer returns the root uiSchema's ui:definitions and ui:globalOptions keys as options (#5527). A form-wide required was never read by the required marker or by validation, which take ui:required from the field's own uiSchema, but it reached the options of a boolean field's widget, of an array field's select, checkboxes or file widget, and of the anyOf/oneOf selector. "Before" is what 6.11.0 gives.

  • schema: { type: 'object', properties: { flag: { type: 'boolean' } } } with uiSchema: { 'ui:globalOptions': { required: true } }: the CheckboxWidget's options.required. Before: true. After: undefined.
  • schema: { type: 'string' } with uiSchema: { 'ui:definitions': {} }: the TextWidget's options.definitions. Before: {}. After: undefined.

A field's own ui:required is still an option. Read the form's definitions and global options from registry.uiSchemaDefinitions and registry.globalUiOptions.

ui:options ignores field and the other keys it doesn't take BREAKING CHANGE​

A field, fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf, definitions or globalOptions in ui:options is ignored, with a console warning, as the exceptions to the equivalence list them. The warning names the key but not the field, and logs once per key, so search your uiSchemas for them rather than waiting on the console. "Before" is what 6.11.0 gives.

  • uiSchema: { 'ui:options': { field: 'MyField' } }. Before: MyField renders. After: the field for the schema's type renders.
  • schema: anyOf with uiSchema: { 'ui:field': 'MyField', 'ui:options': { fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf: true } }. Before: MyField renders alone, in place of the options. After: MyField renders beside the option selector.
  • uiSchema: { 'ui:options': { definitions: {} } }: a widget's options.definitions. Before: {}. After: undefined.

Move the keys out of ui:options:

- 'ui:options': { field: 'MyField', fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf: true },
+ 'ui:field': 'MyField',
+ 'ui:fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf': true,

A layout grid's children entry is affected too, since its extra properties become the cell's ui:options, so a field there moves to ui:field in the cell's own uiSchema entry.

A custom field named by ui:options.field got the template's label and description, and one named by ui:field gets neither. To keep them, declare them under the field's registry key, registering a field given as a component so that it has one.

A custom field named by ui:field isn't handed the select SchemaField now infers for a boolean with labelled oneOf/anyOf options, so one that renders BooleanField shows the checkbox 6.11.0 showed. Set ui:widget: 'select' to get the select.

ui:definitions and ui:globalOptions belong on the root uiSchema. A custom widget that took an option of one of these names through ui:options needs another name for it, since ui:field names a field and getUiOptions() doesn't return ui:definitions or ui:globalOptions.

A typed uiSchema giving one of these keys in ui:options stops compiling, and so does one handing ui:options what getUiOptions() returned, which can hold a field and a fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf. Leave those two out:

- 'ui:options': getUiOptions(uiSchema),
+ const { field, fieldReplacesAnyOrOneOf, ...options } = getUiOptions(uiSchema);
+ 'ui:options': options,

A custom field rendering FallbackField without a plan has the value field draw its label BREAKING CHANGE​

Under useFallbackUiForUnsupportedType, a custom field that renders registry.fields.FallbackField without handing it its presentation has the value field, below the type selector, draw the field's label and description, however the form reached the custom field (#5389). Without a plan, FallbackField can't tell whether the custom field draws a label of its own, so it always has the value field draw one, which a custom field drawing none needs to give its value an accessible name. "Before" is what 6.11.0 gives. With schema: { type: 'object', properties: { val: { type: ['string', 'number'], title: 'Val', description: 'Desc' } } } and a custom field MyField that draws no label or description of its own:

  • MyField named by ui:field. Before: the page runs out of stack, since FallbackField rendered its value through SchemaField with the uiSchema that names MyField, which is now applied once per data path. After: one label, Val, below the type selector, and one description.
  • MyField named by the schema's $id. Before: two labels, Val and Value. After: as above.
  • MyField named by a ui:field that it removes from the uiSchema it passes on. Before: one label, Value, and no description. After: as above.

A custom field that draws its own label and description gets both a second time on every one of those routes, the second description under the same id as its own. Leave the label and description to the value field: draw neither in the custom field, and the value field draws each once.

ui:globalOptions hold only the options RJSF reads there BREAKING CHANGE​

RJSF reads twelve options from the root uiSchema's ui:globalOptions, as fallbacks for a field that sets none of its own: addable, copyable, orderable, removable, label, allowClearTextInputs, duplicateKeySuffixSeparator, enableMarkdownInDescription, enableMarkdownInHelp, enableOptionalDataFieldForType, optionValueFormat and deprecatedHandling (#5607). They are the GlobalUISchemaOptionsKeys type. Every other option is read per field only: the Form builds its registry's globalUiOptions with pickGlobalUiOptions(), which keeps those twelve and the extension keys the form declares, and nothing else. The console warns once about each option RJSF reads per field that ui:globalOptions still sets, such as readonly or widget. A custom component hands getUiOptions() the registry's globalUiOptions, which hold the extension keys the theme and the Form declare. One that reads a root uiSchema's ui:globalOptions of its own instead passes them through pickGlobalUiOptions() with those keys, as its second argument, or it keeps only RJSF's twelve. An option set globally that RJSF no longer reads there moves as follows:

Set in ui:globalOptionsSet instead
widget, fieldthe field's own ui:widget or ui:field, or a replacement for the registered implementation through the Form's widgets or fields, such as widgets={{ TextWidget: MyTextWidget }}
A template override, such as FieldTemplatethe Form's templates
readonly, disabledthe Form's readonly and disabled props
hideErrorui:hideError at the root of the uiSchema, which reaches every field below it
help, title, description, placeholder, classNames, inputType, an array's itemLabel and any other option a field readsthe field's own uiSchema

GlobalUISchemaOptions is closed to those twelve keys, so a ui:globalOptions literal with any other key no longer compiles. Its UserExtensions parameter adds the keys your own components read, which may not reuse an option name RJSF reads for a field, or definitions or globalOptions, which only the root uiSchema's ui: keys set, as ReservedUiOptionName and RESERVED_UI_OPTION_NAMES list them. Declare the options against it, hand them to the uiSchema, which takes them as the plain type, and name their keys in the Form's new globalUiOptionsKeys prop:

import { GlobalUISchemaOptions, UiSchema } from '@rjsf/utils';

const globalOptions: GlobalUISchemaOptions<{ density?: 'compact' | 'comfortable' }> = {
  label: false,
  density: 'compact',
};
const uiSchema: UiSchema = { 'ui:globalOptions': globalOptions };

<Form schema={schema} uiSchema={uiSchema} validator={validator} globalUiOptionsKeys={['density']} />;

Every field then hands the declared keys to its widget in its options, beneath the field's own, as it does RJSF's, and a template reads them with getUiOptions(uiSchema, registry.globalUiOptions). A key that is an option name RJSF reads per field, such as widget, or definitions or globalOptions, which only the root uiSchema's ui: keys set, is not read from ui:globalOptions, and a warning says so.

The themes that read options of their own globally export a type for them, which takes your UserExtensions too: @rjsf/antd's AntdGlobalUISchemaOptions (block), @rjsf/chakra-ui's ChakraGlobalUISchemaOptions (chakra), @rjsf/daisyui's DaisyGlobalUISchemaOptions (daisy), @rjsf/mantine's MantineGlobalUISchemaOptions (gridCols, gridSpacing and gridVerticalSpacing) and @rjsf/mui's MuiGlobalUISchemaOptions (mui). Each of them also exports a UiSchema type whose ui:globalOptions carry its own option and your UserExtensions, so the option compiles there inline, such as { 'ui:globalOptions': { mui: { size: 'small' } } } typed by @rjsf/mui's UiSchema. Each declares its keys as its theme's globalUiOptionsKeys, a new ThemeProps field that withTheme() adds the Form's to, so a custom widget reads the theme's option from its options, and a custom template with getUiOptions(uiSchema, registry.globalUiOptions), as the theme's own do. Any other theme option is read per field only, unless the Form declares it in globalUiOptionsKeys. A theme's type also rejects a UserExtensions key its widgets read as an option of their own: @rjsf/daisyui's color, size and colorGradient, and @rjsf/mantine's wrapperProps, thumbProps, thumbLabel, valueFormat, displayFormat, colorFormat and the InputWrapper options, such as size, labelProps and inputContainer. @rjsf/shadcn exports no such type, but its RangeWidget reads props from its options and folds it into the slider's, so don't name an extension props with it. A Form from @rjsf/core handed a theme's widgets and templates directly, rather than built with withTheme() or the theme's own Form, declares none of the theme's keys, so it reads the theme's option from ui:globalOptions only when its globalUiOptionsKeys name it.

warning

@rjsf/mantine's widgets hand the options they don't recognize to their Mantine component as props, but leave out every key the registry's globalUiOptions hold that the field doesn't set itself, so a key declared for your own components, such as density, never reaches a Mantine input, while a field's own Mantine prop of the same name still does. A Mantine prop set in ui:globalOptions, such as radius or variant, reached the Mantine components of BooleanField's and ArrayField's widgets before, and now reaches none, even when declared: set it in each field's ui:options instead, or as a component's defaultProps in Mantine's own theme.

StringField, and NumberField through it, hand their widget the global options beneath the field's own, as ArrayField and BooleanField already did, so a global allowClearTextInputs or optionValueFormat now reaches every string and number widget.

LayoutGridField no longer copies the globals into each cell's uiSchema, which gave a cell's components globals no field outside a grid got. A cell's ui:options hold its own options and the ui:layoutGrid entry's props, and the cell carries no ui:globalOptions, so its widget's options no longer hold a globalOptions key. A custom field, widget or template in a cell that read a global from its uiSchema reads registry.globalUiOptions instead, as one outside a grid does, or getUiOptions(uiSchema, registry.globalUiOptions). A cell's own option, given as ui:<name> or in ui:options, now beats the global one, where the copy let a global label: false hide the label of a cell that set ui:label: true. Only the root uiSchema's ui:globalOptions are read, so one set on a nested grid's uiSchema no longer applies to that grid's cells.

A forbidden extra key says so on its row BREAKING CHANGE​

An extra key of the data that the object's additionalProperties, unevaluatedProperties or patternProperties forbid, on an object that takes extra keys, such as one matching none of the patternProperties beside additionalProperties: false, used to render a row with no input for its value and no word of why, until a submit reported must NOT have additional properties on the object (#4630). Its row now says The key "%1" is not allowed here from the first render on and right after a rename, without waiting for validation, so a snapshot of such a row gains the error. The message is the new TranslatableString.AdditionalPropertyKeyNotAllowed; a translateString that maps every key needs it. A key that only propertyNames forbids gets no such message. The key input of a forbidden key is now aria-invalid and described by the row's errors, so it is announced as invalid where the message is about it. A custom FieldTemplate that lists the props it forwards to WrapIfAdditionalTemplate one by one has to add the new keyNotAllowed prop to that list for the key to be marked. A custom WrapIfAdditionalTemplate that spreads the props it doesn't use onto an element has to leave out keyNotAllowed, which every theme's FieldTemplate now hands it, or React warns about unknown props on that element.

A dependency anyOf, or a dependency oneOf whose options don't declare the dependency's key, now applies BREAKING CHANGE​

A oneOf under dependencies is a dynamic dependency only when at least one of its options declares the dependency's key in its properties: the option whose properties[key] the data satisfies is merged in, as before. A list where no option declares the key used to be dropped with an ignoring oneOf in dependencies warning, though the validator still enforced it. It now applies as a oneOf beside dependencies does: the option the data matches is merged in, with no option selector, and getDefaultFormState() fills it the same way, so with

{
  "type": "object",
  "default": { "x": { "a": 1 } },
  "properties": {
    "x": { "type": "object", "enum": [{ "a": 1 }, { "a": 2 }], "dependencies": { "a": { "oneOf": [{ "const": { "a": 2 } }] } } }
  }
}

x renders as one select that starts on { "a": 2 } under constAsDefaults always and skipOneOf, as it does when the dependency is written { "const": { "a": 2 } }, and keeps { "a": 1 } under never (#5407). Removing the list brings back the old rendering, but also drops the constraint the validator enforced.

An anyOf under dependencies is merged the same way, as an anyOf beside dependencies is: the option the data matches is merged in, where the list used to stay on the field and render an option selector. An option that declares the dependency's key is merged less that property, as the option of a dynamic dependency is, so the key's own field keeps every value it offers and changing it brings in the option the new value matches. With no selector, the form offers no way to reach an option the data doesn't match: where none matches, the first is merged, so the fields only another option declares don't render until the data matches it. This applies only to the dependencies entry's own anyOf and oneOf: an anyOf that an allOf member or a then/else of the entry holds still renders an option selector, and a oneOf there is still read as part of the dynamic dependency. So to let the user pick the option, wrap the anyOf in an allOf member of the entry, which keeps the selector, keeps the options' properties beside the key's in the data, and still applies only when the key has a value:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": { "a": { "type": "string" } },
  "dependencies": {
    "a": {
      "allOf": [
        {
          "anyOf": [
            { "title": "With B", "properties": { "b": { "type": "string" } } },
            { "title": "With C", "properties": { "c": { "type": "number" } } }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Or make each option declare the dependency's key, so the key's value picks it.

GridType, Operators and TranslatableString are as const objects BREAKING CHANGE​

TranslatableString from @rjsf/utils, and GridType and Operators, which @rjsf/core now exports, are as const objects with a union type of the same name rather than enums. Their values and member access, such as GridType.ROW or TranslatableString.ArrayItemTitle, are unchanged, so code that only reads them keeps working.

Code that uses a member as a type has to name its type with typeof:

-const row: GridType.ROW = GridType.ROW;
+const row: typeof GridType.ROW = GridType.ROW;

The union type itself is still written by name, so GridType, Operators and TranslatableString as types need no change.

mergeObjects() and mergeSchemas() require an object first argument BREAKING CHANGE​

mergeObjects() and mergeSchemas() throw a TypeError when their first argument is undefined or null and the second has keys, where they used to treat it as {}. Their signatures always asked for an object, so this affects only code that called them with a value TypeScript didn't check. Pass {} instead:

-mergeObjects(maybeDefaults, overrides);
+mergeObjects(maybeDefaults ?? {}, overrides);

Where the left-hand value at a key is a primitive or an array and the right-hand one is an object, the right-hand object now replaces it, as a falsy left-hand value already did.

The root field never renders the Optional Data Controls BREAKING CHANGE​

With enableOptionalDataFieldForType, the Optional Data Controls are no longer rendered for the root field. A root anyOf/oneOf used to show its selected option behind an Add button, and now shows it straight away. A nested object or array that a recursive $ref: '#' describes was mistaken for the root and got no controls, and now gets them like any other optional field.

No code has to change. Update tests or snapshots that click the root field's Add button or expect a nested recursive field without one.

An additionalProperties entry never renders the Optional Data Controls BREAKING CHANGE​

enableOptionalDataFieldForType no longer applies to an additionalProperties entry or the anyOf/oneOf options it shows, whether it is set in ui:globalOptions, on the entry or on an option. Their Remove button could only store '', which blocked submit, so an entry is now removed by its own remove button, or stays where a layout grid names its key, which leaves it none, and its object or array no longer has the rjsf-optional-object-field or rjsf-optional-array-field class. An object or array declared inside an entry keeps its controls.

No code has to change. Update tests, snapshots or styles that use an entry's __optionalAdd or __optionalRemove button or those classes, and remove an entry with its own remove button, where it has one, instead.

@rjsf/antd's colSpan is keyed by the widget a property renders BREAKING CHANGE​

A formContext.colSpan record is now looked up by the widget each property renders, even one with no ui:widget, then by the field a ui:field or its $id names, then by its type (#5516). Before, only a ui:widget keyed a property by widget, so a plain string fell through to string and a boolean to boolean. Now a plain string, number or integer matches a text entry, a boolean a checkbox entry, an enum, a boolean with labelled options or a multiple-choice array a select entry, and an array of files a files entry, ahead of their type. A string whose format names a widget, such as date, email, data-url or hostname, matches the entry of that format's name, not text or file, even where it renders the same widget as one of those. A property whose anyOf/oneOf option renders its control matches the entry of the widget that option renders, such as textarea for a ui:widget: 'textarea' the options inherit, or email for an option with that format. One with no type of its own, such as an untyped anyOf, matches the entry of the option's type too, such as object for an object option, which also spans it full width by default, and of a field the option's ui:field names.
